articles.title: Monday briefing: What could Andy Burnham’s reset mean for the UK?
articles.summary:
In today’s newsletter: The prime minister has reopened the debate over a future relationship with a changed EU – as the bloc faces the rise of the far right, a protectionist economic agenda and growing defence ambitions

Good morning. Nobody really wants to think about Brexit any more, save for the original Brexiters, who seem delighted that Andy Burnham’s “reset” with the EU has given them an excuse to get the old gang back together. But arguments about whether the UK should rejoin the EU will reignite in parliament this week, as Burnham briefs MPs on the deal he agreed on Friday.

That deal wasn’t so much a victory as the culmination of Keir Starmer’s incrementalist approach to UK-EU relations. Its core agreements haven’t been ratified by member states yet, and the EU won’t sign them off until Britain resolves a dispute over tuition fees for European students. Burnham is apparently “determined” to take the UK back into the EU, but don’t expect any progress on that before the next general election.

articles.title: Connecting with Britain’s unsung carers has allowed me to feel a deep compassion for my younger self | Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
articles.summary:
Looking after my brother when I was a child was challenging and life-affirming. Now we need to give the next generation of carers proper support

As the years have passed, I have often observed that caring for another person is a responsibility that few human beings completely escape. “Hardly anyone gets off scot-free in this life,” I recently said to a friend, as we discussed our various loved ones and their care needs, the worry and the responsibilities. Whether it’s our children, siblings, friends or parents, some sort of care work is usually required of us on our life’s journey. Illness, disability, mental health issues, ageing, accidents and other vulnerabilities inevitably touch our lives.

There are 5.8 million unpaid carers in the UK, but I suspect there are far more who don’t identify as such, yet regularly care for loved ones or neighbours by helping with bills, shopping, appointments or more personal tasks. If you stood in a busy street in any town or city and stopped a passerby to ask them about the care they’ve given, or indeed the care they have received, many people would have a story to tell.

Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnist

articles.title: The good news out of Cop31? That most of the world’s governments said no to an agreement stripped of meaning | Bill Hare
articles.summary:
Co-chairing global climate talks is clearly not something to be repeated, certainly not by Australia, which is exporting climate pain

The failure of Cop31 in Antalya was a line in the sand moment, a victory for multilateralism as countries stood up to the big fossil fuel producers and said no. The text they rejected barely recognised the catastrophic climate emergency we’re facing, let alone signalled a definitive move away from fossil fuels.

The good news is that most of the world’s governments rejected an agreement stripped of meaning. And the power of one particular fossil fuel producer, Saudi Arabia, needs particular scrutiny. What we also know is that co-chairing global climate talks is clearly not something to be repeated, certainly not by Australia. It didn’t work.

articles.title: The Office for Investment is a true success story for the City
articles.summary:
A year on from its launch, Chris Hayward says the Office for Investment has been a true triumph for financial services

It’s nearly five years since I was elected policy chairman of the City of London Corporation. In that time, I have travelled around the world meeting government leaders and international investors, promoting the wealth of opportunity that can be found in our great nations and regions.

But for too long, international investors have found it difficult to navigate our regulatory and legal landscape, understand who to speak with, and determine where to establish and expand their businesses.

That simply isn’t good enough, not least when our closest competitor in financial and professional services, the United States, has long recognised the importance of providing dedicated support via programmes such as SelectUSA, which has helped attract more than $500bn worth of investment to America, including in banking, insurance and fintech. 

So, in July 2025, following earlier calls from the UK regulators for a concierge service, I urged then Chancellor Rachel Reeves to create the Office for Investment: Financial Services (OfI:FS), a one-stop shop to support international investors looking to establish or expand in the UK. To her credit, she responded quickly, launching the office in October that year. The Financial Conduct Authority and Prudential Regulation Authority were advocates of the concierge service, which was established as a true partnership across government, regulators and industry.

Around a year on from that defining moment, and as chair of the OfI:FS Advisory Committee, I am proud to see the office delivering.

A one stop shop for financial services

OFI:FS has delivered or is currently delivering tailored supportive actions for more than 100 individual firms, encouraging international firms to grow and scale in the UK. This support takes the form of regulatory guidance and business setup to immigration assistance and making connections with government.

This matters because it demonstrates a fundamental shift in how we approach investment. Rather than leaving firms to navigate a complex web of institutions independently, OfI:FS brings together expertise from across government, including HM Treasury, the Home Office, the Financial Conduct Authority, the Prudential Regulation Authority and the City of London Corporation to provide coordinated, practical support. We’re also proud to have KPMG, BDO and Eversheds Sutherland collaborating with OfI:FS, offering tailored support to companies looking to invest in the UK.

Ultimately, OfI:FS is a one stop shop geared towards improving access, helping investors understand the right processes, find the right people and make informed decisions more quickly.

The companies being helped by the Office for Investment

Take the experience of international fintech firm Ramp. Unfamiliar with the UK’s regulatory architecture, the company needed to understand which permissions it might require to operate here. OfI:FS helped clarify the possible routes, allowing the firm to identify an appropriate pathway.

Or consider Rogo, the AI partner for top financial institutions that’s been establishing a London presence. When its founder encountered questions around the appropriate immigration route, OfI:FS connected the company with the relevant government team. Rogo has since built an initial London team of 20, with ambitions to grow to around 50 by the end of 2026.

These examples illustrate why joined-up government working with business is so powerful. Investment decisions are rarely made on the strength of one factor alone. Firms need confidence in regulation, access to talent, suitable locations and the ability to engage with the right institutions.

The prize extends far beyond the Square Mile. OfI:FS is designed to connect international investors with opportunities across all four nations and every region of the UK. This ambition is complemented by initiatives such as Invest Connect, the City Corporation’s new AI investor-led platform connecting UK and global institutional capital with infrastructure and real-asset investment opportunities across the country, helping turn regional investment potential into tangible growth and jobs. Early progress shows what can happen when government, regulators and industry work together towards a shared objective.

Chris Hayward is policy chairman at the City of London Corporation

articles.title: Don’t panic: Prince Harry stands ready to serve his country
articles.summary:
It’s easy to scoff at Prince Harry’s pledge to serve his country again if needed, but his warning on Russian aggression is worth hearing, says Eliot Wilson

There is the faintest flicker of hope that the level of military and geopolitical threat Britain currently faces is beginning to be observed. The Defence Secretary’s catchy warning that we must be “ready for war in 1,000 days” did not move the needle. Public trust in politics and politicians is so low that if Wes Streeting had told the media that East is East, and West is West, social media would currently be aflame with #FakeCompass.

War has become a distant and almost unreal concept to most Britons. Yet if the worst threats on which our military and intelligence services are briefing our politicians are realised, Britain may find itself soon in an unfamiliar, unpredictable hybrid conflict, in which the front line could just as well be the streets of Salisbury as the Northern European Plain or the Arctic Circle. There may be no “home front”, and that is placing a burden on us all.

It may be a long time since anyone outside Montecito was pleased to be notified that “Prince Harry has entered the chat”. But the Duke and Duchess of Sussex have recently relocated from California to the Cotswolds, and the Duke has recently given the media the benefit of his wisdom on international affairs. Making a surprise visit to Lviv last week, he was interviewed by The Daily Telegraph’s “Ukraine: The Latest” podcast.

Prince Harry is not one of the great wordsmiths of his age. Those of you who have not sought Men in Black-style memory erasure may still twitch involuntarily recalling the paean to British values he wrote just over a year ago, the unforgiveably titled The Bond, The Banter, The Bravery: What it means to be British. The phrase “Though currently, I may live in the United States…” was a reminder that he penned his deathless prose from Santa Barbara County, southern California, where the average November temperature is around 20°C.

The Duke is a combat veteran. He spent 10 years in the Army, leaving as a major, and fought in Afghanistan as a helicopter gunner. His interview involved the warning that “we should all be nervous” about Russian aggression in Europe. He made the observation, true enough, that: “Just because there’s not drones, bullets, and rockets flying at us, it doesn’t mean that we’re not at war.”

It is a prompt, albeit a clumsy one, that Russian aggression is not a future possibility but a fact of life now, and for some years. Harry believes Europe has “woken up to the threat” but remains concerned that the continent may yet still “turn in on itself”.

The most unpopular Royals

You and me both, sir. I am less confident that Britain has fully “woken up”: it is as if the electorate now understands the scale of the threat but is yet to feel it. These are conventional sentiments expressed by a retired officer of the Blues and Royals. Yes, you may argue, but think of the reach Harry enjoys! Think of the audience which will hear this!

Up to a point. His media profile is huge, of course. But not all of those who will hear him are a neutral audience, let alone well disposed. At one point the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were the most unpopular members of the Royal Family after Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, and that was when the latter’s image had yet to move from “badly damaged” to “irreparably toxic”. Harry has seemed to many to have placed his own interests before those of his country for some years, and, worse, has done so with bad grace.

One sentence did, hopefully, cut through the murk of triteness and banter. The Duke said, “If asked to sign up again, if the need is there, then I will 100 per cent be there to serve my country”. Before you ask when the Royal Regiment of Wellness or the Honourable Centred-Self Corps were founded, in this case it really is the message rather than the medium. It is not just that we may need to call much more heavily on the Reserves than we have. We need to rediscover the spirit of serving our country, if the need is there.

How much “service” the Duke of Sussex has performed since he and his wife gave the famous-or-notorious interview to Oprah Winfrey five years ago is a matter for each of us to decide. This time, at least, he said some things worth listening to.

Eliot Wilson is a writer and historian; senior fellow for national security at the Coalition for Global Prosperity; contributing editor at Defence on the Brink

articles.title: Crestfallen: Under-pressure housebuilder slumps as cash woes persist
articles.summary:
Shares in Crest Nicholson took a pounding after the beleaguered housebuilder said it will suffer from “challenging” conditions “well into next year”. 

The London-listed builder told shareholders it will meet only the bottom end of its housebuilding targets and deliver a bigger loss than previously expected, as emergency talks with its lenders drag on.

Shares in Crest Nicholson fell by more than 25 per cent to 46.5p in early trading, meaning the stock has lost 67 per cent of its value in the year to date.

UK housebuilders like Vistry and Taylor Wimpey have cut homes targets and slashed jobs in recent months, as higher mortgage rates slow the market, but Crest Nicholson has been among the worst affected. 

The housebuilder said it has built 1,353 homes, at the bottom end of its 1,350-1,400 target. The firm now expects an EBITDA loss of between £30m and £40m, well below its previous £10m guidance. 

Crest Nicholson had previously warned of “subdued” market conditions but said on Monday that these have “deteriorated further” in recent months. Its sales rate slipped to 0.34 in the last two months, significantly below the year average of 0.43.

The group said it “expects the current challenging trading conditions to persist well into next year” and warned of a “prolonged period of weak sales volumes, weak pricing and persistent build cost inflationary pressures”.

The firm said it will review its land bank and downgrade the value of a number of its assets in response to this “deteriorating market environment”. 

Lending talks drag on

Since April, Crest Nicholson has been locked in crunch talks with its lenders in a bid to secure softer borrowing terms. The group delayed its half-year results in July in the hopes of completing these talks but said on Monday that it has still not found a resolution.

The firm said: “The Group remains in constructive discussions with its lenders to amend its covenants and ensure that it has an appropriate level of funding and liquidity going forwards. The Group is also thoroughly exploring alternative sources of debt financing.”

Analysts at RBC Capital Markets said this latest delay suggests “current discussions are not as supportive or constructive as we would have hoped, although the Group is leaving no stone unturned to find the best deal for the business and shareholders”. 

The analysts said they expected Crest Nicholson’s shares to suffer on Monday, though they added that its better debt position, with £240m available, will “mitigate some of the impact”. 

The housebuilder said it welcomed the government’s revival of George Osborne’s Help to Buy scheme, which offered equity loans to help buyers afford the deposit on their first house.

But the government has been criticised for the timing of its Your First Home scheme, which will not take effect until April next year. Analysts suggested that Crest Nicholson would not see an uplift from the programme until the second half of next year.

articles.title: Johnnie Walker’s Keep Walking campaign at 26: ‘For me, it’s a travesty’
articles.summary:
Johnnie Walker has been banging the drum for human progress since 2000 and doubling its sales to just over 20m cases in the process. But is it walking away from this famous campaign wonders creative director Tom Ewart in conversation with Tom Bruce-Gardyne …

The latest advert in Johnnie Walker’s long-running ‘Keep Walking’ campaign features the brand’s new global partner sashaying across the dance floor in a sequined mini-dress clutching a Highball cocktail. The ad is an apparent nod to French new wave cinema, and was made by the guy who directed La La Land. There’s a perky energy beneath its candyfloss glamour, but does it work?

“I don’t see what it has got to do with ‘Keep Walking’,” says Tom Ewart, a leading creative director who recently co-founded 3 Miles, described as a value creation company. “It just looks like Sabrina Carpenter drinking Johnnie Walker in a bar, or have I missed something?” She gets to purr the famous strapline at the end, though it does feel rather an afterthought.

How Keep Walking began in Croydon

‘Keep Walking’ – that great exhortation to progress in life, made its debut in 2000 with the actor Harvey Keitel confronting his demons in the Coliseum in Rome with the words: “You either learn to overcome your fear … or spend your life in the wings.”

There was the Italian footballer Roberto Baggio on missing a World Cup penalty, and countless others in what remains the biggest and most impactful campaign in the history of Scotch. It sprung from Johnnie Walker’s Global Brand Executive which met for the first time in 1999 in Croydon – a venue the Netflix version would doubtless change.

Diageo was formed barely a year earlier, and there was pressure to give its flagship Johnnie Walker whose sales had stalled at around 10m cases, a real sense of direction – something global, and fully coordinated. It dawned on its ad agency, Bartle Bogle Hegarty (BBH) the clue was in the name, and had been from the start.

Up there with Nike’s Just Do It

For Tom Ewart, ‘Keep Walking’ is right up there with Nike’s ‘Just Do It’. “Like all great brands, they found something incredibly simple and motivating that we can all relate to,” he says. “It’s a primal human truth – we all want to feel like we are making progress.”

Over the past 25 years, he has worked on some big drinks, including Guinness and Macallan, for its Masters of Photography series with the brand’s marketing whizz, Ken Grier.

One of his co-founders at 3 Miles worked for BBH on Johnnie Walker, including ‘The Man Who Walked Around the World’ in 2009. As Tom says, it is “well-written and beautifully choreographed,” and is arguably one of the best Scotch adverts ever made. Six minutes long, it defies the belief that our restless eyeballs cannot settle on anything for more than two seconds.

Playing the part of Johnnie Walker, Robert Carlyle begins his walk up a Highland glen by silencing the drone of bagpipes. “Whisky brands are so beholden to their Scottishness, it was a really disruptive thing to tell the piper to ‘shut it’,” says Tom. “It’s like ‘Yeh, we’re from Scotland, but we’re more than that’.”

The film’s self-deprecating humour was sometimes missing in other ads, and the constant call to move forward could feel a little earnest at times. Maybe Diageo sensed this in 2015 when it unleashed ‘Joy Will Take You Further’. It was claimed to be the brand’s biggest campaign ever, and an evolution of ‘Keep Walking’. It felt more like a rejection.

However, this ode to ‘Joy’ with its whiff of Viagra was soon dropped, and Johnnie Walker was back on message. But in 2025 the strapline was split to focus on what Diageo called “the power of ‘Keep’.” We were told to: ‘Keep dreaming, keep wondering, keep playing … keep breathing’ and finally to keep walking.

The Johnnie Walker campaign has ‘lost its focus’

Tom Ewart is unimpressed. “Keep everything is the exact opposite to the original idea. It’s that attempt to appeal to everyone where you end up appealing to no-one,” he says. “For me, it’s a travesty. It’s completely lost its focus and uniqueness.”

Maybe it had simply run its course? I suggest, but he shakes his head. “It feels like someone got bored of the idea. For me, it’s wrong. When you’ve got a platform like ‘Keep Walking’ or ‘Just Do It’, you keep doubling down on it. You try and find new ways to reinvent that story.”

He admits that advertising’s impact on culture has declined since 2000, and that is partly why he set up 3 Miles, which he says “sits somewhere between an agency and a consultancy.”

“The way you create value for brands now, has to be beyond advertising. For me, it’s more a question of – is advertising the right way to express ‘Keep Walking’? The idea of ‘Keep Walking’ and progress is still as true today as it was.”

Mick Mahoney, the creative director who co-wrote ‘The Man Who Walked Around the World’ accuses Scotch commercials of floating in “a sea of same”. As he told me last year: “I think it’s an absolute sitting duck for someone to do something interesting and innovative in terms of communication in the whisky space.”

Tom agrees – “It’s never been easier to come up with an idea to stand out from the crowd. It’s not so easy to convince clients to do the same.” He accepts the reluctance of brand-owners to invest above-the-line in these straitened times, but says: “I’ve heard it time and again, that in a recession when a category is struggling, you need to increase the spend to come out of it better afterwards.”

Award-winning drinks columnist and author Tom Bruce-Gardyne began his career in the wine trade, managing exports for a major Sicilian producer. Now freelance for 20 years, Tom has been a weekly columnist for The Herald and his books include The Scotch Whisky Book and most recently Scotch Whisky Treasures. This content has been produced for Whisky Business in collaboration with WhiskyInvestDirect, the Scotch whisky trading platform for distillers, independent bottlers, and private investors.

articles.title: Zurich warns firms face ‘hidden’ AI risks despite using separate models
articles.summary:
Insurance giant Zurich has warned businesses which rely on multiple AI systems to protect against disruption remain exposed to risks caused by underlying tech failures.

In new research from the Swiss insurance firm and the University of St. Gallen based on interviews with 50 industry and risk experts, Zurich warned that while firms may believe they have hedged their AI risk by using multiple suppliers, those tools often share the same foundational models and digital infrastructure beneath the surface.

Zurich said this means the systems may “behave or fail in similar ways because they draw on similar data, assumptions, architecture or decision logic.”

Recent events, including a wave of cyber attacks which hit high-street retail firms and European supermarket refrigerators, have “demonstrated how digital disruptions can quickly spread across organisations and sectors, highlighting the risks created by shared dependencies,” Zurich said.

The insurance firm warned that correlated AI failures may emerge through otherwise separate industries through waves of complaints, claims, regulatory action or litigation.

AI failures, Zurich said, may “spread across companies and sectors through hidden connections between systems.”

“AI will transform business. The opportunity is enormous, but we also need to understand the risks. Companies need to know where they depend on AI, what can happen when it fails, and be prepared to respond and recover quickly,” Mario Greco, group chief executive officer, Zurich Insurance Group, said.

Professor Dr Karolin Frankenberger, university of St. Gallen, said the challenge posed by AI now “is not simply to innovate faster, but to build systems we understand, can trust and can recover when they fail.”

“That resilience will be critical to economies and societies,” Frankenberger added.

While risks tied to AI are easier to insure against when they can be identified and measured, Zurich said insurance “cannot replace risk reduction or absorb every systemic loss.”

‘Hidden risks’ of autonomous AI and IP

The firm also warned that businesses using autonomous AI systems to negotiate contracts or execute payments without human intervention are creating hidden risks where legal liability is hard to trace when the tech fails.

Another hard-to-measure risk, Zurich said in its report, may hit firms using generative AI without knowing what data the models have been trained on, leaving them potentially exposed to intellectual property issues.

articles.title: Another blow to London as FTSE 100 catering giant departs for New York
articles.summary:
One of the biggest companies in Britain is set to switch its main listing from London to New York, dealing another heavy blow to the UK’s public markets. 

FTSE 100 catering firm Compass, which operates canteens in schools, offices and sports venues, could announce an end to its decades-long primary London listing as soon as Tuesday, according to sources familiar with the matter. 

The Surrey-headquartered firm is poised to launch a consultation on the move which could see the switch take effect in 2028 if approved by shareholders, the Financial Times first reported.

Compass has been listed on the London Stock Exchange since 1988. The group operates in 30 countries but generated about two thirds of last year’s $46bn revenue in North America. The group’s switch to a US main listing would be part of its efforts to capitalise on its opportunities in this market, sources said.

In April, the firm switched the trading currency of its shares from sterling to US dollars in a bid to attract international investors. 

Compass gets a significant portion of its business from the tech sector, where Google, Amazon and Microsoft are among its clients. The group also provides catering for the defence industry, airline lounges and data centres.

In July, the firm said a glut of new outsourcing clients had helped it secure $4.3bn in new business across the previous 12 months, marking a 16 per cent year-on-year uplift.

There would be no impact on the company’s operations in the UK, where it employs about 55,000 people, if the switch was approved by shareholders, it is understood. The firm would retain a secondary listing in London if the move went ahead.

London becoming ‘hostile environment’

Compass is one of the FTSE 100’s 20 biggest companies, with a market value of £43bn. Its shares closed trading on Friday at 33.5p and have gained nearly nine per cent in the year to date.

The firm’s potential main-listing switch to New York would deal another blow to the London Stock Exchange, which has suffered a flurry of high-profile departures in recent years. 

UK-founded fintech Wise, Paddy Power owner Flutter and equipment rental firm Ashstead are among those who have recently ditched primary listings in London in favour of New York. 

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said Compass’s move to quit London shows the UK “is becoming a hostile environment for the welath creators who create jobs and pay for our public services.”

He added: “Too many companies are leaving or never listing in the UK thanks to the red and green tape being imposed upon them.

“We have a ‘listings crisis’, yet far from de-regulate to allow London to compete, ministers plan to force companies to come up with ethnic pay reporting, and have allowed the FCA to go ahead with new environmental reporting that even their own Listing Advice Panel told them not to do.”

London’s recent departures have exacerbated a years-long drought of new listings. The city sits behind Turkey and Malaysia in 12th place globally for the value of new floats this year. 

The government’s attempts to slash red tape to encourage IPOs are yet to rejuvenate London’s public markets. Earlier this month, a Nigerian cement empire owned by Africa’s richest man, Aliko Dangote, scrapped plans for a UK listing.

Compass Group declined to comment.

articles.title: Asian tech sell-off deepens as Wall Street gears up to rebound
articles.summary:
The tech sell-off deepened across Asia during Monday trading as the AI trade continues to falter across the globe, but Wall Street is poised for a rebound.

South Korea’s Kospi tumbled 3.3 per cent to 4,708.5 points, bringing its monthly losses to 15.1 per cent.

The decline was led by index heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, two key suppliers of memory chips needed for AI application, which shed 3.1 per cent and 2.8 per cent respectively.

Benchmark indices for China and Hong Kong both fell over one per cent, but Tokyo managed to avoid further losses as the Nikkei 225 is closed for a public holiday.

But Japan’s tech-heavy index suffered a near eight per cent decline over the course of last week, fuelled by a five per cent drop on Friday, causing it shut at its lowest level in more than seven months.

Taiwan’s Taiex managed to recover from last week’s fall into the red, gaining 2.1 per cent, after the world’s largest chip foundry, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) reported an uptick in share price.

TSMC gained 1.5 per cent over the course of trading, reversing early losses. The chipmaker shed almost 15 per cent of its share price last week.

Anthropic and regulator scramble

Monday’s declines for the majority of the region come after Friday’s bruising sell-off in the wake of Anthropic’s blockbuster New York listing.

The public market debut of the AI lab also sank the Nasdaq 100 into a bear market and caused its worst week since 2020.

The severity of Friday’s sell-off took analysts by surprise, as the region had already suffered from the resignation of Nvidia’s chief executive Jensen Huang, who departed over revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

The extended decline led financial regulators in China, Taiwan and South Korea to roll out measures to support their flagging stock markets, which are heavily exposed to the AI trade and the shift in investor sentiment. 

Measures included the state-backed purchase of stocks, restrictions on short selling and encouragement of share buybacks.

Futures tracking higher

Despite the turmoil in Asia, US shares are poised for a rebound at Wall Street’s opening bell later today.

The S&P 500 is set to rise 2.1 per cent, while Nasdaq 100 futures are tracking 2.8 per cent higher.

“Last week’s stock market sell-off was rapid, brutal and detached from fundamentals,” said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB.

“We believe that investors got ahead of themselves last week. Although the cost of funding AI has changed, and risk appetite for AI stocks has also weakened…however, this has been a real shock for the market and we expect choppy conditions could persist.”

articles.title: ‘We have not delivered’: Capita boss quits after Civil Service Pension Scheme row
articles.summary:
The boss of one of the government’s biggest outsourcing partners has quit after the firm warned its botched handling of the civil service pension scheme was continuing to hurt its profit.

Adolfo Hernandez has stepped down as chief executive of Capita with immediate effect. He will be replaced by current chief financial officer Pablo Andres.

Capita, which has seen its shares more than halve in value since the start of the year, has been blighted by its management of the Civil Service Pension Scheme, a contract it took on in December 2025. The firm has faced intense government scrutiny after members faced delays to payments and trouble accessing their pension documents.

The firm today said its 2027 profit target range, adjusted for businesses being exited, would be £85m-95m, well behind market consensus of £120m, because of “additional costs” in connection with running the scheme.

“I recognise that we have not delivered the service that members of the Civil Service Pension Scheme deserve,” Hernandez said in a statement. “I remain confident in Capita’s future.”

In June, the National Audit Office (NAO) began an investigation into Capita’s management of the scheme, while earlier this month, the Public Accounts Committee launched an inquiry into what it described as “the chaos that continues to engulf” the scheme.

“Despite a two-year transition period to prepare for taking over the scheme, Capita has struggled to administer the scheme effectively following the transfer,” the NAO said.

“Key service levels have been repeatedly missed, leaving many members struggling to access the information they need to plan for their retirement.”

Capita also said on Monday it was seeking to raise as much as £190m from shareholders in a bid to shore up its finances and “allow the business to move forward from a more stable foundation.”

The firm also said it would need to adjust the terms of its debt covenants in order to get the equity raise over the line.

Capita said it would “continue to look at all options available to the group to deliver improved stakeholder value, including determining the right portfolio configuration going forward.”

Capita shares collapsed more than 50 per cent to 115p following the update. The stock is down 71 per cent since the start of the year.

articles.title: FTSE 100 Live: Stocks jump as London and Wall Street dodge Asian tech sell-off
articles.summary:
Welcome back to City AM‘s FTSE 100 liveblog.

London’s blue-chip index is making gains on Monday morning as investors brush off the fresh tech sell-off which weighed on markets in Korea and Japan overnight. Wall Street looks to have brushed off AI fears too, with the Nasdaq gaining in premarket trading.

Stick with us for all the latest business and economic news from global markets.

Here’s a few of our top headlines this morning:

Burnham’s public control push is ‘code for renationalisation’, CBI boss warns

articles.title: RFU gets Twickenham boost as Mayor handed veto over Nimbys
articles.summary:
The Rugby Football Union has received a major boost in its bid to stage more concerts at its Twickenham home thanks to new powers granted to the Mayor of London.

Objections from some local residents have held up the RFU’s application to host up to 15 non-rugby events a year – a five-fold increase on its current allocation.

But the new strategic licensing veto means that Mayor Sadiq Khan can now overrule Nimbys and grant permission if it is deemed important to London to do so.

The move could be transformative for the RFU’s finances, following three consecutive years of losses totalling £50m despite a lucrative stadium naming rights deal with Allianz.

It also has implications for other major venues in London, such as Wembley Stadium, the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Emirates Stadium and London Stadium.

“London’s major stadiums are among the best venues in the world,” said James Small-Edwards, Labour’s Planning Spokesperson on the London Assembly.

“But too often, they face regulatory barriers to hosting the events that could generate significant additional revenue, support jobs and strengthen London’s position as the premier global destination for sport and entertainment.

“World-class venues like Twickenham Stadium should be able to host more major events. The additional revenue would support grassroots rugby, create jobs locally and give a boost to London’s cultural offer. 

“The Mayor now has the powers to make a difference. He must use them to help some of London’s biggest venues finally reach their full potential.”

Why concerts can be game-changer for London venues like Twickenham

The new powers were confirmed by the Mayor’s Deputy Chief of Staff, Richard Watts, during a meeting of the London Assembly’s Budget and Performance Committee meeting last week.

Extra concerts and third-party events have proven a big driver of additional revenue in Tottenham, where live music, boxing and NFL game have generated £55m in annual revenue for Spurs, and could do the same in Twickenham.

The loss-making London Stadium was last week granted permission to increase its annual non-sporting event allowance from 10 to 24, potentially easing the taxpayer burden of the former Olympic Games venue.

Current Mayor Sadiq Khan has repeatedly billed London as the world’s sporting capital but that status has been impeded by red tape, leading major events such as next month’s long-awaited boxing match between Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury to be held in Cardiff instead.

The Mayor’s new powers rest on certain criteria, such as economic importance, and are still in draft form but due to be finalised and implemented imminently, sources said.

articles.title: Rents to outpace house price growth as rates and politics weigh on sales
articles.summary:
Rents are set to rise faster than house prices while political instability and higher borrowing costs dampen buyer demand, according to two property firms’ fresh forecasts.

The rate of rental price growth for newly-let properties is expected to be around double the pace of house price growth over the next three years, Hamptons said.

Across Britain, the property firm said it expects private rents paid on newly-let properties to spike by 14.2 per cent on average between the fourth quarter of 2026 and the fourth quarter of 2029, while over the same period, it forecasts house prices to increase by 7.2 per cent.

Private rents paid on both newly-let rental properties and those where there is a tenant already in place are expected to rise by 10.9 per cent over the next three years.

“With fewer homes entering the rental market, competition between tenants is likely to keep rents rising faster than house prices over the next few years,” Aneisha Beveridge, head of research at Hamptons, said.

“For landlords, that creates a delicate balancing act because higher costs do not automatically translate into higher rents,” Beveridge said.

She added that this does, however, present “a silver lining for investors” as rents rise faster than house prices and yields begin to improve.

“In London, that has already started to tempt some landlords back into the market,” Beveridge said.

Price expectations hit as ‘political winds blow harder’

Property firm Knight Frank has pointed to a similarly bleak picture in its latest UK Residential Market Forecast.

The estate agent has downgraded its price growth expectations from 3 per cent to 1 per cent for 2027, as a more uncertain political backdrop, higher borrowing costs and ongoing geopolitical instability weigh on buyer demand and market confidence. 

Prime markets are anticipated to face even stronger headwinds, with prime central London prices forecast to fall by 3 per cent next year amid tax pressures and political uncertainty under Andy Burnham’s government.

However, while sales markets remain subdued, the lettings outlook is markedly different.

Knight Frank said it expects continued pressure to weigh on rental supply, with UK rents forecast to rise 18.1 per cent over the next five years and London rents to spike up to 19.2 per cent.

“We have downgraded our price forecasts as the macroeconomic and political headwinds blow harder. Meanwhile, upward pressure on rents will persist,” Tom Bill, head of UK residential research at Knight Frank, said.

Bill added that when the firm issued its last house price forecasts in April, “Keir Starmer was prime minister, and few people expected the Middle East conflict to last beyond November’s US mid-term elections.”

“Seven months on, neither is true,” Bill said. First, UK politics has become more unpredictable. Andy Burnham took over from Starmer in July but is operating within the confines of the 2024 manifesto. It feels like an untenable position that is fuelling speculation about an early election.”

articles.title: Louise Haigh to tell top bosses ‘public control is not anti-business’
articles.summary:
Andy Burnham’s deputy Louise Haigh is expected to tell top bosses at the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) Annual Conference that “public control is not anti-business.”

In her speech at the CBI conference on Monday, Haigh, the government’s first secretary of state, will make a case for stronger public control of utilities, including water and energy.

“This government will put pragmatism and public interest ahead of failed political ideology. Public control is not anti-business – it’s about getting the foundations right, so that private enterprise can do what it does best,” Haigh is expected to say.

Government ministers and opposition politicians are due to speak at the event, which is attended by top business figures.

It is anticipated Haigh will also point out that foreign governments own “significant stakes in our water, electricity and gas networks with returns paid to their taxpayers”.

During the speech, Burnham’s deputy will lay out the government’s vision for “a new partnership with private capital built on clear rules, clear expectations and a fair return on investment”, promising stronger government support to support British businesses growth and investment opportunities.

She will also look to blame generations of previous politicians for “ducking difficult decisions” and “outsourcing responsibility to a sprawling web of regulators and arms-length bodies”.

Challenging the idea that public control equates to full-scale nationalisation, Haigh will argue this approach is not about whether or not markets work, but instead look at how effective monopolies have led to a lack of genuine competition. 

“Labour think nationalisation is a magic wand for every industry and every problem. The only trick they know is splurging ever more taxpayers’ money,” Andrew Griffith, Tory shadow chancellor, said.

Griffith added that if Labour “were really serious about getting bills down and Britain building, they would ditch their net zero obsession, give Rosebank the green light for cheap and reliable energy and get spades in the ground at Heathrow.”

“Instead they are writing a blank cheque to be paid for through taxes and borrowing,” he said.

“With hard-working families facing ever higher costs, the test for any public service is whether it brings bills down. Rail nationalisation is failing that test, with passengers facing higher fares and worse services. Why should anyone believe nationalised water, energy or infrastructure would be any better?,” Griffith said.

CBI chief: Budget ‘left too many question marks’ over economy

During the conference, which comes just weeks after John Healey’s Autumn Budget, the boss of the CBI is expected to say the country must move on from a “steady as she goes” Budget that “left too many question marks over our economy”.

CBI chief executive Rain Newton-Smith will tell the organisation’s annual conference in London that unlocking investment is the only way to escape the “financial straitjacket” of high tax and low growth.

“In the last few years, we in the UK have been too ready to talk ourselves down. To put on our gloom-tinted glasses. They don’t sit well on me,” Newton-Smith will say, adding, “The biggest contribution business can make to this country is not paying more towards our debts but investing in the growth that gets us out of them.”

articles.title: Jim O’Neill joins calls to reform ‘utterly nonsensical’ council tax system
articles.summary:
Lord Jim O’Neill has joined campaigners calling on Andy Burnham to launch a review into property taxes as part of the government’s 10 year plan.

The former Goldman Sachs chairman and economist has joined a group urging the government to commission an independent review of property taxes as households across the country face rising bills, councils struggle with funding pressures, and the outdated tax system stifles economic growth.

MPs are due to debate the proposals in parliament on Monday following a petition signed by more than 100,000 people calling for a reform of council tax and stamp duty. Dozens of Liberal Democrat MPs have signed a separate motion also calling for a property tax review.

Ahead of the debate, a coalition of MPs, think tanks, economists and charities including Lord O’Neill have written to No 10, urging Burnham to consider commissioning an independent review of property taxation to look into alternatives to council tax and stamp duty.

“There is widespread agreement that we have an utterly nonsensical approach to the taxation of property,” O’Neill said.

“The owners of higher-value homes can pay far less council tax as a proportion of their property’s value than people at the other end of the scale, while stamp duty discourages people from moving and holds back economic activity,” he said.

O’Neill added that “now is the time for bold action to fix the property tax system once and for all.”

Council tax valuations nearly 50 years out of date

The letter warns that without the government taking any action over the next decade, council tax will continue to be based on property values from 1991, with valuations almost 50 years out of date. 

On current trends, low and middle-income households could face a £900 increase in their council tax bills over the next decade. 

Councils face mounting financial pressures, while households are dealing with the prospect of even more substantial increases.

Neal Lawson, director of left-wing group Compass, said Burnham has “committed to taking on the big challenges where other politicians have failed, and the inequality at the heart of our property tax system should be absolutely central to that.”

“We need an independent review to consider the options and deliver for the working people that put their trust in Labour to deliver real change,” Lawson said.

articles.title: CBI boss warns Burnham’s public control push is ‘kryptonite to investors’
articles.summary:
Andy Burnham’s pledge to expand public control “sounds like code for renationalisation”, the boss of Britain’s most influential business group has warned, as she called on the Prime Minister to clarify that private investment would boost growth.

At the body’s flagship conference on Monday, Confederation of British Industry chief Rain Newton-Smith will warn the Prime Minister against sidelining investors in his 10-year plan address in December.

The industry grandee will argue that employers back ambitions to reduce youth unemployment and advancing devolution – but needed “reassurance” that the government would not stamp out the private sector.

“To some, ‘public control’ sounds like code for renationalisation,” Newton-Smith will tell CBI member organisations that include some of the biggest listed companies, banks and manufacturers in the country.

“That is kryptonite to investment. We know that’s not what’s coming – but give us the reassurance we need. Show this is a model built on partnership, not primacy, that the government wants private capital at the table – not heading for the exit.”

‘Burden of doubt’ hangs over public control plans

The CBI’s annual conference is set to feature addresses from top government figures and opposition leaders, plus the likes of Alan Milburn, who led the recent youth unemployment review, and Heathrow chief executive Thomas Woldbye.

In an opening speech, Newton-Smith is expected to say that people across the country had been “too ready to talk ourselves down”, praising Burnham for bringing a “dose of hopes to our politics”.

But she will warn that the UK is stuck in a “financial straitjacket” due to a sky-high tax burden, a range of spending demands and threats to borrowing costs.

She will argue that John Healey’s recent Budget “left too many question marks over our economy” before saying that upcoming decisions at the Spending Review and Burnham’s 10-year plan should provide “action” to lift economic spirits.

“The biggest challenge is not the burden of one tax or regulation – it’s the burden of doubt,” Newton-Smith will say.

“We need more than mañana – because time wasted is investment lost. We have the answers. We know how to electrify. So use the 10-year plan to show how we start delivering, work with us to get British business competing again.”

Burnham’s AI gamble

Burnham’s speech is scheduled to take place before a Christmas break although a date has not yet been agreed.

The government is taking advice from a range of experts both from within the government and at independent groups to lay out plans for “greater public control” and re-wiring the state.

Over the next year, the UK is set to take the G20 presidency. Burnham has said he wanted to write up an “AI code” to be adhered to by the world’s largest economies.

Newton-Smith will say that widespread adoption could turn “British business into global companies” and that the UK could still “catch the economic lightning” from advances in technology.

articles.title: Slumping London flat prices spark landlord return
articles.summary:
Falling flat prices and rapidly rising rental returns are drawing buy-to-let investors back to London’s property market.

Surging rents and cheaper prices for property purchases are leading to landlords buying flats in London at their quickest rate in recent years.

According to estate agent Hamptons, the share of investors based in the capital purchasing flats in London has spiked to an 11-year high to 39 per cent, up from 34 per cent last year, as reported by the Telegraph.

Analysis by the estate agent shows gross rental yields on freshly purchased London flats have risen to 7 per cent, up from 6 per cent last year and the highest recorded level since Hamptons began its dataset in 2015.

Alongside this, the amount of landlords seeing 10 per cent yields on flats has more than doubled, with the share of landlords climbing from 7 per cent in 2025 to 15 per cent this year.

It marks the first time the figure has reached double digits since at least 2025, and stands against the share just being 1 per cent five years ago.

Hamptons’ research director, Aneisha Beveridge, said higher yields “seem to be tempting some investors back into parts of the London market, particularly where prices have adjusted but rents remain strong..”

The data suggests the government’s buy-to-let crackdown, which was launched a decade ago with a three-percentage-point stamp duty surcharge on any additional homes, might be running out of steam in the capital.

Healey’s landlord crackdown on rental income

In his maiden Autumn Budget, chancellor John Healey set out a crackdown on landlords as the UK government looks to increase tax rates on rental income.

Property experts and estate agents told City AM in October that John Healey’s hike to tax on rental income is the latest blow in an assault on landlords, which is already pushing many in the capital to sell up.

articles.title: British Airways owner tells Burnham Heathrow’s third runway ‘doomed to failure’
articles.summary:
The owner of British Airways’ parent company has told Andy Burnham Heathrow airport’s proposed expansion is not affordable in its current form and is “doomed to failure.”

Luis Gallego, chief executive of International Airlines Group (IAG) raised concerns over the £49bn expansion plans for Heathrow’s third runway in a letter to the prime minister, according to The Times.

IAG, which also owns Aer Lingus, Vueling, and Iberia, said in the letter it and Heathrow have been unable to close a £19bn gap between the airport’s predicted costs of the expansion and what IAG believes passengers would be willing to pay through hiked airport charges.

“Unfortunately, in our view and given our knowledge of a market that is so important to us, we are convinced that the preferred scheme for expansion to date is too expensive and, as it stands, is unaffordable and doomed to failure,” Gallego said in the letter.

Private investment ‘will not be enough’

Gallego said the airline group still supports expanding Heathrow, but warned private investment alone would not meet the amount needed to fund the scheme at an acceptable cost.

He told Burnham that “if we want to move forward with the current project, private investment will not be enough.”

IAG has suggested using extra air passenger duty revenues yielded by the expansion to help fund construction costs, or direct government investment to help cover land purchases and finance early engineering work.

Gallego also pushed back on Burnham’s claim the expansion was “a matter for London and Londoners” and said it was a “project of national importance that will benefit every region and nation of the UK.”

A Heathrow spokesperson said: “We welcome IAG’s support for a third runway and are working more closely than ever with airlines to make expansion affordable.”

“We’ve made good progress in narrowing the gap, but there’s more to do. We’re going through the plans together line by line, challenging costs and stripping out anything that doesn’t deliver value.

Expansion must be affordable for airlines and passengers, as well as financeable for investors, and we’re determined to deliver it.”

articles.title: ‘Accept Brexit and move on’, Theresa May warns Burnham
articles.summary:
Former prime minister Theresa May has warned Andy Burnham must “accept Brexit and move on”.

Speaking to the BBC, May said she was “aghast” that the prime minister could be considering rejoining the EU after he said at the Brussels summit this week he wanted to “brainstorm” ideas on the future of Britain’s relationship with the bloc.

May, who was prime minister between 2016 to 2019 before being forced to resign after failing to complete a Brexit deal after spending three years negotiating one, urged Burnham to “just get on” with today’s challenges rather than rehashing Brexit conversations.

“When I was prime minister I was very clear, we should deliver on that vote. So I’m afraid my message to him really is, you know, people voted for Brexit. Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on,” May said.

Speaking to the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg, May said Burnham “wants to pat people on the head” by suggesting Brits “got it wrong” with the vote.

May, who was replaced by Boris Johnson after her tenure as prime minister, said:  “What I saw was that the extent of those negotiations, the hours that have to be put in – it’s across the whole of government.”

“It’s not just prime ministerial time, cabinet ministers’ time, officials’ time, to-ing and fro-ing on those negotiations. Because you have to negotiate hard in order to make sure that you’re getting out what you want,” she said.

May added: “And that’s one of the reasons why I look slightly aghast at what Andy Burnham is talking about, further negotiations of going into the EU. And also we, as a country, we voted for Brexit.”

Burnham agrees youth migration for 100,000 to UK

On Friday at the Brussels summit, Burnham agreed to allow 100,000 young people from EU nations to spend three years travelling, working or studying in Britain in an agreement that could face intense scrutiny.

Burnham argued that a wide-ranging deal with the EU tackled the “biggest challenges of our time” as he hailed alignment on food standards and carbon emissions markets, plus efforts to share data on illegal migration.

articles.title: Sandpapergate: Cricket Australia can’t keep ducking a fresh independent inquiry
articles.summary:
Getting to the bottom of things is part of the job of a litigation lawyer. The same can be said for police officers, investigative journalists and even doctors in search of a diagnosis. A question being posed Down Under is whether it is also part of the job for Cricket Australia.

In 2018, during a Test match between South Africa and Australia in Cape Town, the Australian fielder Cameron Bancroft was caught by TV cameras applying sandpaper to roughen up one side of the ball so it would move more in the air. This was cheating.

Cricket Australia conducted an immediate investigation and relatively quickly singled out three players for punishment. Bancroft, the captain Steve Smith and vice-captain David Warner (all batsmen) were banned for between nine months and a year.

However, questions remained. Why were no bowlers found to have been involved? It was the bowlers who would exploit the altered condition of the ball.

In 2021, following some unwelcome media coverage, the bowling group issued a denial around the use of sandpaper on the field of play.

Now Usman Khawaja says the whole team knew about the scheme. Bancroft says he deliberately withheld evidence of the team’s wider knowledge from the original investigation. Chadd Sayers, a fast bowler, says he took sandpaper off the field during the previous Test at Port Elizabeth and was never interviewed as part of the original investigation.

Pat Cummins, now Australia’s captain, continues to deny knowing about the scheme.

Cricket Australia today is run by different people, who were not involved in the previous investigation. Failing to re-examine what happened runs a serious risk of digging an even deeper hole.

Cricket Australia has proposed a “forum” where players and staff can come forward to give their accounts of what happened. This, however, is a mistake.

While led by an independent lawyer, it is voluntary and confidential. There has even been a suggestion that different versions of the truth may be contemplated.

Why a new Sandpapergate inquiry is unavoidable

What Cricket Australia should do is set up a fresh, truly independent inquiry. Such a process would start by looking at how the original investigation was run and what it was trying to achieve.

Who was interviewed? Who was left out and why? What documents were called for, what was handed over and what has been preserved? The investigators should have access to the original interview records and match footage, and their remit should cover both Tests.

It is surely important to establish why Bancroft chose to hold back information (if indeed he did), whether he was encouraged to do so and, if so, by whom. If the wider group did know about the sandpaper, did the three players who were singled out take a disproportionate share of the blame?

The investigators should test the reliability of the evidence, give those they propose to criticise a fair chance to respond and publish reasoned findings. The findings may be painful for Cricket Australia, but it is essential for the integrity of the organisation going forward that they should be aired.

Indeed, by failing to do this, Cricket Australia risks an external intervention which could be far more uncomfortable.

If this were happening in England and the same scandal was engulfing the England and Wales Cricket Board, I suspect there might be calls for parliamentary intervention. The House of Commons could require the attendance of witnesses and the production of documents – and it may not be long before an Australian senator triggers a move for an inquiry of a similar sort.

One thing is clear: if Cricket Australia does not grip Sandpapergate now, it will forever be a blight on both its game and its administration.

Simon Bushell is senior partner at Seladore Legal and has extensive experience in complex cross-border disputes and investigations.

articles.title: Inflation voters’ top concern as Iran war bites
articles.summary:
A vicious bout of inflation set off by the US’s war in Iran is now British voters’ top concern, according a closely follwed poll that laid bare the scale of economic pessimism that continues to stalk the UK.

Nearly four in 10 (37 per cent) UK adults listed price rises as a big issue facing the country, according to a poll by Ipsos, taking it level with immigration as the issue households are most concerned about.

The score is the highest level recorded since August 2023, when the country was still recovering from a wave of double-digit inflation unleashed by Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

“With levels of inflation in Britain reaching a year-long high this month, it is perhaps no surprise that we see a sharp rise in public concern about inflation,” Ipsos research director Mike Clemence said. “It is now as big an issue for the public as immigration, which has been the front-runner issue for much of 2026.”

Inflation adds to economic pessimism

Last month, the Bank of England chose to raise interest rates for the first time in three years in a bid to get ahead of an acceleration price pressure at the start of next year. Inflation is on course to reach nearly four per cent in May, double the Bank’s two per cent target, driven largely by ballooning energy costs from elevated oil prices.

Bills are expected to jump by some 26 per cent in January, when the energy price cap next changes, sparking speculation rate-setters may look to tighten monetary policy again at their next decision in December.

The Ipsos poll, which is the longest running gauge of public concerns in the UK, also found economic pessimism remained rife among voters. Just 13 per cent expect the economy to improve over the next 12 moths, compared with 67 per cent who believe it will get worse.

The finding provides a net economic optimism score of -54, four points lower than October’s figure of -50, researchers said.

“As we approach the end of the year, economic optimism remains weak with two-thirds expecting Britain’s economic performance to worsen,” Clemence added. “This suggests economic and inflationary concerns are likely to remain elevated into the New Year.”

articles.title: Exclusive: Timms welfare review to dismiss change to Pip eligibility
articles.summary:
A government-led review into disability payments will not demand a tightening on eligibility to claims, according to people briefed on the matter, setting Andy Burnham up for a clash between welfare reform for under 25-year-olds and other adults. 

Sir Stephen Timms’ welfare review, which is set to be published on Tuesday, will suggest that claimants of  disability benefits should not be compelled to take up support offered to help people into work, volunteering or other activities, City AM understands.

People claiming personal independence payments (Pips) should also retain access to cash support, the report is expected to conclude. Timms, who is the disability minister, was not mandated to deliver savings ahead of writing the report as he was told to publish findings according to existing projected spending levels. 

The total welfare bill excluding pensioner spending is set to total about £183bn this year, with the Office for Budget Responsibility showing that Pips contribute to about £50bn of the spending figure. Disability benefits are also set to grow as a share of GDP between the years 2026 and 2032. 

Both the Milburn and Timms reviews’ reflections on spending figures have come into focus due to the rise in borrowing costs, a near-record high tax burden and pressures for the Chancellor to fund defence and public infrastructure around the country.

Ahead of the report’s publication, the Institute for Fiscal Studies’ senior research economist Eduin Latimer said that report “should expect claimant numbers to rise and therefore be clear about how eligibility or generosity would be reduced in order to control the costs of the system”.

Burnham’s welfare ‘philosophy’

Timms’ recommendations could put Burnham in a difficult position after the Prime Minister suggested he wanted to apply the “philosophy” behind Alan Milburn’s report on youth unemployment to the wider welfare system. 

Earlier this week, Milburn recommended that benefits for young people should be cut by about £3.6bn a year by tightening eligibility criteria, which could involve some people with anxiety, depression or ADHD to “get less financial support at the beginning of their benefit claim than under the current system”. 

Cuts to benefits on the health element of Universal Credit will be superseded by a near-£6bn injection of investment in employment support under Milburn’s plans. 

The Tony Blair-era health secretary has now been appointed to a government role to lead reforms of the welfare and employment system for those aged between 16 and 24. 

On Friday morning, it was reported in the Financial Times that there could be reforms introduced to distinguish different health conditions. 

The Timms review has focused on increasing capacity for face-to-face assessments, ensuring that people can access the welfare system by easier means, and curb the number of reviews for people with lifelong or degenerative conditions. 

Tricky territory for Labour

The disability minister was commissioned to write the year-long review after Labour backbenchers rebelled against Sir Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves’ plans to slash the benefits bill by about £5bn in mid-2025. 

The cuts divided the party and severely weakened support for the former Prime Minister. 

Cabinet ministers Louise Haigh and Anneliese Midgley were in the 127-strong rebel group that  signed an amendment opposing the cuts. 

Burnham has insisted he wanted to “get the welfare bill down” but would not impose “crude cuts”. 

Opposition figures have meanwhile pledged drastic welfare reforms in order to fund proposed tax cuts. 

Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whateley has pledged to cut the bill by £36bn if the Tories are elected, mainly by tightening eligibility for claimants, slashing access to some foreign nationals and re-introducing a two-child benefit cap. 

Reform UK has meanwhile promised to cut the bill by £50bn through more radical reforms. 

A DWP spokesperson said: “Supporting disabled people to participate fully in life will always be our top priority.

“The Timms Review interim report made clear, PIP is no longer fit for purpose.

“When the final report is published, we will consider the recommendations alongside the Milburn review.”

articles.title: Image rights: HMRC’s new tax rules for footballers take the biscuit
articles.summary:
As well-known sports personalities, footballers can make a lot of money from exploiting their image, especially in the age of social media. As a bonus, they can put structures in place to minimise the tax take on these earnings.

Not for much longer, though. HMRC has been scrutinising these arrangements, and from April 2028, new rules mean revenue from image rights “related to an employment” (ie: deriving from their club activities) will be treated as employment income. As a result, payments will be subject to PAYE and National Insurance Contributions (NICs) for both player and club.

While sensible on paper, this raises questions over implementation: what do the new rules catch, and who polices them?

Why image rights can be lucrative – for the taxman

Consider the tax at stake when a footballer receives £100,000 from their club for image rights exploitation. Currently, the club can claim it as an allowable expense, saving Corporation Tax, and the payment goes into the player’s image rights company, attracting Corporation Tax at 25 per cent.

Treated as employment income, the payment would cost the club NICs at 15 per cent, and cost the player tax and NICs at 47 per cent.

No wonder HMRC wants to change the rules: it expects additional tax receipts of £40m-£45m annually from 2028, plus an extra £10m in the preceding two tax years, presumably due to agreements being amended ahead of time.

The rules go beyond payments from clubs to players, and cover third-party payments arranged or facilitated by the club or received “by reason of… employment”. But the scope of the legislation’s wording here is uncertain and open to interpretation that ultimately will be settled by the courts.

However, HMRC’s guidance sets out its view: a player obtaining the club’s permission to enter a third-party agreement would not be caught by the rules, nor would an employer simply providing a player with contact details to a brand.

Yet if a club recommends or selects a player for an opportunity, negotiates on a player’s behalf, or receives remuneration as part of any agreement, this would fall within the new rules. Clubs must be careful in their dealings with brands to ensure they do not inadvertently breach these conditions.

Fair play?

HMRC provided an example that considerably widens the potential scope of the rules. In its hypothetical scenario, a club wins the league for the first time, prompting a local biscuit brand to sponsor the captain.

The biscuit brand is named after the same location as the club, uses similar colours in its branding as the club, and uses the term “for winners” in its advertising. HMRC says this is sufficient for sponsorship payments to be treated as employment income, even though the club was not involved in the agreement in any way.

But how is the club to know of its obligations in this situation? Should it check all output involving players for potential links that could create a tax charge? What if the biscuit brand’s colour scheme was already similar to the club’s? Is it possible that different tax outcomes could arise for a team captain who has won numerous trophies to another that won just one, and is this fair?

Some would argue that, rather than the sponsorship being based on team achievements, success on the pitch enhanced the individual players’ image: therefore, exploitation is not team (or employment)-specific.

HMRC guidance is not law, merely its interpretation of the legislation. The courts will decide how these rules are applied.

The taxman’s strict approach may be designed to encourage an overly cautious approach from clubs: after all, they expect to raise £10m before the rules are even introduced.

What happens next will be closely watched by everyone with skin in the game.

Adam Jefferies is a Private Client Director at PKF Littlejohn.

articles.title: JP Morgan boss Jamie Dimon to set ‘example’ after Healey’s bank tax hike
articles.summary:
The boss of JP Morgan has warned he will seek to claw back the costs of John Healey’s bank tax hike after branding the move “unfair”.

Jamie Dimon, regarded as one of the most influential figures in finance, said at an event in London on Thursday he would look to find ways to offset the Chancellor’s tax rise on the banking sector.

Healey doubled the UK banking surcharge, which sits on top of corporation tax, to six per cent in his Budget for a 15 month period to strum up cash for an energy support package.

Dimon said he plans to set “an example so that [governments] understand the trade-offs of these unfair penalties”.

He added that any move to offset the bank tax would be “more in sorrow” than anger, in comments first reported by the Financial Times. He did not specify what areas he would target to claw back costs.

JP Morgan quickly became one of the most vocal critics in the aftermath of Healey’s Budget. The lender said at the time that the tax increase “lacks principle” and hit out at Labour for singling out the banking sector.

Budget watchdog warned bank profits could be driven overseas

The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) has forecast the hike will raise around £1.5bn, with surcharge receipts pulling in £2.4bn in 2027. But the watchdog warned around £190m in receipts would be wiped out as some banks move profits out of the UK in response to the higher rate. It added that the total size of profits lost was “uncertain”.

JP Morgan has laid out plans for a new mega-tower in Canary Wharf, which is expected to inject £10bn into the local economy and create 7,800 industry jobs.

Dimon warned ahead of the Budget that any tax increases on the industry would have “adverse consequences”.

The Wall Street giant also has a major campus in Bournemouth, where it employs some 5,300 staff processing more than $1tn of global transactions each day.

There was speculation ahead of the Budget that the banking surcharge could be returned to its eight per cent rate. Share prices rallied following Healey’s announcement as the tax hike came in lower than expected.

David Postings, the boss of trade body UK Finance, told a City audience this week: “It may be a smaller increase than some called for but a tax rise is still a tax rise, making an already uncompetitive regime even less competitive.”

JP Morgan declined to comment.

articles.title: City of London Christmas lights: Lord Mayor switches on Cheapside as King Kenny lights up Fleet Street
articles.summary:
The Lord Mayor of the City of London Bronek Masojada this week switched on the Cheapside Christmas lights at the Royal Exchange before a crowd of City workers, with St Paul’s Cathedral’s children’s choir singing.

The lights went on at the grand Royal Exchange pillars and six festive trees around Bank Junction, as well as installations along Cheapside and Threadneedle Street.

The event was run by Cheapside Business Alliance, the City’s first Business Improvement District (BID) in collaboration with the Royal Exchange, Fortnum & Mason, St Paul’s Cathedral, Mansion House and the Bank of England.

St Paul’s Cathedral’s children’s choir on the steps of the Royal Exchange (Cheapside Business Alliance)

Cheapside Christmas lights: A first for the Royal Exchange

Charlotte Fletcher, chair of Cheapside Business Alliance, said: “It’s wonderful to see so many of you here for the first Cheapside lights switch-on at the Royal Exchange, and the start of the festive season in the heart of the City, [where] Cheapside has brought together history, business and community for centuries.”

The lights on the Royal Exchange’s columns were funded by owner The Ardent Companies and the building’s retailers, and designed by Fier & Folk. Fortnum & Mason decorated the Christmas tree, which was funded by Cheapside Business Alliance.

The Royal Exchange Christmas tree, decorated by Fortnum & Mason (Cheapside Business Alliance)

Choirs, carols and mince pies

St Paul’s Cathedral’s children’s choir performed before and after the countdown. Gospel group Keynotes Choir, who have performed with Emeli Sandé and Sam Smith, then did an hour-long set, and singer Emmanuel Kelly closed the night with his new single, Christmas Love (Marry Me). Fortnum & Mason handed out hot chocolate, mulled wine and mince pies.

Gospel group Keynotes Choir performed an hour-long set (Cheapside Business Alliance)

Fleet Street Quarter Christmas lights

The next evening King Kenny – best known from The Traitors – switched on Fleet Street Quarter’s lights at Ludgate Circus alongside Lady Lucy French OBE, chief executive of Fleet Street Quarter.

The event also launched the Dennis & Gnasher Mega Mischief Trail, 12 sculptures made with Beano and Wild in Art to mark 75 years of Dennis the Menace, which runs until 15 January 2027.

French said: “Fleet Street has been home to Beano since 1938.”

King Kenny said: “As a Londoner, it’s an honour to switch on my first Christmas lights in the city.”

King Kenny and Lady Lucy French OBE at the Fleet Street Quarter switch-on (David Parry/Assignments/PA)

The City of London Christmas lights switch-ons follow Davina McCall lighting up London’s tallest Christmas tree last week.

articles.title: Brexit: Rejoin and leave campaigns can’t win with yesterday’s arguments
articles.summary:
Brexit is back on the agenda, but research shows leave and rejoin campaigners will need new arguments to win over today’s voters, says Morgan Jones

Today, as you will likely be aware, the EU-UK summit will be taking place in. It’s the most tangible step so far in Andy Burnham’s re-opening of the conversation about rejoining the bloc. The Prime Minister’s clear language about the failures of Brexit indicates that this is likely to be a key theme over the coming years and indeed at the next general election. In response to this new push to rejoin, we have also seen the launch of new campaigns, “Stay Out” – more Tory aligned – and “Enough Official” – more Reform aligned – which will look to strengthen and re-affirm the leave case. Despite its triumph at the ballot box a decade ago, most polling now suggests that a plurality of Brits favour rejoining and a majority consider Brexit a mistake.

At Persuasion UK, we aim to get behind headline figures like this and test, as much as is possible, how they translate when mapped onto the messy processes of the real world. Testing opinion on Brexit is exactly the kind of thing that requires this approach, because so much of what people feel about being in or out of Europe was created through the process of the referendum and subsequent debates. As political scientists Sarah Hobolt and James Tilley have compellingly argued, Brexit created, rather than brought to the fore, the tribes of “leaver” and “remainer”. How will the toplines we’re currently seeing – where the success of Brexit is rated catastrophically low even by leave voters, and where demographics alone swing the population into a pro-EU position – be acted on by a live campaign? What issues can we expect to be most salient?

Voter exhaustion

The main beat “Stay Out” hit in their first press release was about the increased cost of membership of the EU. The figures at the heart of this – not unlike certain other numbers associated with the leave cause – are disputed, but our research clearly showed that budget contributions are an area of significant concern for the public, with hostile media on this sinking rejoin numbers by nine points amongst the sample shown them. Any suggestion that Britain might have to join the Euro is also a point of real difficulty. However, despite the centrality of immigration in “Enough Official”’s launch video, our research suggests free movement clearly no longer provides the attack line it did a decade ago. While immigration might have been at the core of the case Farage and others made about the EU in the 2010s, our testing suggests it would not be particularly potent at destabilising rejoin sympathies today, particularly given people’s deep frustrations with increased barriers to travel since Brexit.

One area of concern for rejoiners, which might be described as process rather than policy, is voter exhaustion. In our research, the longer you tell people a process of negotiating and rejoining will be, the less appealing it is. This chimed with things I found while writing a book on the People’s Vote campaign: the committed activists campaigning for a new referendum often struggled to internalise the fact that even if many people basically agreed with them, their primary preference was to simply have the whole thing over and done with.

A lot has changed in ten years. Both sides of the issue will have to learn to play new games and make new arguments. Arguably this is even more true for the leave side, simply because arguments which were successful beforehand are naturally more tempting than those which failed you. But any campaign re-heating past points will quickly find that yesterday’s arguments don’t necessarily map onto today’s political terrain.

Morgan Jones is the deputy director of Persuasion UK and the author of “No Second Chances: The inside story of the campaign for a second EU referendum

articles.title: Anthropic shares plunge as AI fears erase debut gains
articles.summary:
Anthropic’s shares plunged at market open on Friday, as investors’ fears over the AI boom wiped away most of the gains from its record-breaking debut.

The Claude maker’s shares fell as much as 10 per cent per cent to $87.8 (£66.9) after Wall Street’s opening bell, a sharp reversal from its 17 per cent surge on Thursday.

Anthropic’s shares opened 33.4 per cent higher than its IPO price yesterday at $111, before easing somewhat to close at $97.1.

But the decline extended in early trading on Friday, as the AI lab was swept up in a tech-wide rout that has dominated global equity markets for the past week.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 was down 1.5 per cent in early trades, while the S&P 500 tumbled 0.4.

Dashing hopes

Anthropic’s listing was initially billed as a defining moment for the AI boom and wider global markets, giving investors the chance to gain exposure to a company at technology’s frontier.

But analysts said its debut would likely not be enough to dissipate growing fears on the sustainability of the debt-fuelled boom.
