articles.title: Iran regime's execution spree continues as twins face death penalty, decades in prison after alleged torture
articles.summary:
Two Iranian twin sisters imprisoned for participating in anti-government protests came face-to-face with the very official they accused of torturing and sexually assaulting them when they appeared in court to seek justice.

They discovered he was the judge assigned to hear their complaint, their U.S.-based cousin told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview.

Masoud Nourmohammadi, the cousin of Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, alleged that the official had been involved in their interrogation and subsequently presided over the complaint they filed against the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

"As soon as they walk in, they see the exact person who tortured them and sexually assaulted them is the judge," Nourmohammadi said.

IRAN'S REGIME CAME FOR TEENAGE TWINS; THEIR FATE OFFERS A GLIMPSE OF TEHRAN'S WIDENING DEATH CAMPAIGN

He claimed the complaint was immediately dismissed by that same official.

"The judge was their prosecutor during the building (of) the case, and he was the one that did the sexual assault on the kids and tortured them as a prosecutor and for the lawsuit he was assigned as a judge for that lawsuit," Nourmohammadi said.

Fox News Digital has not independently verified the allegations or reviewed the court documents.

The twins, now 21, were arrested after January anti-government demonstrations in Isfahan. According to the Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA), Taraneh was sentenced to death and an additional 11 years in prison, while Romina received a 36-year prison sentence. The sentences were issued in the so-called Shohada Square case involving 16 defendants.

IRAN TO EXECUTE FIRST FEMALE PROTESTER TIED TO ANTI-REGIME UNREST

Nourmohammadi said the sisters' legal situation has become increasingly precarious. One of their attorneys has been arrested, another withdrew from the case and the family has since secured a new lawyer to pursue the appeal of the criminal verdict.

He also described alarming new reports about their health.

"We just heard from another inmate who was with them in the same prison that the girls have been throwing up, vomiting blood in the night," Nourmohammadi said.

He claimed Taraneh had previously been unable to walk after allegedly being tortured and that both sisters were being denied necessary medical treatment.

Their case comes amid growing international concern over Iran's use of the death penalty against people arrested during nationwide anti-government demonstrations.

IRANIAN PROTESTER HANGED HOURS AFTER MARRYING HIS IMPRISONED FIANCÉE OVER JAIL PHONE LINE

A Nov. 16 report by Norway-based Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO) documented at least 121 protest-related death sentence cases after January's demonstrations, including six women and at least five people who were minors at the time of their alleged offenses. The organization cautioned that some sentences had subsequently been overturned or referred for retrial.

According to IHRNGO, 41 protesters have been executed since March 18, including 39 connected to January's protests and two linked to the earlier Woman, Life, Freedom movement.

"Despite the execution of more than one protester every week on average since March, the international response has failed to raise the political cost of these executions sufficiently to deter the Islamic Republic," IHRNGO Director Mahmood Amiry-Moghaddam said.

The warning coincided with the U.N. General Assembly's Third Committee adopting a resolution Wednesday condemning Tehran's human rights record, with 76 countries voting in favor, 27 against and 64 abstaining.

UN WATCHDOG SLAMS POTENTIAL ELECTION OF IRAN TO PANEL WITH HUMAN RIGHTS SWAY: 'LUNATICS RUNNING THE ASYLUM'

Explaining the U.S. vote, Ambassador Dan Negrea said Washington believed the text did not go far enough in holding the Iranian government accountable and contained language that distracted from its central purpose.

"Let no one mistake our abstention for any softening toward Tehran," Negrea said. "For 47 years, the regime has ruled through torture and terror. It crushes dissent with public executions and beatings. It remains the world’s leading state sponsor of terrorism, and its repression does not stop at its own borders. It pursues those who dare to speak up against it and hunts them down around the world.

"Today, it unjustly executes more people than any other country. The United Nations has documented these human rights violations and abuses at length, and responsibility for them belongs to the regime alone."

Iran's U.N. mission rejected the resolution, accusing its sponsors of politicizing human rights and ignoring the consequences of sanctions and military conflict.

Nourmohammadi, who lives in Utah, said he has contacted congressional representatives seeking help but has not received a response.

He said Tehran uses executions to intimidate Iranians considering further demonstrations.

"That's one of the reasons that the Islamic Republic is executing people is just to create that fear," he said.

The cousin said the family remains focused on fighting the sisters' sentences and securing medical treatment for them.

articles.title: Iran-backed Houthi 'terrorist attack' hits Riyadh's tallest skyscraper and HQ of Saudi Public Investment Fund
articles.summary:
A "terrorist attack" by the Iran-backed Houthis damaged multiple floors at the tallest skyscraper in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, which houses the headquarters of the Saudi Public Investment Fund on Thursday, authorities and reports said.

Entrances leading into the King Abdullah Financial District were closed and people were being evacuated from the area following the strike by a suspected Houthi missile, according to Reuters.

The news agency reported that the attack on the Public Investment Fund Tower, which is 80 stories tall, destroyed windows across up to eight floors of the building and bent portions of its metal facade.

"One of the towers of the Financial Center in Riyadh was targeted in a terrorist attack by the terrorist Houthi militia, causing material damage but no injuries — praise be to God," the General Directorate of Saudi Civil Defense wrote on X as it shared a photo of the damage.

HOUTHIS KILL 14 AT SAUDI AIRPORT AS EXPERT WARNS OF 'RAPID TARGETS' AMID MIDDLE EAST WAR

The incident unfolded after the Houthis attacked a building belonging to Saudi state-owned oil company Aramco, in the same area on Nov. 8, Reuters reported.

Saudi-led coalition spokesman Col. Turki Al-Malki said Thursday that Saudi air defenses "intercepted and destroyed 4 ballistic missiles launched by the Houthi terrorist militia toward the southern region."

He also said the coalition went on offense in Yemen, destroying a ballistic missile launch platform in Dhamar that was used by the Houthis "in an attempt to attack Riydah today."

HOUTHIS EMERGE AS GLOBAL THREAT BEYOND IRAN CONTROL AMID SAUDI STRIKES, FORMER ENVOY WARNS

The Houthis have been escalating attacks on Saudi Arabia during the U.S.-Iran war.

The U.S. Embassy and Consulates in Saudi Arabia warned Americans earlier this week that they "should exercise heightened vigilance due to the increased threat of armed attacks by Iranian-supported Houthis and Iranian efforts to target U.S. government officials and facilities in the region.

"Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," it added. "These hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area."

articles.title: Trump, Putin, Xi issue 4-point declaration after historic summit
articles.summary:
President Donald Trump issued a joint "peace declaration" with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday following the trio's trilateral meeting during the 2026 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, China.

"The three heads of state had an in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation and committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security," the White House said in a statement, titled "U.S.-Russia-China Heads of State Declaration toward Peace." 

Russia's Foreign Ministry and China's Chamber of Commerce to the EU confirmed the pact in near-identical statements, which also highlighted the three countries' commitment to reducing nuclear proliferation, increasing global petroleum production and upholding international institutions.

TRUMP'S HISTORIC SUMMIT WITH XI, PUTIN MARKS DIPLOMATIC MILESTONE, BUT BREAKTHROUGHS REMAIN ELUSIVE

"The three countries plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations. They reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows," each of the U.S., Chinese and Russian statements read.

China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs also released a more expansive statement on the meeting.

TRUMP'S CHINA TRIP: HISTORIC XI-PUTIN TALKS, 'SUPERINTELLIGENCE' BOAST AND OTHER TOP MOMENTS

"President Xi noted that it is a groundbreaking move for the top leaders of China, Russia and the United States to hold the first-ever meeting in history. History tells us that peace among major countries brings stability to the world, while their contention would only lead to chaos in the world. Peace has been an enduring pursuit of humanity," the statement read.

The statement referred to the theme of the historic meeting between the three leaders, the first time in history the three nations' heads of state met collectively, as "Safeguarding World Peace and Promoting Strategic Stability in Major-Country Relations."

CHINA'S XI SURPRISES TRUMP AT TARMAC, RECIPROCATING GESTURE SHOWN MONTHS AGO

"More than 80 years ago, China, Russia and the United States, the key anti-fascist forces in the world, fought shoulder to shoulder and achieved great victories, winning peace and tranquility for the world. History is the best textbook; we must remember history, and learn from it to shape the future," the Chinese statement continued.

TRUMP CANNOT DETER XI AND PUTIN’S NUCLEAR GOALS WITH A STRATEGY DESIGNED FOR JUST ONE

All three countries' statements affirmed a commitment to nuclear harm reduction, with each including language stating that "a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought."

Additionally, China's readout of the meeting stated that President Trump noted how many eyes around the world would be on the summit.

KIM JONG UN'S NUCLEAR BUILDUP SPARKS 'SERIOUS CONCERN' AHEAD OF TRUMP-XI-PUTIN SUMMIT

"President Trump noted that the U.S.-China-Russia summit draws attention from across the world. It is very important and has made history. The three countries are all nuclear-weapon states, and have a special and important responsibility to safeguard world peace and stability," the Chinese statement read.

An earlier Chinese readout of the meeting revealed topics covered on the agenda, which included Russia's war in Ukraine, ongoing tension in the Middle East and the Korean Peninsula.

CHINA BLOCKS BLOOMBERG REPORTER FROM TRUMP-PUTIN-XI MEETING OVER QUESTION TO TRUMP

China also stressed that the summit was "positive, constructive and very productive."

"President Xi emphasized that the seeds sown at the summit today among the three presidents will surely take root, sprout, bloom and bear fruit," the statement concluded.

articles.title: China could exploit US technology to threaten American forces, congressional watchdog leaders warn
articles.summary:
China's military could exploit advanced American technology, including through espionage and unauthorized access to artificial intelligence infrastructure, to develop weapons that could ultimately threaten U.S. forces, two congressional China watchdog leaders warned in an interview with Fox News Digital.

The officials raised concerns that Beijing is seeking to acquire sophisticated U.S. semiconductors and access powerful AI data centers, potentially strengthening its military capabilities without the knowledge or involvement of the American companies behind the technology.

Those concerns are underscored by the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission's 2026 annual report, which says Beijing is seeking to circumvent American export controls to obtain advanced semiconductors for military modernization.

BEYOND KILLER ROBOTS: CHINA'S REAL AI THREAT TO AMERICA IS ALREADY HERE, EXPERTS WARN

Citing an April 2026 assessment by Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology, the commission reported that China's People's Liberation Army was soliciting advanced Nvidia chips for AI-enabled military capabilities.

The report describes Beijing's push toward "intelligentized warfare," integrating AI into weapons systems, targeting, military command and logistics.

Mike Kuiken, the commission's vice chairman, warned that the threat extends beyond chip exports to access to computing infrastructure abroad. "Anytime the Chinese gain access to advanced chips, we are helping them," Kuiken told Fox News Digital.

Commission Chairman Randall Schriver acknowledged the risk, pointing to permitted sales of dual-use technology, inadequate cybersecurity protections and American investments.

"I think we need sort of a comprehensive look at how the Americans are either wittingly or unwittingly contributing to Chinese military modernization," Schriver said.

Kuiken warned that Chinese AI developers or military institutions could also gain access to powerful data centers. "If we're doing it knowingly, we need to bring it to an end," he said.

TWO TOP TRUMP CABINET OFFICIALS GO TO WAR OVER CHINA SPY SCANDAL AMID EXPLOSIVE ACCUSATIONS: REPORT

The warnings come amid heightened scrutiny of Nvidia's relationship with China. Reuters reported Nov. 18, 2026, that Nvidia had stopped shipping licensed Hopper-generation AI data center chips to Chinese customers, according to interim CEO Colette Kress.

The findings also come amid a separate controversy surrounding Nvidia co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned in November following revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, whom U.S. authorities have suspected of having intelligence ties to Beijing.

Jensen Huang has denied knowing about her alleged intelligence connections, while Beijing has rejected the espionage accusations. Nvidia's board launched an independent investigation. U.S. authorities have not conclusively established that Alice Huang was spying for Beijing, and Fox News Digital could not independently verify the allegations.

The commissioners also warned that China's advances extend beyond acquiring American hardware.

"Denial and deception is part of the CCP's standing doctrine, and that extends to the PLA, so I'm sure there are things we have yet to discover," Schriver said.

FOREIGN SPY ‘HONEYTRAPS’ TARGETING AMERICA’S TECH ELITE SPARK ALARM AMID NVIDIA CEO SCANDAL

He pointed to China's growing use of AI-enabled military systems, including autonomous unmanned platforms.

Kuiken warned that Beijing is increasingly integrating advanced AI into existing military technology. "We are absolutely seeing the PLA take the technologies that they have on the shelf today and figuring out how they can deploy the most advanced artificial intelligence capabilities into that ecosystem so that they can gain advantage," he said.

Against those concerns, China's Foreign Ministry struck a more cooperative tone regarding AI security in a Nov. 19, 2026, statement following a meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump in Shenzhen.

CHINA WATCHDOG WARNS TRUMP FACES ‘2-ON-1’ SHOWDOWN WITH XI, PUTIN AS TAIWAN RISKS MOUNT

"China and the United States should strengthen communication and coordination, prevent the security risks of AI, and ensure that AI is always under human control," the ministry said in its account of Xi's remarks.

The commission also identifies protecting American data as a leading national security priority, warning that AI could make it easier to identify cybersecurity vulnerabilities and compromise sensitive information, amid a series of high-profile technology outages affecting major U.S. companies and government systems.

Asked about the recent disruptions involving the NSA, Apple and Chase Bank, Kuiken warned that increasingly sophisticated AI models are making it easier to identify cybersecurity weaknesses.

"These frontier models are incredibly good at cyber, which means they're good at coding and coding means it's very easy to find vulnerabilities in things," Kuiken told Fox News Digital. "You're basically seeing these leading organizations around the world do everything they can to lock down their organizations to make sure they're not vulnerable."

Kuiken emphasized that the commission's leading recommendation this year focuses on protecting American data, describing it as both a national security priority and an economic resource. "One, we want to protect it to keep ourselves secure and two, we wanna deploy it in the models that we have with the democratic world, controls to get economic benefit from it," he said.

The commissioners did not establish any connection between the recent technology outages and Chinese cyber operations.

In response to Fox News Digital's request for comment, a spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington defended Beijing's technological development and criticized U.S. export restrictions. "China’s sci-tech progress relies on independent innovation and open cooperation," the spokesperson said. "China opposes politicizing and instrumentalizing trade and tech issues, opposes abuse of export control measures, which disrupt the stability of global industrial and supply chains and serve no one’s interests."

"China and the U.S. need to work together to deliver on the important common understandings between the two presidents and uphold the momentum of steady development of China-U.S. economic and trade ties," the spokesperson added.

The White House did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment in time for publication.

articles.title: Russia's Putin vows a response 'far more painful' after Ukraine attacks prized bridge in Crimea
articles.summary:
Russian President Vladimir Putin vowed Thursday to respond to Ukraine in a "far more painful" manner after Volodymyr Zelenskyy's forces heavily damaged the Kerch Strait bridge that has become a symbol of Russia's annexation of Crimea.

The warning was issued as Ukraine's president said he arrived in Berlin, Germany for talks with more than 40 partners aimed at ending the war, including with President Donald Trump's son-in-law and advisor Jared Kushner and U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff.

"We will respond to these strikes. And I want everyone to know this: I believe our response will be far more painful than what the Kyiv regime did to the bridge," Putin said after meeting with President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping for trilateral talks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, China, according to Reuters.

"We will, of course, restore the bridge. The road section suffered serious damage," Putin reportedly added.

UKRAINE RELEASE VIDEO SHOWING DAMAGE PUTIN'S PRIZE BRIDGE FOLLOWING 'UNPRECEDENTED OPERATION' IN CRIMEA

Ukraine attacked the bridge for the third time this week prior to Putin making his remarks, Reuters reported.

A Russian official told The Associated Press that the latest strike on the bridge linking Russia to Crimea halted rail traffic.

On Tuesday, the Security Service of Ukraine released videos showing the aftermath of a drone strike on the bridge, which destroyed one of its two arches and a roadway underneath it.

Putin said Thursday that he discussed with Russia's Security Council a potential stoppage of attacks at sea and against energy facilities, and "asked everyone to give it further thought and come back to it, hoping that perhaps some kind of agreement could be reached," according to Reuters.

"But after the strikes on the Crimean Bridge, there will be no agreements," Putin added.

TRUMP HISTORIC SUMMIT XI, PUTIN MARKS DIPLOMATIC MILESTONE, BUT BREAKTHROUGHS REMAIN ELUSIVE

Zelenskyy has described the bridge as the "main military crossing from Russian territory into our Ukrainian Crimea."

Ahead of Thursday's Coalition of the Willing meeting in Germany, Zelenskyy said "Ukraine’s priorities are strengthening our air defense, energy and financial support, the diplomatic track, and the next steps toward ending the war and guaranteeing security.

"Bilateral meetings with European partners are also planned, and, of course, with Chancellor Friedrich Merz. There will also be a format involving the American side and European national security advisors," he added.

Kushner said on X that the U.S. priorities for the trip "are to further strengthen our close coordination with Ukraine and Europe, work toward a unified position on the key elements of a lasting peace, and to jointly prepare the agenda and proposed format for the next round of multilateral negotiations."

Kushner declared that Trump is "determined to end this terrible war and create a lasting peace that makes all of Europe safer."

articles.summary: French far-right leader Marine Le Pen Sunday denied receiving confidential information from a civil servant suspected of leaking details of investigations to her National Rally (RN) party, while acknowledging she could not say whether others in the party had benefited.

articles.title: COP31 climate talks in Turkey collapse
articles.summary: EU member states on Sunday objected to adopting an 11th-hour deal that omitted explicit references to fossil fuels, the bloc's presidency said. The issue remains a major point of contention at the summit, which is taking place amid soaring energy prices and geopolitical tensions fuelled by the war in Iran.

articles.title: Drone strikes hit homes, United Nations building in Sudan's capital
articles.summary: Drone strikes damaged residential homes and a United Nations building in Sudan's capital Khartoum early Sunday, with the army accusing neighbouring Ethiopia of launching the attacks. The strikes came as drone warfare intensifies in the country's conflict, now in its fourth year.

articles.title: Russian ship attacked near Benghazi in suspected drone attack
articles.summary: Authorities in divided Libya's east said a Russian ship docked at the Benghazi port was hit on Sunday in a suspected drone attack, causing a blast but no casualties. There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the strike, but it comes as Ukrainian forces have stepped up their long-range barrages against Russia far beyond the front lines.

articles.title: Israel’s Eisenkot slams ‘Jewish terrorism’ after attacks by settlers in West Bank
articles.summary: Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot on Sunday condemned arson attacks by settlers on Palestinian villages in the West Bank as “Jewish terrorism”. Israeli police said they opened an investigation into the attacks, which came nearly a month after an inconclusive election stripped incumbent Prime Minister ⁠Benjamin Netanyahu of his majority.

articles.title: Democrat Hubbard wins North Carolina recount, clinching historic House majority
articles.summary: Democrat Chuck Hubbard was elected to the US House of Representatives from North Carolina on Sunday after defeating veteran Republican Virginia Foxx, who chairs the powerful House Rules Committee. His victory gave Democrats their best general election result in decades, winning at least 258 seats in the 2026 US midterms.

articles.title: Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drone at Benghazi naval base, Libyan officials say
articles.summary: A Russian navy corvette docked at the Benghazi naval base ​in eastern Libya was hit on Sunday by a Ukrainian sea drone, according to local officials, hours before a cargo ship was also hit by a sea drone in a second attack. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday confirmed that his country's military was behind the strikes.

articles.title: Burnham, 'Brejoin' & the Ghosts of Brexit
articles.summary:
“The people of Britain have spoken, and the answer is: we are out.”

The words of David Dimbleby at 4.40am on 24 June 2016, as the Brexit referendum result became clear.

But nearly a decade on, is Britain changing its mind?

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has reopened talks with Brussels, exploring options for a closer relationship with the EU. But the move has drawn criticism from key figures behind Brexit, including Theresa May and Boris Johnson.

So what is driving this rethink, and where might it lead?

France 24's Gavin Lee speaks to John McTernan, veteran Labour strategist and former adviser to Tony Blair.

articles.title: Le Pen denies receiving leaked information from French interior ministry official
articles.summary: French far-right leader Marine Le Pen on Sunday said she did not receive, nor ask for, confidential information on an investigation into her party from a senior interior ministry official. She however could not say if other party members had benefited from the leaks. Hugues Moutouh, the civil servant under suspicion, has denied the allegations and asked to be relieved of his duties pending a probe.

articles.title: Ligue 1: PSG extend winning run at Nice (3-2) but lose Désiré Doué to injury
articles.summary: A bittersweet victory for PSG at Nice on Saturday evening. The Parisians strengthened their grip on top spot in Ligue 1, but lost Désiré Doué for several months after the forward suffered a serious knee injury.

articles.title: Drone strikes hit homes and UN building in Sudan's Khartoum
articles.summary: Drone strikes damaged residential homes and a United Nations building in Sudan's capital Khartoum early Sunday, with the army accusing neighbouring Ethiopia of launching the attacks. The strikes came as drone warfare intensifies in the country's conflict, now in its fourth year.

articles.title: West Bank attacks: Opposition leader Eisenkot decries "Jewish terrorism"
articles.summary: Israeli authorities have opened an investigation after Palestinian vehicles and properties were set on fire in three villages in the occupied West Bank. Israeli soldiers were deployed to the area following the attacks, which local residents said were carried out by Israeli settlers. Gadi Eisenkot, a rival of outgoing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, condemned the acts on X, describing them as “Jewish terrorism”. Antonia Kerrigan reports.

articles.title: Russian strike kills 2 in Kyiv
articles.summary: A Russian attack struck an apartment building in the village of Dymer, just north of Kyiv, on Sunday, killing at least two people and wounding four others. The morning strike destroyed a five-storey building, while rescuers evacuated nine people, including a child. At least 11 others are believed to remain trapped under the rubble.

articles.title: The week in pictures: Xi hosts Trump and Putin, COP31 and new French protests
articles.summary: From the unprecedented Shenzhen summit in China that saw President Xi Jinping host his US and Russian counterparts, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, to tough talks at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey and another week of French protests over the cost of living, FRANCE 24 looks back at some of the most striking images from the past week.

articles.title: 'It can take years': Why the AI Riemann proof is far from settled
articles.summary: Artificial intelligence claimed another major scalp in maths on Friday, as Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge published what he says is proof of the Riemann hypothesis, a Millennium Prize Problem, in 17 million lines of code that no human has read in full. Physicist Tony Padilla tells Tech 24 that verification could take years, and that Alpöge should share how he got there.

articles.title: 'GTA VI': When the biggest-ever entertainment release becomes the biggest headline
articles.summary: This week FRANCE 24's media show "Scoop" looks at how the press covered the release of "Grand Theft Auto VI". Pre-orders and first-day sales totalled more than $2.3 billion. What does the game and the franchise's success mean for the future of entertainment? Our guest is Margaret Wallace, a video game developer and an associate professor of the practice of media innovation at Boston University.

articles.title: Anthropic shares slide on second day of trading as AI jitters fuel tech sell-off
articles.summary: Anthropic's much-hyped arrival on Wall Street fizzled out on Friday as ​nosediving tech stocks showed that even a blockbuster listing could not shake the gloom hanging over the sector. Shares in the AI firm dipped below $90, one day after soaring to over $110 during a record-breaking Nasdaq debut.

articles.title: Anthropic goes public after blockbuster IPO but fails to revive AI trade
articles.summary: Anthropic has become the first pure-play AI developer to be publicly traded on the stock market, following a record-setting IPO. The stock opened 34 percent higher, briefly valuing the company at more than $2 trillion, before ending its first day of trading up 17 percent. However, Wall Street indexes closed sharply lower as investors took profits, reflecting underlying market jitters about the AI trade.

articles.title: How much do businesses want to pay for AI?
articles.summary: Four years after ChatGPT went mainstream, generative AI is transforming how we live and work. It's also been a major driver of economic growth, with massive amounts of money poured into expanding global computing capacity. But now, there are signs of a slowdown in AI spending as companies take a reality check: are they getting sufficient returns on their investments and how much artificial intelligence do they actually need?

articles.title: Anthropic blows past $2 trillion in Nasdaq debut, beating SpaceX's June listing
articles.summary: Anthropic hit $2 trillion in market value as its shares soared in their Nasdaq debut on Thursday, with investors rushing to own a stake in the maker of the Claude chatbot, the world's first publicly traded frontier AI company. Shares began trading at $111.5, 34% higher than the IPO price of $83.

articles.title: AI lab Anthropic sets stock market record with $81 billion IPO
articles.summary: Anthropic becomes the first "pure play" AI lab to go public, with an eye-watering $1.5 trillion valuation, a bellwether moment amid growing concerns of a financial bubble in the sector. Meanwhile, a scientific study shows US data centres are emitting as much greenhouse gas as entire nations.

articles.title: Inside Limoges city hall, devastated by arson attack during French riots
articles.summary: Work is underway to restore the city hall of Limoges, in central France, which was devastated by an arson attack during riots on October 17. More than €1.7 million has been raised through an online fundraising campaign in the wake of the disaster. Also on the show, the highly anticipated video game "Grand Theft Auto VI" has finally been released, with gamers in Oceania among the first to get a taste of the latest instalment in the franchise.

articles.title: 'Extreme wealth can become a type of brain damage': Journalist Alexander Hurst
articles.summary: An international journalist who poured his meagre savings into highly risky options trading at the start of the Covid-19 pandemic and quickly made $1.2 million, before losing it all again, has spoken to FRANCE 24 about his experience. Alexander Hurst works for a number of media outlets, including the Guardian as a correspondent based in Paris.

articles.title: 'Failures, incompetence, broken promises': Deutsche Bank exposed in major leak
articles.summary: PRESS REVIEW – Wednesday, November 18: A joint investigation following the leak of 15 million documents shows that Deutsche Bank turned a blind eye to the criminal activities of some of its clients. Next, for its 175th birthday, The New York Times has chosen the top 10 stories that made history. Wired is focusing on the moments that defined 2026. Finally, we bring you a story about American parents whose children dream of becoming Formula 1 drivers. But how much does that dream cost?

articles.title: Nvidia posts blockbuster quarterly results amid leadership crisis
articles.summary: AI chipmaker Nvidia posted Q3 revenues double those of last year and 20 percent higher than last quarter, while the company board says it has no intention of reinstating disgraced former CEO Jensen Huang. Also in this edition: gaming tourists flock to Miami amid a marketing blitz for the upcoming release of the latest edition in the "Grand Theft Auto" franchise.

articles.title: Germany's Early Start Pension: Can child investment accounts help?
articles.summary: Germany plans to pay €10 a month into investment accounts for children to encourage long-term retirement saving. Economists say the measure may help build wealth but won't solve the country's pension funding challenge.

articles.title: COP31 climate talks end without consensus on how to fund vulnerable countries or move the world away from coal, oil and gas use
articles.summary: After two weeks of tough talks, the COP31 climate summit has closed without a consensus on how to quit fossil fuels or fund countries struggling to adapt to a hotter world.

articles.title: China, ASEAN countries struggle over South China Sea code of conduct
articles.summary: The Philippines wanted a South China Sea code of conduct in place by 2026. But persistent disagreements between China and ASEAN countries are slowing progress toward a deal.

articles.title: Dozens missing as deadly fire tears through Indonesian candy factory
articles.summary: At least 24 people were killed in a devastating fire at a confectionery factory on Java. Officials said many more people remain unaccounted for, prompting fears of a much larger tragedy.

articles.title: Mexican special forces arrest drug kingpin 'Chapo Isidro'
articles.summary: The alleged leader of the Beltran Leyva gang and one of the FBI's most wanted fugitives, known as "Chapo Isidro," was captured by the Mexican military following a raid and a shootout in the coastal state of Sinaloa.

articles.title: Russian helicopter suspected of violating Finnish airspace
articles.summary: Finland's Defense Ministry thinks the incursion is linked to a drone strike earlier Saturday on a Russian cargo ship, which is on a US sanctions list.

articles.title: EU and Indonesia sign trade deal
articles.summary: A deal covering 730 million people promises lower tariffs and new investment opportunities as the European Union seeks to diversify trade ties amid growing global economic tensions.

articles.title: New EU budget proposal aims at tax gobal tech giants
articles.summary: European Council President Antonio Costa has proposed a smaller EU budget for 2028-2034, including a 3% tax on major digital firms to ease member states' contributions. France has already rejected the plan as inadequate.

articles.title: Russia strikes Zelenskyy's hometown, killing 2
articles.summary: The attacks follow Russian President Vladimir Putin's vow of a "painful" response to Ukraine's attacks this week on the Kerch Bridge, linking Russian-occupied Crimea.

articles.title: Anthropic researcher uses AI to solve math's greatest riddle
articles.summary: The proposed breakthrough could reshape mathematical research, but still needs independent verification. It's the latest in a string of cases where AI has outpaced humans in solving famous maths problems.

articles.title: Man convicted of arson over deadly 2025 Palisades fire in Los Angeles
articles.summary: A 30-year-old man has been convicted of causing one of the most destructive wildfires in the history of Los Angeles. The verdict came after the case was retried.

articles.title: Brazil ex-President Jair Bolsonaro taken to hospital over abdominal pain
articles.summary: Jair Bolsonaro has been hospitalized in Brasilia with intestinal obstruction. The former far-right Brazilian leader is receiving pain medications, his son Carlos said.

articles.title: Russian ornithologist jailed over small donations to Navalny's foundation
articles.summary: Sofia Rosenfeld has devoted her life to studying Arctic birds. A Russian court sentenced her to 3.5 years in a penal colony over donations to Navalny's foundation. Friends and family are fighting for her release.

articles.title: COP31: No agreement on climate science, disinformation spreading
articles.summary: Attacks on climate science and disinformation risk delaying key measures at COP31 in Antalya. As the UN climate talks draw to a close, how will that affect efforts to come to an agreement?

articles.title: Can German auto manufacturing recover after Mercedes and VW cuts?
articles.summary: German automakers are pulling back on investments at home, sparking fresh anxiety about the auto sector's future. Some industry watchers think there is still a narrow window to stem the decline. But how?

articles.title: Lufthansa to cut 1,000 jobs, citing ongoing losses — reports
articles.summary: According to a letter obtained by the media, Lufthansa's executive board said the German company is losing €20 million every month. In addition to job cuts, operational cuts are also planned.

articles.title: Have we missed our chance to stop climate change?
articles.summary: From record-breaking heat to devastating floods and wildfires, the warning signs are everywhere. Can rising temperatures still be brought under control?

articles.summary: Funding from wealthy countries to help deal with the impacts of climate change hasn't materialized, says Uganda's environment minister. The East African country is hoping oil and carbon credits will help boost finances.

articles.title: Iran balances ties with China and Russia as Trump ramps up pressure

articles.summary: The sharp sell-off in tech stocks after the US midterms and the Nvidia scandal has cast doubt on Anthropic's IPO. Yet with hundreds of billions still being invested, some think the AI party is still in full swing.

articles.title: How industrial cooperation strengthens Europe’s defense readiness
articles.summary:
Europe’s defense industrial sector is evolving as governments, manufacturers and suppliers work together to strengthen production capacity, technical expertise and long-term resilience. Across the continent, collaboration between European and North American industry is helping expand manufacturing networks, support highly skilled jobs and develop the capabilities needed to sustain critical defense programs over time.

As policymakers focus on readiness, industrial resilience and security, cooperation across borders is becoming increasingly important. Advanced manufacturing, engineering expertise and long-term investment depend on extensive networks of suppliers and technology partners working together to support shared objectives.

One example of this cooperation can be seen in the Patriot program, led by Raytheon, an RTX business. Patriot brings together a broad network of industrial partners across Europe and supports collaboration among companies that contribute specialized expertise and capabilities from across the continent.

Maintaining and producing Patriot technology in Germany through this partnership is an excellent contribution to support Germany and NATO partners while strengthening industrial capabilities across Europe.”

Developing, delivering and deploying truly integrated air and missile defense systems depends on Europe’s aerospace and defense engineers, suppliers and production facilities. Technological interoperability and availability among European and NATO partners rely on shared engineering standards, coordinated production processes and aligned sustainment pathways.

With the support of 24 European suppliers, Raytheon is not doing this alone. A cornerstone of this expansion is COMLOG, Raytheon’s joint venture with MBDA Deutschland, which will begin production in Germany by 2027. This initiative will boost output, increase in-region sustainment capacity and further anchor production within Europe and expedite deliveries on both sides of the Atlantic.

“Maintaining and producing Patriot technology in Germany through this partnership is an excellent contribution to support Germany and NATO partners while strengthening industrial capabilities across Europe,” explains Jürgen Koneczny, Vice President Program Patriot at MBDA Deutschland GmbH and Managing Director of COMLOG GmbH. “This collaboration strengthens industrial and military capabilities in Europe, creates jobs in Germany and strengthens supply chains that benefit European partner nations.”

Expanding industrial capacity and strengthening supply-chain resilience are becoming increasingly important priorities across Europe. Bayern Chemie, a key German supplier supporting the Patriot program, plays an essential role in building manufacturing capacity and diversifying sources of critical components.

“Our partnership with RTX’s Raytheon is a strong example of how U.S. and German industrial cooperation can accelerate innovation, deepen co-production and reinforce the technological strength of the Western defense industrial base,” says Dr. Wolfgang Rieck, Managing Director of Bayern Chemie GmbH. “By bringing together complementary expertise, advanced technologies and shared industrial capabilities, we are well positioned to support evolving defense and security requirements across Europe and for customers worldwide.”

Europe’s defense readiness depends on the ability to sustain critical systems throughout their operational life.”

Beyond production, European governments are increasingly focusing on sustainment, the maintenance and modernization capacity that keeps systems operational over decades. In the Netherlands, Fokker Techniek provides specialized maintenance, repair and overhaul support for Patriot units. In Poland, Wojskowe Zakłady Elektroniczne (WZE) delivers electronics modernization and testing capabilities that help improve readiness and expand national industrial expertise.

“Europe’s defense readiness depends on the ability to sustain critical systems throughout their operational life,” says Roland van Dijk, CEO of Fokker Techniek. “Through our partnership with Raytheon, Fokker Techniek brings decades of Dutch MRO expertise to help ensure long-term readiness, reliability and availability. Together, we are strengthening the resilience of Europe’s defense industrial base while supporting the security and operational readiness of The Netherlands, NATO and its allies.”

For WZE, participation in the Patriot program represents both industrial growth and strategic value:

“Our cooperation with Raytheon represents an important opportunity for Wojskowe Zakłady Elektroniczne to further develop its technological and industrial capabilities. Through our participation in an international supply chain, we have strengthened specialized expertise, contributed to the growth of Poland’s defense industrial base and supported the development of modern capabilities for Poland and allied nations. This collaboration demonstrates the value of long-term industrial partnerships in fostering innovation, strengthening industrial resilience and enhancing collective security across the Alliance,” says Damian Gorzelany, WZE President.

Today, 24 European partners support Patriot-related work, making the system an increasingly co-produced and co-maintained asset built in Europe for Europe.”

Together, these partnerships reflect a broader shift in Europe – a move toward more distributed production, resilient supply chain and deeper industrial cooperation among allies. With 21,000 employees across 65 locations and 13,500 suppliers in Europe, RTX is woven into this ecosystem. Today, 24 European partners support Patriot-related work, making the system an increasingly co-produced and co-maintained asset built in Europe for Europe.

For companies across Europe, these collaborations are about more than production. They help sustain specialized expertise, create high-value employment opportunities and reinforce the interconnected industrial ecosystem that supports security, innovation and economic growth across the region.

articles.title: Ukraine sank Russian warship off Libya, Zelenskyy says
articles.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday credited his intelligence services with sinking a Russian warship in the Libyan port of Benghazi, calling it “an exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to the Russian war.”

Libya’s eastern-based administration said Sunday that a suspected drone attack had caused an explosion on a Russian ship docked in Benghazi, and that a second vessel was hit off the city’s coast that evening. Satellite images, published by Vantor and distributed by AP, showed the corvette Merkury capsized in port.

“Despite all the enemy’s attempts to counter them, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk,” Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram. According to his post, a Ka-27 combat helicopter was also destroyed along with the ship.

The operation used seven Ukrainian-made sea drones and also hit the cargo ship MV Angara, which Kyiv accuses Moscow of using to carry weapons.

Moscow has not yet commented. The U.N. mission in Libya called for an independent investigation.

In March, Russia accused Ukraine of launching sea drones from Libya against the Arctic Metagaz, a sanctioned LNG tanker that was hit around 240 kilometers north of the Libyan port of Sirte and left damaged and drifting in the Mediterranean.

The Libyan strikes occurred a day after a drone hit the Russian cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland. Finland’s defense forces said Ukraine was likely behind that attack.

“War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity,” Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo wrote on X on Saturday. “Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.”

Overnight, Russia launched 153 drones at Ukraine, the air force said. In the Kharkiv region, eight people were injured when drones hit a kindergarten and a hotel, regional officials said.

articles.title: “Faire des milliardaires les méchants de l’histoire” : à Paris, les gauches occidentales tâchent de faire front commun
articles.summary:
PARIS — Dans la salle Nina Simone, au sous-sol du Théâtre de la Concorde, à Paris, Sophie Binet, secrétaire générale de la CGT, passe la parole à Paul Nowak, son homologue britannique du Trades Union Congress. Parmi ceux qui les écoutent, au pied de la scène : les représentants démocrates américains fraîchement réélus, Pramila Jayapal et Ro Khanna, ou encore Elle Bisgaard-Church, chief of staff du maire de New York, Zohran Mamdani, qui hoche religieusement la tête.

Aussi présents au théâtre : des chercheurs, dont plusieurs prix Nobel d’économie, militants, conseillers politiques ou chefs de partis, tous réunis pour débattre de la taxation des ultrariches, ainsi que de la régulation de l’intelligence artificielle et de l’indépendance des médias.

L’affiche était belle. C’était bien l’un des objectifs du sommet contre l’oligarchie internationale organisé samedi 21 novembre par l’économiste Gabriel Zucman — ardent défenseur de la taxe du même nom — à l’occasion du lancement du Manifeste de Paris (éditions Seuil), un ouvrage collectif initié par lui et cosigné par 115 chercheurs : prouver qu’il y a “un momentum”, comme veut le croire Claire Trottier, présidente de Patriotic Millionnaires Canada.

“On voit une idée jugée radicale il y a dix ans faire son chemin et être de plus en plus perçue, comme on dit en Québécois, comme du gros bon sens”, a-t-elle confié à POLITICO en marge de l’événement.

Internationale de la taxation

Comme tous les participants interrogés par POLITICO, Trottier nourrit l’espoir qu’un front mondial voit le jour.

“Elon Musk, Peter Thiel, Steve Bannon… ils organisent tous leurs mouvements de droite et oligarchiques au-delà des frontières, et se rassemblent autour d’une vision commune de ce qu’ils veulent accomplir. Si nous voulons les combattre, nous devons nous unir autour de notre propre vision”, estime ainsi Pramila Jayapal. 

Si la question fiscale reste le point de départ, le public du jour s’accorde à dresser un tableau plus large, dans lequel les milliardaires, par le pouvoir que leur confère leur fortune, représenteraient une menace directe pour la démocratie et son bon fonctionnement.

Aux Etats-Unis, la victoire des démocrates aux midterms peut leur permettre d’imposer le sujet de la taxation des ultrariches au niveau fédéral. “On a gagné ce débat, poursuit Jayapal. Même si des propositions diverses existent, avec trois ou quatre propositions de loi, elles visent toutes à taxer la fortune. Reste la question du comment, combien et sur quelle période.”

Son collègue Ro Khanna, élu de Californie — où Gabriel Zucman a été l’artisan d’un référendum visant à instaurer un prélèvement exceptionnel de 5% sur le patrimoine des milliardaires, finalement rejeté début novembre — prévoit de déposer “dès la première semaine” de la mandature un Tax Billionnaires Act cosigné avec le sénateur Bernie Sanders, indique-t-il à POLITICO. Une façon d’“ouvrir la voie sur la taxation et de prouver au monde que c’est possible”, selon Khanna.

Plusieurs élus européens avaient aussi fait le déplacement, comme l’eurodéputée espagnole Hana Jallous, le socialiste belge Paul Magnette ou les élus néerlandais Jesse Klaver, Luc Stultiens et Ufuk Khaya.

D’autres leaders de gauche ont pris la parole. Le maire de New York Zohran Mamdani et Bernie Sanders se sont exprimés via un message vidéo. La chef du Parti démocrate italien Elly Schlein ou celui du parti écologiste anglais et gallois Zack Polanski étaient sur scène.

Des Français aux abonnés absents ?

Les Français étaient plus rares, bien que le sommet ait été organisé avec la bénédiction du maire socialiste de Paris, Emmanuel Grégoire, qui a prononcé le discours d’ouverture. Les eurodéputées Aurore Lalucq (Place publique) et Manon Aubry (LFI), le député Eric Coquerel (LFI), le premier secrétaire du PS Olivier Faure étaient présents. 

Trop peu, aux yeux d’un conseiller politique américain chevronné, présent lui aussi. “C’est quand même curieux, alors qu’on se trouve dans la capitale d’un pays qui a connu des soulèvements si importants, souligne-t-il sous couvert d’anonymat. Cela pose la question de la coalition qu’on peut construire. Pour l’instant, on fait de l’épistémologie, plus qu’on ne lance un mouvement.” 

Dans la campagne présidentielle française, seule La France insoumise reprend la proposition de Gabriel Zucman d’un impôt plancher de 2% sur les plus gros patrimoines. La mesure figurait bien au programme élaboré par le PS avant la primaire de la gauche, mais pas dans les premières mesures dévoilées par Raphaël Glucksmann (Place publique). Sa lieutenante Aurore Lalucq assure à POLITICO que rien n’est encore acté.

Des débouchés encore incertains

“On voit un soutien extrêmement large dans l’espace intellectuel, qu’il nous faut consolider dans le monde politique”, concédait Gabriel Zucman, interrogé par POLITICO à quelques jours du sommet.

L’économiste assure s’adresser aussi aux partis de centre et de centre droit, dont il dit espérer qu’ils s’empareront des propositions formulées dans son manifeste. “La question que je veux leur poser, c’est : qu’attendez-vous ? Trouvez-vous normal que des milliardaires puissent ne payer aucun impôt personnel ?”, poursuit-il.

Pour contribuer à imposer le sujet, Patriotic Millionnaires prépare son lancement en France, peut-être avant la fin de l’année, indique Alexandre Naulot, recruté en septembre par la directrice générale de ce mouvement né aux Etats-Unis. Son but : trouver des Français millionnaires prêts à prendre la parole dans les médias et à aller toquer aux portes des politiques pour augmenter la fiscalité des ultrariches.

Les mouvements sociaux, comme celui que connaît la France, nourrissent aussi les espoirs des partisans de la taxation, qui y voient le possible point de départ d’une future victoire politique. “C’est à cela que ça tient, malheureusement : au degré de mécontentement, de cruauté et d’iniquité que les gens expérimentent”, estime Pramila Jayapal, qui appelle à pointer du doigt les plus fortunés.

“Lorsqu’on peut faire des milliardaires les méchants de l’histoire, on canalise la colère vers la bonne cible. Ce travail consiste à amener les gens à comprendre qu’ils ont été trahis : l’argent ne manque pas, il suffit de taxer les ultrariches.”

Sur scène, le Néerlandais Jesse Klaver a lui aussi haussé le ton. “En arrivant, j’ai vu Bernard Arnault faire sa promenade du soir, a-t-il assuré. J’ai d’abord cru que vous l’aviez invité, ce qui aurait été une très bonne idée. Il aurait pu constater l’énergie dans cette pièce, et voir qu’il a du souci à se faire.”

articles.title: EU ETS must finance European aviation’s transition to net zero
articles.summary:
The EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) must become the main mechanism to finance aviation’s transition to net zero rather than the blanket tax it is today. Every euro that passengers and airlines pay into the ETS should be reinvested in off-taking sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and in new aircraft, engine and air traffic management technology.

At least 500 million SAF allowances in 2029-40

SAF is not simply another operational cost for European airlines. First- and second-generation SAF costs 2-5 times more than conventional jet fuel, and the eSAF that becomes mandatory from 2030 costs 10-13 times more. Passengers and airlines alone cannot pay the SAF bill that the EU has legislated in ReFuelEU Aviation.

SAF allowances under the ETS cover part of this price gap. Without them, passengers pay the difference.

If European governments and the European Parliament want to show the same levels of ambition for aviation as for industrialized sectors such as cement and steel, at least 500 million SAF allowances should be allocated under the EU ETS revision.

And yet, the European Commission is proposing 110 million SAF allowances for 2029-40, equivalent to just 13 percent of what passengers and airlines will pay into the extended scope during that time. Where does the rest go?

If European governments and the European Parliament want to show the same levels of ambition for aviation as for industrialized sectors such as cement and steel, at least 500 million SAF allowances should be allocated under the EU ETS revision.

Europe has the most ambitious SAF targets in the world. As a result, the cost of traveling in Europe and from European hubs is higher than for other parts of the world where there is no obligation to offtake SAF. On a flight within the EU, the passenger pays for ETS and SAF on both legs of their journey. When travelling outside the EU, around 70 percent of the seats offered by European airlines are subject to SAF mandates, compared with only around 15 percent for their global competitors, putting them at a disadvantage in offering competitive prices.

With only 110 million SAF allowances, and with the strict conditions around when these allowances can be claimed, European airlines will have to pay the SAF bill and pass on the cost to the passenger.

The cost of SAF with the Commission’s ETS proposal would add up €18.4 Billion in 2030 and €73 Billion in 2035. Limiting the types of SAF that can benefit from SAF allowances will not help manage the cost. The allowances should cover all types of SAF, not just the third-generation eSAF. Fuel suppliers will still be supplying first and second-generation SAF as part of the fuel mix in 2030 and 2035, and all these types of SAF will be helping to reduce emissions. Made in EU can be a bonus instead of a pre-requisite.

Maintain today’s scope

The European Commission is also proposing that the 110 million SAF allowances are part of a package that extends ETS to flights leaving the EU to destinations up to 5,000 km away.

In fact, there is no link between the scope of EU ETS and the amount of SAF allowances.

Extending the scope of EU ETS will increase costs and divert passengers to non-European destinations and non-European hubs, on board non-European carriers.

SAF allowances are not a handout — they are a way of reinvesting the ETS payments that passengers and airlines already make into decarbonizing aviation. In 2025, airlines claimed 5.2 million SAF allowances, equivalent to only 11% of what passengers and airlines paid into EU ETS in 2025.

Applying a regional system like EU ETS to a global problem undermines CORSIA (Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation) and will not reduce emissions. Aviation is the only transport sector to have a global system to address its environmental impact: CORSIA, under the International Civil Aviation Organisation. Extending the scope of EU ETS will increase costs and divert passengers to non-European destinations and non-European hubs, on board non-European carriers.

Putting our money where EU policy is

In these negotiations on the EU ETS revision, national governments and Members of the European Parliament have the choice to put our money where EU policies are: maintain our commitment to CORSIA, maintain today’s scope and SAF allowance conditions, and increase the number of SAF allowances to at least 500 million.

Transitioning to net zero has a cost, and airlines and passengers cannot be left to carry it alone. Making EU ETS the investment mechanism for decarbonizing aviation will help keep flying accessible to all and will keep Europe connected and European airlines competitive.

articles.title: Using carbon footprint evidence to support better healthcare decisions
articles.summary:
This article has been developed and funded by GSK.

“Health belongs at the heart of climate action” was the opening statement made by the UN climate chief at the recent COP31. The reality is that healthcare systems face a difficult challenge: improving patient outcomes while reducing their carbon impact and becoming climate resilient. As health systems work toward their net zero goals, there is growing need to understand where emissions occur and, more importantly, where action can make the greatest difference.

Over the past few years, GSK has assessed the carbon footprints of medicines and vaccines across our portfolio. These assessments have revealed surprising insights about where emissions are generated, where reductions are possible, and how healthcare systems and industry can work together to build more sustainable models of healthcare.

Most importantly, they have shown that measuring carbon footprint is only the beginning. The real opportunity lies in using that evidence to transform patient care.

Three lessons from measuring the carbon footprint of medicines and vaccines

The biggest carbon impacts are often hidden

At GSK, we consider multiple environmental impacts at the product level, including carbon footprint, material use, biodiversity and animal-derived materials. But when people think about the environmental impact of medicines, packaging is often the first thing that comes to mind. It’s visible to healthcare professionals and patients alike, making it an obvious target for concern.

Yet product carbon footprint assessments can tell a different story. Our data show that packaging is not a major contributor to carbon emissions. Packaging initiatives can make a positive environmental contribution, especially if considering waste reduction and circularity in a healthcare setting. But when viewed through a carbon lens, our analysis indicates that larger emissions reduction opportunities exist elsewhere in the value chain.

As health systems work toward their net zero goals, there is growing need to understand where emissions occur and, more importantly, where action can make the greatest difference.”

Depending on the product, the key sources of product emissions may come from a propellant, the manufacture of active pharmaceutical ingredients, energy-intensive biologics production or device components. In many cases, the parts of a medicine that patients see are not the parts driving the majority of emissions.

This matters because assumptions can lead us to focus on the wrong solutions. Measurement helps identify where interventions can achieve the greatest environmental benefit. The most appropriate solution also depends on the environmental outcome being targeted, and may be different if you want to tackle the carbon footprint, waste or water use, for example.

Data only matters if it drives action

The value of a carbon footprint is not the number itself. Its value lies in what organizations do with it.

At GSK, we have assessed approximately 80 percent of our product-related emissions across vaccines, small molecules and biologics, enabling us to identify carbon footprint hotspots and focus investment where it can have the greatest impact.

One example is respiratory care. For metered-dose inhalers, the propellant used to deliver medicine is responsible for a significant proportion of emissions and represents close to half of GSK’s overall carbon footprint. Understanding that hotspot has shaped investment in next-generation, lower-carbon footprint propellants and the manufacturing infrastructure needed to support them.

In other cases, the opportunity lies elsewhere. For one of our respiratory biologics, carbon footprinting identified drug-substance manufacturing as a key source of emissions. By transitioning to renewable electricity and implementing a higher-yield manufacturing process, we are aiming to nearly halve the product’s carbon footprint by 2030.

Patients may never notice these changes. Some of the most significant sustainability improvements occur behind the scenes.

Depending on the product, the key sources of product emissions may come from a propellant, the manufacture of active pharmaceutical ingredients, energy-intensive biologics production or device components.”

Product carbon footprints are valuable, but they are not the whole picture

As useful as product carbon footprints are, they represent a snapshot in time. Supply chains evolve, suppliers change, electricity grids decarbonize and transport routes shift. Treatment duration, dosing schedules and patterns of care can also significantly influence the overall environmental impact.

A carbon footprint therefore should not be viewed as a definitive measure of sustainability or used in isolation to compare products.

Instead, it should be treated as one important piece of evidence that helps guide better decisions alongside clinical, patient and health-system considerations.

Moving beyond products to patient pathways

The next frontier for sustainable healthcare is not simply reducing the footprint of individual products. It is understanding the carbon impact of entire patient journeys.

A medicine’s carbon footprint tells us how emissions are distributed across its lifecycle. Healthcare systems, meanwhile, hold crucial information about how patients access care, how often they interact with services and what outcomes different approaches deliver in practice.

When these perspectives are combined, new opportunities emerge.

The question shifts from “How do we reduce the carbon footprint of a product?” to “How do we reduce the carbon impact of care while continuing to improve outcomes for patients?” For example, we completed a study that showed a respiratory vaccination program could reduce associated healthcare emissions by around 22 percent versus no vaccination. By preventing disease, it is possible to improve patient outcomes and reduce environmental impacts.

This is where collaboration becomes essential and, encouragingly, is already underway. Initiatives such as the BSI PAS 2090 standard, developed with support from the Sustainable Markets Initiative Health Systems Task Force and the Pharmaceutical Environment Group, has helped create a consistent approach to measuring pharmaceutical product emissions. The Sustainable Healthcare Coalition and Patient Care Pathway Consortium have also developed a methodology for assessing the carbon impact of patient pathways.

These shared frameworks help move the conversation beyond measurement and toward action.

Turning ambition into impact

The healthcare sector is still in the early stages of developing environmental data and understanding impacts. With discussions considering how, when and why product carbon footprints might be required by health systems, the opportunity is to ensure they are used in a practical way that drives meaningful action.

Product carbon footprints provide an important starting point, but it is by combining them with a real-world understanding of the footprint of patient care that they can become a powerful tool for designing more sustainable healthcare systems. Together we have an opportunity to translate environmental ambition into practical improvements that benefit both patients and the planet.

The next frontier for sustainable healthcare is not simply reducing the footprint of individual products. It is understanding the carbon impact of entire patient journeys.”

articles.title: Europe recognizes refining’s strategic role: Now it must act
articles.summary:
A strategic step was taken for Europe’s economy and its citizens, as well as for energy security, defense and strategic autonomy, at the end of this October.

The European Commission launched the first Strategic Dialogue on refining, recognizing a reality that has too often been overlooked: refining is not simply an industry of the past. It is strategic to Europe’s economy, energy security and autonomy, defense, and transition.

The discussion, chaired by Commissioners Dan Jørgensen and Andrius Kubilius, brought together industry, the European Union Military Committee, NATO and other stakeholders. Commissioner Andrius Kubilius put the security dimension plainly: “Defense without fuels is not possible.” The defense community also stressed the need for domestic production capacity as European military demand for fuels increases.

More importantly, the dialogue looked beyond today’s pressures. The Commission announced a joint roadmap for the transformation of the sector, dedicated technical workstreams and continued political engagement toward a European Refining Strategy.

That is a significant step. Now we need to understand what is at stake.

New analysis by Oxford Economics provides the numbers. In 2025, Europe’s fuel manufacturing and refining industry supported €200 billion in EU GDP, equivalent to around 1.1 percent of the EU economy. It sustained 1.8 million jobs and generated more than €83 billion in tax revenues.

Europe cannot strengthen its resilience while allowing the industrial capacity underpinning it to disappear. Yet that capacity is already shrinking.

But its importance extends far beyond its own economic footprint.

Refined products remain critical to transport, aviation, shipping, agriculture, construction and the chemical industry. Moreover, in most cases, petrochemical units and refineries are integrated industrial complexes. Six major sectors heavily dependent on refining products together account for €1.6 trillion in GDP and 38 million jobs while petrochemicals1 themselves provide inputs to around 95% of manufactured goods.

This is why the Strategic Dialogue matters.

Europe cannot strengthen its resilience while allowing the industrial capacity underpinning it to disappear. Yet that capacity is already shrinking. Across the EU-27, Norway, Switzerland and the United Kingdom, conventional refining capacity fell by 19 percent between 2009 and 2025, while the number of conventional refineries declined from 117 to 83.

Meanwhile, Europe’s exposure to imports is growing. Gross imports of refined fuels increased by 39 percent between 1990 and 2025. For jet fuel and kerosene, imports now account for 61 percent of EU consumption, compared with 36 percent in 1990.

The issue is not about defending the status quo.

Decarbonization will reshape Europe’s demand for fuels. The challenge for our industry is to transform its production and infrastructure to meet growing demand for renewable and low-carbon alternatives. Yet, the real question is whether the renewable and low-carbon fuels Europe will continue to need are increasingly made in Europe, using European infrastructure, skills and investment, or imported from elsewhere.

That distinction matters because today’s refineries are the best-positioned industrial platforms for tomorrow’s fuels. Their assets, logistics, hydrogen infrastructure, industrial clusters and skilled workforces can support the production of biofuels, renewable hydrogen and e-fuels. Converting these sites can reduce capital expenditure by an estimated 30-50 percent compared with equivalent greenfield projects.

Once those sites disappear, much of that transformation potential disappears with them.

Oxford Economics has examined what a faster and more disruptive decline could mean. In a scenario where EU refinery capacity falls by around 30 percent by 2035, rather than around 16 percent in its baseline, and closures are not sufficiently replaced by converted biorefineries and e-fuel plants, the EU’s GDP would be nearly €25 billion lower than the baseline. Around 120,000 jobs would be lost and government revenues would be approximately €14 billion lower.

A European Refining Strategy should combine two objectives that are sometimes wrongly treated as contradictory: maintaining a competitive European industrial base and accelerating its low-carbon transformation.

The same scenario would also turn the EU from a net exporter of refined products in the baseline into a net importer by 2035, increasing exposure to global supply disruptions and price volatility.

The simple conclusion is that competitiveness is not an alternative to decarbonization. It is a precondition for delivering it in Europe.

Our industry is already transforming. EU production of liquid biofuels reached 18 million metric tons of oil equivalent in 2024. Companies are developing sustainable aviation fuels, renewable diesel, renewable hydrogen and e-fuels. But Europe is not the only destination for these investments. If we want new low-carbon production to be built here, Europe must offer a competitive investment environment.

This is where the Strategic Dialogue can make a difference.

A European Refining Strategy should combine two objectives that are sometimes wrongly treated as contradictory: maintaining a competitive European industrial base and accelerating its low-carbon transformation. That means effective protection against carbon and investment leakage, broader access to sustainable feedstocks, long-term markets for renewable and low-carbon fuels, simpler and more coherent regulation, and instruments capable of reducing the risks of major industrial investments.

Europe has learnt the hard way over the past few years the value of resilience, strategic autonomy and domestic industrial capacity. The Strategic Dialogue shows that these principles are closely linked to the refining industry.

The task now is to turn recognition into action.

Our choice is not between maintaining yesterday’s refining industry and building tomorrow’s clean energy system. It is whether we transform the industrial base we already have or lose it and become more dependent on industrial capacity elsewhere.

Europe can decarbonize while strengthening competitiveness, resilience and strategic autonomy. The Strategic Dialogue has opened the door.

A European Refining Strategy must now turn that political momentum into investment and industrial transformation.

1 There is strong integration between the refining and petrochemical sectors, with 14 integrated sites in operation.

articles.title: Surging left-wing Basque separatists brace for showdown with Spain’s right
articles.summary:
Spain’s impending general election is set to reshape politics not only in Madrid but also in the northern industrial region of the Basque Country, where the bitterly divisive question of independence is boiling up again.

A right-wing coalition is on course to form Spain’s next government after the Nov. 29 vote, but polls in the Basque region project a strong electoral performance by the left-wing separatist EH Bildu coalition.

The two camps appear to be on a politically combustible collision course.

Bildu’s rise has mirrored the Basque Country’s own transformation. Over the past decade, the rugged coastal region of 2.2 million people has increasingly shed its association with ETA, the separatist militant group that waged a decades-long campaign of violence before disbanding in 2018.

As the shadow of political violence has receded, the Basque Country has consolidated its position as one of Spain’s most politically progressive and economically dynamic regions. It is now internationally recognized as an economic powerhouse — energy giant Iberdrola and banking group BBVA are both headquartered in Bilbao — and a global destination for high-end gastronomy.

“The majority of the Basque Country is socially progressive and sovereigntist,” Gorka Elejabarrieta, a Bildu lawmaker running for the Spanish parliament in Gipuzkoa, told POLITICO. “Our coalition and movement bring together those two ideas, which are hegemonic in Basque society.”

Spain’s political right has long opposed Basque separatism, but its hostility toward EH Bildu is particularly pronounced. It regards the party as “ETA’s heir” and has repeatedly questioned its legitimacy as an actor in democratic politics.

Challenging the old order

Within the Basque Country, this month’s election is also a contest to determine who will shape the region’s relationship with Madrid and its political future, with the resurgent Bildu challenging the decades-long dominance of the center-right Basque Nationalist Party (PNV).

For the past 45 years the PNV has taken a pragmatic approach to regional autonomy. Closely tied to the region’s all-important business community — the comparatively wealthy Basque Country represents about 6% of Spain’s economy — it has sought to preserve economic stability for the region in its dealings with the national government.

But Bildu has chipped away at the PNV’s dominance by appealing to both pro-independence voters and a broader left-wing electorate.

Center-right figures such as People’s Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo — Spain’s expected next prime minister — and Madrid’s conservative regional president, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, frequently link Bildu to ETA and use its parliamentary agreements with Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to attack his legitimacy elsewhere in Spain.

But ETA’s deadly legacy has receded as a concern for Basque voters. Some 15 years after the group ended its armed campaign, polling indicates terrorism no longer figures among the public’s main concerns, with housing, employment and health care taking precedence.
