That shift benefits Bildu, which has lately focused its messaging on quality-of-life policies.

A late-October poll by the Basque government’s Sociological Prospection Office projected that Bildu will win seven of the 18 seats allocated to the Basque Country in Spain’s parliament. The PNV is forecast to take just four — its worst result in a general election since Spain’s return to democracy — and fall short of the five MPs needed to form its own parliamentary group.

Elejabarrieta said a strong result would strengthen the party’s hand in pressing Madrid for a new settlement recognizing the Basque Country’s status as a nation and its right to decide its future. That, however, is where Bildu could find itself crossing swords with a government formed by the PP and the far-right Vox party.

Elejabarrieta said his party would fight any attempts to curtail the Basque Country’s linguistic rights or autonomy. “If they attack us, if they try to undercut our self-government or sabotage our political activity, they will encounter a wall — not just from EH Bildu, but from Basque society as a whole,” he said.

From social policy to sovereignty

Between 1968 and 2010, ETA’s campaign for independence from Spain claimed the lives of 853 people. 

Months after the group announced a “definitive cessation of its armed activity” in 2011, Bildu emerged as a new vehicle for Basque nationalism, uniting pro-independence, radical-left groups that included former members of Batasuna — a banned party closely associated with ETA — with more moderate nationalists and figures from the non-nationalist left.

Political scientist Eva Silván said Bildu began “a conscious and real evolution” after a sizeable number of Basque voters unexpectedly backed the left-wing Podemos party in 2015, “revealing there was an electorate in the Basque Country that was left-wing but not tied to nationalism or independence.”

Bildu has courted those voters by focusing on social and economic measures championed by progressive and green-left parties across Europe. Silván said that shift has allowed the party to present itself as a “fresh” option alongside the PNV, which she said was viewed as out of touch with the concerns of younger voters.

“Independence has not disappeared from its ideology, but it no longer occupies a prominent place in its agenda,” she said.

Elejabarrieta acknowledged Bildu had shifted its focus toward issues affecting voters’ everyday lives, but stressed it had not abandoned its “openly sovereigntist and independentist” commitments. “For us, the social struggle and the national struggle are two sides of the same coin,” he said.

The PNV is not blind to Bildu’s success with the Basque Country’s increasingly left-wing electorate, and has sought to counter portrayals of itself as old-fashioned.

In a recent interview with the Onda Cero radio network, party leader Aitor Esteban said the PNV — which has historically maintained close ties with the Catholic Church — was “very progressive on social issues,” while acknowledging that it remained “very traditional” on economic matters.

Aitor Esteban speaks at the Spanish parliament in Madrid on May 31, 2018. | Oscar del Pozo/AFP via Getty Images

That balancing act is exemplified by the party’s position on housing: While it backed legislation to protect vulnerable families from eviction, it voted against measures to automatically extend existing rental contracts, arguing they would hurt small landlords.

Esteban has repeatedly questioned the accuracy of gloomy polls, pointing to small sample sizes and large numbers of undecided voters. Privately, however, people in the PNV have been more candid about the challenge, with one party insider recently telling Spanish newspaper El Diario: “We’re fucked.”

Awakening a pro-independence giant

Elejabarrieta said if Sánchez is reelected, EH Bildu would be keen to continue working with his government on progressive legislation, including the minimum-income and rent-control measures introduced during the current term, while also exploring “ambitious” options for the Basque Country’s future.

But a PP-led government in Madrid would be a different story.

The center-right party wants to reinforce the central state’s presence in the Basque Country by expanding its administrative, police and military footprint, and has proposed dissolving parties that promote independence or illegal referendums — a central plank of Bildu’s political mission. 

The party also wants to restore Spanish as the language of debate in Spain’s parliament and scrap the interpretation and translation service for Basque and other co-official languages.

The far-right Vox party, which the PP will likely need as a coalition partner, similarly aims to dismantle much of the Basque Country’s autonomy and has explicitly called for Bildu to be outlawed.

Silván warned that a PP-Vox government could sharply polarize the region’s politics and reignite dormant tensions. “The Basque Country is a place where people still mobilize on the streets, and you can bet that trade unions and common people will stand up,” she said. 

Elejabarrieta said Bildu was acutely aware of the threat a possible right-wing government in Madrid would pose to “our national institutions, our language and our self-government,” and said the prospect had reinforced his party’s commitment to working with other progressive forces.

He likened the current situation to that of the Basque government ruled by PNV leader José Antonio Aguirre during the Spanish Civil War. Aguirre led a coalition of center-right Basque nationalists, left-wing Spanish republicans and communists while besieged by Francisco Franco’s forces. 

“Just as they did in 1936, we now face an exceptional situation, and we must respond exceptionally and together,” he said.

Elejabarrieta also warned that any attempt to undermine Basque self-government, institutions or national symbols would swell support for independence in both Catalonia and the Basque Country.

“If they go down that road, we will soon become an enormous factory for pro-independence supporters,” he predicted.

articles.title: What is the Riemann hypothesis and why is its solution so monumental?
articles.summary:
Bernhard Riemann set out a problem mathematicians have been trying solve for more than a century

The Granger Collection/Alamy

The cadence of prime numbers has a pattern; it isn’t simply chaos. Mathematician Bernhard Riemann suspected this was the case, but he never proved it conclusively, and his mathematical successors have spent more than a century trying to demonstrate that he was right. The Riemann hypothesis may now be proven, and it could reveal the most basic structure of our number system, while also opening the door for a new understanding of the vast world of mathematical functions.

Read more

Mathematicians and AI in behind-the-scenes battle over what’s true

In 1859, Riemann made a casual remark about a mathematical function in his memoir, qualifying a statement about it as “very probably” true. The fact that he never proved it more definitively has held the world of mathematics in suspense ever since, and the “Riemann hypothesis” became the field’s most famous and stubbornly unsolved problem – until now. A new AI-assisted proof by Levent Alpöge at Anthropic may have just ended a whole era of mathematics by confirming Riemann’s hunch from nearly 200 years ago.

“This result, if true, will be the culmination of a struggle thousands of mathematicians have attempted in the past,” says Christopher Hughes at the University of York in the UK. The proof of the Reimann hypothesis is also one of the Clay Mathematics Institute’s Millennium Prize Problems, each of which comes with a $1 million prize for a solution.

Advertisement

The Riemann hypothesis has loomed so large over mathematicians for decades because it concerns mathematics’ most simple yet hard-to-understand objects: prime numbers. These are numbers that aren’t divisible by any number other than 1 and themselves, and any number can be built by multiplying primes. In this way, primes are the bones of all systems of numbers; everything is built on top of them. But how primes are distributed among all numbers is, on the face of it, unpredictable. This is where Riemann made an intervention.

He hypothesised that the way primes are spaced throughout the number line can be inferred from another set of numbers, now tied to a mathematical function called the Riemann zeta function. These numbers are complex – so each is actually a pair of numbers, one called real and one called imaginary – and when they are plugged into the Riemann zeta function, the function spits out zero. Confusingly, these numbers that result in a zero from the function are called “non-trivial zeros”. Riemann discovered that summing over a sequence of these complex numbers allowed him to predict the distribution of primes up to a certain high number. Effectively, he came upon a formula that could make sense of primes’ seemingly random appearances among numbers.

But the formula only works if all the zeros always sit on the same vertical line when plotted in a coordinate system where the horizontal axis tracks their real number constituents and the vertical axis their imaginary ones. Riemann calculated some of these zeros, which confirmed his idea, but could not prove the hypothesis more generally. It became the biggest unsolved problem in all of mathematics. “It is a legendary problem, the queen of all the Millennium Problems,” says Scott Armstrong at Sorbonne University in Paris. “For the whole field of mathematics, there could not be a bigger theorem.”

In the intervening years, mathematicians used computers to verify that the first 12 trillion nontrivial zeros line up on Riemann’s vertical line and much work has gone into proving that the zeros at least must lie in a strip of the coordinate systems around this line. In fact, a previous release of AI proofs by OpenAI on 6 October contained the proof of a weaker version of the Riemann hypothesis, placing the non-trivial zeros in the neighbourhood but not exactly on the line Riemann predicted.

In a statement released to the public, Alpöge wrote that his proof, developed with Anthropic’s Claude AI, is over 250,000 pages long, and it has not yet been fully read, digested or understood by the mathematics community. Even its translation into the language of the proof-checking software Lean is 17,000,000 lines long. That means it will take time to carefully adjudicate. “I have not had a chance to read the 17 million lines of Lean, so cannot speak to their truth,” says Alex Walker at University College London. And the announcement didn’t illuminate the details of the method, he adds.

The most interesting mathematical discoveries in OpenAI’s 722 new papers

OpenAI has released hundreds of papers claiming to make progress on the biggest open problems in mathematics – here are some with the most potential

Consequently, it is currently unclear exactly what mathematical tricks the AI leveraged, though early commentators suggest that it drew on a vast swathe of mathematics spanning several fields including number theory and arithmetic geometry. Some have suggested the AI made connections across these fields that don’t already clearly exist in the literature.

The Lean code is in the process of being adapted to efficiently run on a computer that can review it, which will provide a crucial check on the new proof. “While Lean itself has some issues, so far none of the AI results with Lean certificates have had to be retracted,” says Scott Aaronson at the University of Texas at Austin. Still, it may take years to unravel all the details of the new proof and reap any of its mathematical insights, he says. But the ramifications will certainly be enormous and extensive.

Notably, it resolves the biggest open question of number theory by finally making primes make sense. Numerous results also build on the assumption that Riemann was right and will now stand on firmer ground. And then there are implications for functions similar to the Riemann zeta function, known as the generalised Riemann hypothesis. “An extremely large number of results have previously been proven subject to the generalised Riemann hypothesis,” says John Nicholson at the Max Planck Institute for Mathematics in Germany. He says there are also a number of fast algorithms for computing quantities in algebraic number theory whose correctness depends on the generalised Riemann hypothesis. The Riemann hypothesis even has ties to theories of chaos in quantum systems in physics.

“The failure of the Riemann hypothesis would create havoc in the distribution of prime numbers,” wrote Enrico Bombieri at Princeton University when outlining the Millenium Problem more than a quarter of a century ago. Now, thanks to a combination of human ingenuity and relentlessness, and the computational power of AI, that distribution may have been shown to be not that dangerous after all.

articles.title: Anthropic mathematician claims AI-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis
articles.summary:
The Riemann hypothesis describes a pattern within the prime numbers

ROBERT BROOK/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Alamy

A mathematician at AI company Anthropic claims to have discovered, and verified with formalisation, a proof of the Riemann hypothesis – one of the most infamous and thorny problems in all of mathematics.

The Riemann hypothesis was first put forward in 1859 by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It proposes an origin for the prime numbers, namely that they follow a certain pattern. The question is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems, which will award a $1 million prize for an accepted solution.

Read more

OpenAI has dumped 722 maths papers – now it must clean up the mess

Levent Alpöge at Anthropic published a statement today claiming to have solved the problem with the aid of Anthropic’s Claude AI.

Advertisement

“I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis,” writes Alpöge. “It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.” In August, Anthropic announced previous work on the Riemann hypothesis, but that stopped short of a full proof.

Alpöge hasn’t published a human-readable version of the proof, saying it would be “obviously inappropriate to attempt to post some massive unreadable travesty of ‘slop'”, though he says an unpublished version ran to more than 250,000 pages.

Instead, Alpöge has released a version of the proof written in Lean, a computer code mathematicians use to mechanically verify proofs as a series of logical steps in a process called formalisation. This process is so thorough that if a theorem comes through intact, meaning that the code compiles, it is considered to have been proved correct beyond all reasonable doubt.

However, the process isn’t without vulnerabilities, and the code and mathematics will need to be thoroughly checked by humans. “Let’s see if it compiles first,” says Kevin Buzzard at Imperial College London, reacting to the news. “Might be a while before we find the relevant experts who are able to tell us the thrust of the argument, assuming it’s all true, of course, which it probably will be because of course Alpöge will have [a] huge amount of egg on [his] face if the Lean code doesn’t compile or is deficient in some way.”

A golden age of maths is dawning and mathematicians are freaking out

Mathematicians are stunned at the progress AI is making in solving advanced problems, leaving some questioning whether there will still be room for humans

Alpöge says the proof may also help solve the generalised Riemann hypothesis (GRH), which widens out the concept to different properties of prime numbers, and could expand our understanding of a broader family of mathematical structures. “There are numerous results that are conditional on the generalised Riemann hypothesis, and now those are theorems!” says James McKee at Royal Holloway University of London. “I suppose most mathematicians believed, or the more cautious ones merely suspected, that GRH was true, so its proof will not be unsettling. What is both unsettling and tremendously exciting, is the rapid progress in recent months towards automated proofs of significant mathematical results. It is both a wonderful time and a terrible time to be a research mathematician.”

Alpöge has been involved in a number of recent discoveries involving AI. In July, he announced that the Jacobian conjecture – which academics have spent decades trying to prove was true – is actually false, giving a tiny, 216-character counterexample as proof.

He and Tristan Buckmaster at New York University also announced that they had cracked three significant problems considered “stepping stones” to the Navier-Stokes problem, hours before OpenAI controversially revealed a full solution.

Anthropic listed on the stock market on 19 November, and Alpöge appears to suggest that he waited to announce the proof until after. “The precise timing is horrible. If I could have, I’d have finished this all much earlier,” he writes, saying that he spoke to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and determined that “there was a constraint to respect” before the announcement could be made.

articles.title: The BepiColombo spacecraft is finally entering orbit around Mercury
articles.summary:
Artist’s impression of BepiColombo orbiting Mercury

ESA/ATG medialab

After a long and ponderous journey, the BepiColombo spacecraft will finally enter Mercury’s orbit on 21 November. Over the course of the next year, it will investigate the planet’s geology, its tenuous atmosphere and its magnetic field in an effort to understand how it formed and evolved over time.

BepiColombo, a joint mission of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), launched in October 2018. Mercury’s proximity to the sun makes it incredibly difficult to reach without overshooting the planet and falling into the sun, so the spacecraft had to take a long and looping path over the past eight years, flying past both Venus and Mercury several times and using their gravity to make subtle tweaks to its trajectory. In 2024, an issue with the thrusters lengthened that journey even further, pushing the arrival date back from 2025 to 2026. Now, it has finally arrived.

Read more

6 of the most fascinating moments in the life of our solar system

While it is arriving at Mercury as a single spacecraft, BepiColombo actually comprises two separate orbiters: ESA’s Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA’s Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO, or Mio). In December, the two will split apart and move to different orbits – MPO on a near-circular path that takes 2.3 hours to complete an orbit, and Mio on a more distant elliptical orbit, where it will take 9.3 hours to circle Mercury.

Advertisement

Those split orbits complement the differing scientific objectives of the two spacecraft. MPO is more than twice the size of MMO, and its 11 scientific instruments focus largely on studying Mercury itself. Its instruments include several types of spectrometer to measure the makeup of the surface, a laser altimeter to map its terrain and instruments to study the makeup of Mercury’s extremely thin atmosphere, called an exosphere.

Mio’s more distant orbit will allow it to study a broader area around Mercury. It has five sets of scientific instruments to study the magnetic field and atmosphere of the planet, as well as the solar wind that blows strongly in the area close to the sun.

Free newsletter

Sign up to Launchpad

Sign up to newsletter

Now that the BepiColombo spacecraft are entering orbit, their primary mission is expected to last only one Earth year, which is a little more than four Mercury years. The mission could potentially be extended for another year, but beyond that the combination of limited fuel and extreme temperatures will make it all but impossible to keep going.

Over the course of the year, researchers hope that BepiColombo will provide enough data to solve some of Mercury’s many mysteries. Mercury’s magnetic field is bewildering, because it originates 400 kilometres above the planet’s centre and should have faded away long ago. Its atmosphere must be continuously supplied with material from the surface, but we are unsure exactly how that occurs. And its enormous iron core, much bigger proportionally than the core of any other planet in the solar system, makes its very formation and evolution a puzzle. If all goes well, BepiColombo will start to unravel the convoluted tale of our solar system’s smallest planet.

articles.title: Big tech may finally face legal consequences for AI’s actions
articles.summary:
California has filed a lawsuit against OpenAI for the Hugging Face incident

Chris Jung/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

Can you send a computer to jail? No, obviously not. That’s a stupid question. And yet it is one that AI firms seem to want us to ask when faced with tales of “rogue agents” breaking into other peoples’ computers. As is so often the case with our current AI moment, storytelling has got in the way of reality.

Thankfully, that may be starting to change. This week, California announced that it is filing a lawsuit against OpenAI over an incident that occurred earlier this year, when another AI firm, Hugging Face, was hit by an attack that turned out to originate from OpenAI’s servers.

Read more

The real reasons we keep seeing big tech outages – it isn’t just hackers

In OpenAI’s telling, the Hugging Face hack was “driven by a combination of OpenAI models”, models that were “hyperfocused” on achieving a goal and found ways to “cheat” by stealing the answers for a test from Hugging Face’s servers. It is easy to come away with the impression that seemingly no humans were involved, and certainly not to blame. But in the words of California Attorney General Rob Bonta, the attack “was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability”, and he explicitly dismisses “science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok”.

Advertisement

Ever since the Hugging Face attack occurred, I have struggled to understand why OpenAI has yet to face legal consequences for what would seem to be a crime – unauthorised computer access under the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act – if conducted by a human. So far, the legal answer to this seems to be a lack of intent, which the law requires, and it remains an untested legal question whether an AI can have intent, according to an analysis by US firm Ballard Spahr. California is instead bringing a civil suit, alleging that OpenAI created a risk to public safety and violated the state’s Unfair Competition Law, which prohibits harmful or fraudulent business practices even when there is no intent to deceive.

OpenAI has objected to the lawsuit. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab,” said OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri. As legal defences go, “everyone is doing it” doesn’t seem like a very good one to me, but that will be for the courts to decide.

What is clear is that we need an agreed understanding of liability when it comes to AI, but what I don’t think we need are special AI laws when our existing ones work just fine. For example, in 2024, Air Canada was held liable for misleading information given to a customer by its AI chatbot. A tribunal ruled that Air Canada had effectively tried to argue that the chatbot was a legally separate entity that it was not responsible for – an argument that did not wash.

In my view, any similar claims that AI can have its own legal agency should be dismissed. The argument that an AI is a legal actor serves AI companies in two ways, neither of which benefits society at large. The first is that it attempts to swerve responsibility, while the second is that it adds to the story of AI being an all-powerful, unknowable being. That second story is at the heart of the current AI revolution, but it isn’t one we have to listen to.

Read more

How preppers plan to save us if the whole internet collapses

I prefer a different argument. For the past year or so, Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor at Princeton University have put forward the idea of “AI as Normal Technology” – transformative, yes, in the same way as the internet or electricity, but not something that requires re-engineering the ordinary functions of society. As a normal technology, normal laws can apply. Writing about the Hugging Face attack earlier this year, the pair said that “AI companies should be liable for what their agents do” and, like Bonta, blame OpenAI’s internal culture and lack of human oversight for the incident.

The most high-profile example of existing laws being applied to AI companies is a class-action lawsuit against Anthropic, alleging that the firm used pirated copies of books to train its Claude AI models. Anthropic settled, and is now in the process of paying out to affected authors from a $1.5 billion fund. The wider question of whether training an AI on copyrighted material is illegal or counts as fair use remains open, and I really can’t believe that, four years after the launch of ChatGPT, we don’t yet have an answer to what is probably one of the most fundamental legal disputes of our time. OpenAI has previously said it would be “impossible” to create the kind of AI we have now without using copyrighted material, so this is an existential question for the AI firms.

Existing laws can also be tweaked to make it clear that they apply to AI. The European Union has done just that, updating a 1985 consumer rights directive to produce the 2024 Product Liability Directive, which explicitly makes it clear that software, including artificial intelligence, is a product and that people writing software are liable for any defects. The law doesn’t come into force until 9 December, when EU members must implement it, and it remains to be seen how it might be used against AI companies.

In other words, we don’t have to try to send a computer to jail. We’ve got humans who should be liable instead. As Bonta says, “While the technology OpenAI develops may be new, California’s prohibitions against conduct that harms the public and laws against unfair, deceptive, and fraudulent business practices are not.”

Further AI reading

After much fanfare, Anthropic has listed on the stock market at $83 a share, giving it a valuation of around $1.5 trillion. It is the second big AI firm to go public this year, following SpaceXAI in June.

The Economist has a great piece on whether the AI industry can ever make enough money to survive. It calculates that it must produce $3 trillion in revenue by 2030 to cover the costs of planned data centres. That is roughly equivalent to a tenth of all wages in high-income countries, or similar to the amount spent on food. Are people really going to buy as much AI as they do food?

The Cambridge Dictionary has named “human” as word of the year, as a pushback against the growth of AI. It feels a bit like trying too hard to be relevant, in my view.

As the COP31 climate summit continues, only nine countries have signed a pledge aimed at limiting the environmental impact of AI. As I have written previously, we cannot afford to run this 21st-century technology on a 20th-century energy supply.

articles.title: Turmeric supplements offer little benefit for knee osteoarthritis
articles.summary:
Turmeric capsules are touted as remedies for joint problems

olga Yastremska/Alamy

Turmeric supplements seem to have little to no effect on pain and mobility problems caused by knee osteoarthritis. That’s according to one of the most rigorous assessments of the evidence yet, which focused on four randomised controlled trials comparing the supplements to placebo pills.

Osteoarthritis, which affects more than 500 million people worldwide, is caused by damage to cartilage that cushions the ends of bones, resulting in pain, stiffness and inflammation. Standard treatments include painkillers and anti-inflammatory drugs that can ease symptoms. “But many people see little or no benefit,” says Philip Conaghan at the University of Leeds, UK, who wasn’t involved in the latest review.

Read more

There are only a few anti-ageing supplements that actually work

Turmeric supplements are often touted as an alternative therapy. They contain curcumin, a compound that gives turmeric its yellow colour and is thought to have anti-inflammatory properties. Yet such beliefs are often based on prior flawed studies, says Ivan Shirinsky at the Research Institute of Internal and Preventive Medicine in Novosibirsk, Russia.

Advertisement

Shirinsky and his colleagues analysed results from four randomised controlled trials, collectively involving more than 370 participants with knee osteoarthritis. Participants were randomly assigned to take either a supplement containing turmeric extract or placebo pills two or three times per day, for between eight weeks and three months. Each trial used a slightly different supplement containing a different curcumin dose. “We looked at the most rigorous evidence available,” says Shirinsky.

Among those who took a placebo, knee pain decreased by 1.6 points, on average, on a scale from 0 to 10 by the end of the study. Those taking turmeric supplements experienced an average 2.3-point decrease in pain, meaning the difference between the turmeric and placebo groups was half that required to be meaningful to patients based on prior studies, says Shirinsky.

Free newsletter
