Glofs and glaciers are blind, they do not know whether to fall on the right or the left,” he said, highlighting the shared threat climate change poses to both neighbours.

He further said, “You have called me for culture and civilisation [discussions]. I am your guest, you are my host […] You have asked me the same question a 100 times and I have responded to it a 100 times.”

In his remarks at the SCO forum on Saturday, Malik had termed climate change an “enemy” of civilisations and pointed out its impact on South Asian countries that bore the brunt of climate destruction.

Water and the IWT remain a contentious issue between Pakistan and India, following New Delhi’s unilateral abeyance of the accord in April last year after the Pahalgam attack, which was followed by the four-day military conflict between the two sides.

Following India’s move, Pakistan termed any attempt to suspend its water share an “act of war”, noting the IWT had no provision for unilateral suspension. It later argued that New Delhi’s action was a violation of the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties.

Backing Islamabad’s stance, the Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) on Aug 31 ordered New Delhi to uphold the IWT, declaring that the treaty remained fully in force, as India had no justification for ending or suspending the agreement.

The IWT, brokered by the World Bank in 1960, allocates the three western rivers — Indus, Jhelum and Chenab — largely to Pakistan, and the three eastern rivers — Ravi, Beas and Sutlej — to India.

The treaty has survived wars, crises, and political tensions for more than six decades and is considered a rare example of durable water-sharing cooperation between the two neighbours.

articles.title: Netanyahu and Eisenkot’s parties resume talks to form coalition govt in Israel
articles.summary:
HERZLIYA: The parties of caretaker Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his rival Gadi Eisenkot launched a new round of talks on Sunday over whether to form a coalition government, with Netanyahu’s party insisting on keeping his main policies.

Delegations from Eisenkot’s Yashar party and Netanyahu’s Likud began their confab at a hotel in Herzliya, near Tel Aviv, a journalist on the scene said, following a first round of talks last Sunday.

A former army chief of staff, Eisenkot has until Dec 6 to form a government, with the possibility of a 14-day extension, after October elections failed to give either camp an absolute majority.

His 48-member bloc, which needs 61 lawmakers to reach a majority, remains divided over whether to build a coalition through an alliance with ultra-Orthodox parties, a rapprochement with Arab parties, or a national unity government with Likud.

Netanyahu is pushing for a national unity government, which could see a rotation of the premiership between the two men, a mechanism already tried in Israel. Such an arrangement could allow Netanyahu to keep his political protection against the corruption charges he faces, as well as continue to oppose the creation of an independent commission of inquiry into the security failures that preceded the Hamas raid of Oct 7, 2023.

But that prospect runs up against Eisenkot’s refusal to serve in a cabinet led by Netanyahu, against whom he centred his campaign. His ally Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister, also reiterated on Saturday his refusal to join a coalition with “Netanyahu or his bloc, under any circumstances”.

National ‘unity’?

On Saturday, Yashar presented the resumption of talks as “a genuine commitment to forming the broadest possible government”, saying that Eisenkot had asked his representatives to explore all options. But Likud immediately laid down several conditions for its participation in a unity government, a formula backed by Netanyahu.

Among other things, it demands an end to “all personal attacks and incitement to hatred” targeting the outgoing prime minister and his government. It also called for bringing together “all the parties that support the existence of the State of Israel as the nation-state of the Jewish people”, without the participation of Arab parties.

Netanyahu and his allies regularly target Arab parties, which secured a record 19 seats in the legislature and are opposed to Netanyahu remaining in power. Likud is also demanding agreement on several major policy positions, notably rejecting the creation of a Palestinian state, maintaining Israeli control over territories in Syria, Lebanon and the Gaza Strip, and a compromise on conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jews, a particularly sensitive issue in Israel.

On Friday, Eisenkot warned that he would not allow the talks to drag on, saying he was ready to submit to parliament an “emergency national government”.

Although he did not spell out how, his statements suggest a two-stage plan: the swift formation of a minority government based on the core opposition parties, and then broadening it.

A minority Eisenkot government could receive support from the 19 Ar­­­­ab party lawmakers but Eisen­kot’s right-wing ally Avigdor Liber­man rejects working with them and instead advocates an alliance with ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties.

Published in Dawn, November 23rd, 2026

articles.title: Lahore ranked after Islamabad, ahead of major cities in safety perception index
articles.summary:
LAHORE: Lahore has scored ahead of several major international cities, including New York, Paris and New Delhi but lower than Islamabad in the recent Numbeo’s 2026 Mid-Year Crime and Safety Index with safety and crime indexes at 63.8 and 36.2 respectively.

A report in this regard was presented to Punjab Inspector General of Police (IGP) Abdul Kareem during his visit to the Lahore Police Lines, Qilla Gujjar Singh here on Sunday, where he held a high-level meeting on the crime situation in the city.

Capital City Police Officer (CCPO) Bilal Siddique Kamyana, DIGs Faisal Kamran, Zeshan Raza, all the SSPs, SPs and other senior police officers were present. A senior official told this reporter that the meeting discussed various other key issues including criteria of posting the station house officers (SHOs), deteriorating response time of police on helpline 15 calls, shortage of Dolphin Force bikes and mishandling of some cases, such as a police raid at the residence of Attorney General for Pakistan (AGP) Mansoor Usman Awan.

During the session, he said, the DIG operations presented Numbeo’s report which has placed Lahore in the “Low” to “Moderate” crime range based on user-submitted perception surveys.

“Lahore scores lower on crime than Karachi (Crime Index 57.8–57.9) and Rawalpindi (51.8), while Islamabad scores lower on crime (30.8–31.1)”, said Mr Kamran while quoting the report. He added that the provincial capital also scored lower on crime than many major Western cities.

“These figures are based on visitors’ perception on this website,” he said, adding that a total of 380 cities of the world were included in the surveys.

IGP holds high-level meeting and discusses posting of SHOs, deteriorating response on helpline 15, shortage of Dolphin Force bikes, mishandling of cases

The CCPO told the meeting that Lahore was the only city in Punjab without any no-go area, major land-grabbing mafia, gangsters or hooligans as the police had eradicated them to bring peace in the city. He told the meeting that the crime situation of the city had improved significantly during the last four years.During the meeting, the official said, the IGP expressed displeasure over the deteriorating response time of the police on 15 calls, saying that it had dropped to 22pc across the province. He declared it a matter of serious concern and said that as per reports, the callers were being asked to reach police stations to file their reports.

The official said that DIG operations clarified that the response time of the police in Lahore was recorded 66pc. However, Abdul Kareem declared the response time of the Lahore police at 15 ‘still insufficient’ as Lahore police possessed significantly more resources than those in other cities.

The official said that Mr Kamran cited shortage of bikes for Dolphin Force as a major reason for low response time. He further elaborated that the Dolphin Force were patrolling on bikes of various police stations as a makeshift arrangement.

Mr Kareem revealed that Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz had approved procurement of new bikes for the provincial police at a cost of Rs300 millions with Lahore Police getting as many as 300-400 bikes by December.

According to the insider, the IGP said that inspectors were complaining that they were not being considered for SHO posts in the provincial capital. He said that they were worried that a majority of junior officials, sub-inspectors, were serving as SHOs.

In response to these complaints, the DIG operations said that two-thirds of SHOs were sub-inspectors and it was meant to produce a pool of trained officials for sensitive jobs.

About the complaints of missing women, the DIG investigation told the IGP that out of thousands of such cases, less than 100 were yet to be traced.

Published in Dawn, November 23rd, 2026

articles.title: PTV asked to disclose details of foreign trips at public expense
articles.summary:
ISLAMABAD: The Pakistan Information Commission (PIC) has directed Pakistan Television Corporation (PTV) to disclose details of foreign trips undertaken by its officials at public expense since January 2025, ruling that information about the utilisation of public funds cannot be withheld merely by declaring it confidential or sensitive.

Allowing an appeal filed by journalist and Right to Information (RTI) activist Saddia Mazhar, the commission directed PTV’s managing director to provide the complete information sought in her request within 10 days of receiving the order, with a copy to be submitted to the commission.

The order was signed by Information Com­m­issioner Ijaz Hassan Awan and Chief Information Commissioner Shoaib Ahmad Siddiqui.

Ms Mazhar had submitted an information request on June 21, 2026, seeking details of PTV officials and other officers who had travelled abroad at public expense to cover or attend various events from January 2025 onwards.

She specifically sought the names of the officials concerned, the composition of teams deputed for foreign assignments, the nature of their assignments and the expenditure incurred by the government or PTV.

Journalist seeks names of officials, assignments, expenditure since January last year

However, PTV resisted disclosure, maintaining that the information formed part of the corporation’s official and confidential records.

In its written response submitted to the commission on Aug 25, 2026, the state-owned broadcaster argued that disclosure could involve matters relating to official deployments, security considerations, operational arrangements and other sensitive aspects of high-level official engagements.

PTV also invoked exemptions under Section 16(d)(ii) and (iii) of the Right of Access to Information Act, 2017, requesting the commission to allow it to withhold the information.

The corporation maintained that its officials were deputed on foreign tours for official assignments, including coverage of prime ministerial visits, high-level government engagements, international conferences and other important meetings. It said specific teams were allocated according to the nature and requirements of these engagements.

Ms Mazhar challenged PTV’s position, arguing in her rejoinder that the information concerned public expenditure and did not fall within the exemptions invoked by the broadcaster. She maintained that the records constituted public information under the RTI law.

After hearing the arguments and examining the available record and relevant legal provisions, the commission rejected PTV’s objections.

In its order, the commission observed that the requested information fell within the ambit of Sections 5(g) and 6(b) of the Right of Access to Information Act, 2017, as it related to expenditure incurred on foreign tours by officials from the allocated budget of a public body.

“Such information pertains to the utilisation of public funds and, therefore, constitutes public information subject to disclosure under the Act,” the order stated.

The commission also rejected PTV’s argument concerning the potential impact of disclosure on its financial interests and commercial activities, observing that the corporation had failed to establish how providing the information would damage its financial interests or adversely affect its lawful commercial activities.

It also observed that merely describing information as confidential or sensitive, without establishing the applicability of the relevant exemption under the law, was insufficient grounds for withholding it.

Published in Dawn, November 23rd, 2026

articles.title: Independent media not as 'independent' as it could be: Mehdi Hasan
articles.summary:
• US journalist says news gatekeeping has been outsourced to Silicon Valley
• Says every journalist ‘needs to be’ a content creator now

DOHA: Journalism has undergone a major transformation since the advent of social media and independent news platforms, bringing both opportunities and challenges. These changes were the focus of a talk titled The New Gatekeepers by British-American journalist Mehdi Hasan at the Doha Film Festival.

Drawing on his experience at mainstream outlets including the BBC, CNN, Al Jazeera, Sky News and MSNBC, Hasan discussed the changing media landscape and his move towards independent journalism through his own media company, Zeteo, after his MSNBC show was cancelled.

Speaking about news gatekeepers, he said that historically only a handful of people could communicate with mass audiences because billionaires, corporations and governments controlled the technology and resources needed to spread information. That has now changed.

“It’s good that we have democratised access to the news. Today anyone in this room can go out with a microphone, camera and a WiFi connection and potentially reach more people than a BBC, CNN or an Al Jazeera journalist,” he said.

However, Mr Hasan stressed he was not opposed to gatekeeping itself, arguing that journalism still needed fact-checking and professional standards. “I am still a journalist, not a YouTuber or content creator. I am still on YouTube, but I do fact-check. The problem with the old gatekeepers was not the gates. It was that they were opening the gates to the powerful and shutting them to the powerless.”

Citing a Reuters Institute survey, he noted that, for the first time, more people were getting their news from social media than from news websites and apps. “We are already in a brave new world,” he remarked.

But the democratisation of information had not eliminated gatekeeping; instead, it had transferred much of that power to Silicon Valley, where technology executives such as Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg exercise considerable influence.

Hasan described it as “insane” that platforms controlled by Zuckerberg, including WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook and Threads, were used by a substantial proportion of the world’s population, with many relying on them for news.

He warned that algorithms could undermine the news business, as had already happened to numerous publishers.

Asked whether independent media was truly independent, Hasan acknowledged that it was not as independent as it could be. Although such outlets were often free from corporate, government or billionaire ownership and relied on subscribers rather than advertising, they faced another pressure: “audience capture”.

“If you are fully funded by your subscribers, then you would tell them what they want to hear,” he said.

He cited his own experience at Zeteo, where subscribers cancelled their subscriptions during the 2024 US election for diametrically opposed reasons, illustrating the difficulties of maintaining an independent editorial space.

On whether every journalist now had to become a content creator, Mr Hasan said the two roles had increasingly overlapped. “I think every journalist does have to be a content creator now, which is a double-edged sword. But I don’t think every content creator or YouTuber is a journalist.”

Addressing the crisis of trust in information, he argued that journalism itself was not responsible for the decline in public confidence. “I don’t think journalism is inherently bad, evil or has lost trust. I think institutions, people and journalistic practices have lost trust. People are craving journalism, facts, evidence, information and news about the world,” he said.

Mr Hasan also rejected the idea that corporate media was dead, arguing that established organisations remained essential because independent outlets lacked the resources and expertise for large-scale news gathering, foreign coverage and extensive investigative reporting.

He said he could not undertake the kind of investigative journalism produced by The New York Times due to lack of resources. However, he said, mainstream media had failed audiences in several areas, creating demand for alternative sources of information.

Agenda, objectivity

On editorial agendas and objectivity, Mr Hasan admitted that he had his own agenda, arguing that no media organisation was entirely neutral. “I don’t believe that there is any neutral media outlet, but my position is that journalists are allowed to have opinions as long as they are based on facts. I believe in objectivity. Neutrality and objectivity are not the same. I don’t believe you should be neutral between good and evil.”

He identified another major challenge for independent journalism: audiences’ reluctance to pay for news. Without subscriptions or paywalls, he argued, it was difficult to fund the reporting and information gathering needed to sustain quality journalism.

Published in Dawn, November 23rd, 2026

articles.title: PM to attend ECO moot in Iran after Russia trip
articles.summary:
ISLAMABAD: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif will undertake his first official three-day visit to Rus­sia from Nov 30, aiming to strengthen bilateral ties and secure energy and inve­stment agreements bef­ore travelling to Iran for the 18th Economic Coo­peration Organisation (ECO) Summit on Dec 3 and 4.

During his meeting with Russian President Vladi­mir Putin, discussions are expected to focus on ene­rgy cooperation, defence, trade, regional security and investment, a source in the Prime Minister’s Office told Dawn.

The revival of Pakistan Steel Mills, established with Russian assistance, is also likely to feature prominently, alongside potential Russian investment in Pakistan’s oil and gas sectors.

The two countries are likely to examine possibilities for Russian cooperation in restoring the industrial facility, alongside broader initiatives aimed at supporting Pakistan’s industrial development.

Following the Russia visit, Prime Minister Shehbaz will represent Pakistan at the ECO summit in Tehran, where leaders of 10 member states will discuss regional trade, connectivity, energy, tran-sportation, investment and industrial cooperation.

The summit comes ahead of Pakistan assuming the ECO chairmanship for 2026-27.

Published in Dawn, November 23rd, 2026

articles.title: Govt moves to overhaul ‘weak’ audit system
articles.summary:
• FBR task force flags weaknesses in existing review framework
• Cabinet approves SECP Amendment Bill 2026 after consultation
• Proposed legislation aims to strengthen independent audit oversight

ISLAMABAD: The government has decided to overhaul the country’s ent­ire audit system after the Prime Min­ister’s Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) Task Force described the existing framework as weak, saying it discourages local and foreign investm­ent and limits access to capital markets.

Documents seen by Dawn suggest the government plans to introduce legislative amendments in parliament to reform the existing audit system.

The proposed amendments will be introduced in the light of recommendations made by the Prime Minister’s FBR Task Force, which has already raised serious concerns over weaknesses in the existing audit framework, according to the document.

In this regard, the government will introduce legislation, including the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) (Amendment) Bill, 2026. A similar bill was passed by the National Assembly in 2021 after scrutiny and recommendations by the NA Standing Committee on Finance. However, it was withdrawn from the Senate in 2022 for resubmission. The federal cabinet has now approved the proposed bill again after extensive consultations and reviews by three ministerial-level committees.

The task force has also recommended amendments to the Audit Oversight Board (AOB) law to improve tax collection.

The process of reforming the AOB was already underway, but market-related concerns continued to highlight weaknesses in audits. Pakistan’s existing AOB law did not comply with international standards, an official briefing document said.

“Investors and lenders rely on audited accounts, but weak audits discourage local and foreign investment and access to capital markets.

“The International Organisation of Securities Commissions (IOSCO), the securities market standard-setter, declared Pakistan non-compliant with independent audit oversight. The European Union (EU) also withdrew Pakistan’s equivalence status for independent audit oversight,” it added.

The report cited Unity Foods and SE Foods as examples of companies affected by weak audits and prospectus disclosures. It also highlighted concerns over Hascol’s audited accounts.

The report said developed and developing countries had amended their laws and shifted from self-regulatory oversight by accountancy bodies to independent audit oversight. Even smaller jurisdictions, including Sri Lanka, Mauritius and Botswana, are compliant members of the International Forum of Independent Audit Regulators (IFIAR), it added.

It has been learnt that the proposed system will end the dominance of private auditors.

The document said the federal cabinet had approved the draft legislation following a comprehensive review by the FBR Task Force, IFIAR, SECP and AOB, along with extensive consultations with stakeholders. The proposed legislation is expected to strengthen Pakistan’s international recognition and establish an effective audit oversight system.

The salient features of the SECP Amendment Bill, 2026, are as follows:

The independence of the nominating committee responsible for appointing AOB board members will be strengthened by including the FBR chairman in place of the president of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Pakistan (ICAP).

AOB board members will not be permitted to have any association with audit firms.

The AOB board will be responsible for policy matters, while management, operations and adjudication will be handled in line with governance principles and the board’s regulatory functions.

The AOB will conduct regular, risk-based inspections of auditors of Public Interest Companies (PICs) to assess compliance with professional auditing standards.

Accountancy bodies will continue to conduct regular inspections and Quality Control Reviews (QCRs) of non-PIC audits under the oversight of the AOB.

The AOB will directly investigate complaints and references from the SECP, State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) and FBR after approval by its board or a designated committee.

Standard action will be taken against individuals who refuse to provide required information, while the AOB will also be empowered to file complaints concerning criminal offences involving falsification.

Published in Dawn, November 23rd, 2026

articles.title: Why foreign investment continues to elude Pakistan
articles.summary:
Pakistan has secured a hard-won stability, yet foreign investors continue to look the other way. Net foreign direct investment (FDI) fell 34 per cent in FY26 to $1.64 billion, against more than $5bn in FY07 and FY08. At about 0.5pc of GDP, the FDI is barely visible in an economy of 250 million people.

This is not for want of macroeconomic progress: the State Bank’s reserves have climbed from under $3bn in early 2023 to about $21.5bn, and the fiscal deficit is at a multi-year low. But this stability remains fragile, and investors base their decisions on the next 10 years, not the last two. On that horizon, three major factors have kept investments away.

First, Pakistani industry pays roughly 13 to 15 US cents per kilowatt-hour (kWh), nearly double India (6 to 9 cents) and Vietnam (8 cents), and well above Bangladesh (9 cents). Industrial gas costs $13.5 per MMBtu, against $6.5 in India and $10 in Bangladesh. According to the regulator, about half of the average tariff is capacity payments for the power plants that often sit idle. That legacy cost falls on the very consumers who could grow the economy. For an export-oriented investor comparing sites, this single line in the spreadsheet easily ends the conversation.

Second, corporations in Pakistan pay 29pc corporate tax plus super tax. Workers’ Welfare Fund and Workers’ Profit Participation Fund take the effective rate near 46pc; add dividend tax, and rates exceed 50pc. Banks paid an effective 54pc in FY25. By contrast, Vietnam’s corporate rate is 20pc, Indonesia’s 22pc and Malaysia’s is 24pc. India cut its rate to 22pc in 2019, and as low as 15pc for new manufacturers. This year’s budget removed the lower super-tax slabs and cut the top rate from 10 to 8pc. That is welcome, but it remains an annual negotiation, not a trajectory an investor can model.

25 multinationals have exited or downsized since 2022; investors hate policies that keep changing after capital is committed; Pakistan needs a framework that outlasts budgets and governments

Last but not the least, what investors hate most is not mediocre policies, or even high tax rates, but policies that keep changing after capital is committed. Pakistan has given them real reasons to fear.

The state spent years promoting net metering and capacity grew from about 300MW in 2021 to over 2,800MW by FY25. In March 2025, the buyback rate was cut from Rs27 to Rs10. In February 2026, net metering was scrapped for new users, with buyback at Rs8.13 and contracts cut from seven years to five.

Industries that built gas-fired self-generation now face an off-grid levy designed to force them back onto the costliest grid in the region. Captive gas use in the export sector has collapsed from 180 to 26 mmcfd.

Agreements with independent power producers, backed by sovereign guarantees, were renegotiated or terminated in 2024 and 2025. Lenders everywhere noted that a sovereign contract in Pakistan is open to revision. The super tax arrived in 2022 as a one-time levy, applied to a year already closed, and has been retained and re-slabbed in every budget since.

Layered on this is regulatory overreach in almost every sector: price controls, overlapping federal and provincial regulators, discretionary licensing and sudden import curbs. By one count, 25 multinationals have exited or downsized since 2022. Each cited its own reasons; together they read as a clear verdict on predictability.

For the solution, Pakistan doesn’t need another incentive package or investment conference. It needs a framework that outlasts budgets and governments. The recently announced national tariff plan exemplifies such a framework. For investments to meaningfully return to Pakistan, more predictable plans are needed, built on three commitments:

First, it should reward productive investment, including direct incentives to manufacturing, exports, technology and mining through accelerated depreciation and investment allowances, not exemptions for real estate and trading.

Second, the country needs to clear the path for the green energy transition and publish a decade-long roadmap to cost-reflective industrial tariffs of around nine cents, free of cross-subsidies, with stable rules for solar, storage, wheeling and a competitive power market.

Third, it needs to achieve regionally competitive taxes by 2030 and legislate a glide path that brings the corporate rate to 25pc and phases out the super tax, so investors can build it into their models.

This bears repeating that investors do not need Pakistan to be cheap, they need it to be predictable. Capital will only come when investors see a policy framework that is clear, written into law and not subject to change with the latest whim, crisis or budget cycle.

The writer is President of American Business Forum

Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, November 23rd, 2026

articles.title: Capitalising on Middle East conflict
articles.summary:
Rarely does a government in Pakistan respond swiftly and purposefully to a crisis by bringing public and private stakeholders together, building consensus and implementing corrective measures. The US-Iran conflict presented such an opportunity, forcing Pakistan to protect its maritime supply chains while opening new possibilities for its ports and shipping industry.

The prime minister constituted two committees to address the emerging challenges. This article focuses on the committee headed by Federal Minister for Maritime Affairs Muhammad Junaid Anwar Chaudhry, of which the writer was a member. Its mandate is to protect maritime trade flows and energy supplies while identifying opportunities arising from disruptions to regional shipping.

The committee met regularly, sometimes daily, to address operational bottlenecks and develop a coordinated response. It helped maintain oil supplies and secure some liquefied natural gas (LNG) cargoes from Qatar despite force majeure following attacks on its production facilities and disruption of the Strait of Hormuz.

One of its earliest initiatives followed an approach by the Pakistan Ship’s Agents Association (PSAA), which pointed out that disruption at major regional transshipment hubs offered Pakistan an opportunity to attract cargo previously routed through competing ports. Despite having a transshipment policy for more than two decades, Pakistan had failed to attract significant business because of restrictive customs procedures and uncompetitive port charges.

US-Iran conflict is pushing Pakistan to protect its maritime supply chains and opening new possibilities for its ports and shipping industry

The committee engaged customs authorities to remove these impediments. Rules were amended to allow transshipment cargo to be stored at off-dock terminals, easing pressure on congested on-dock facilities. The requirement for mandatory scanning of all containers moving to off-dock terminals was also replaced with a risk-based non-intrusive inspection system. Customs procedures were further revised to accommodate non-containerised break-bulk and roll-on/roll-off cargo.

New feeder shipping services to Gulf and Red Sea ports were also encouraged to maintain outlets for Pakistani imports and exports amid disruption to established shipping routes.

Another significant achievement came on July 29, when the Joint War Committee of Lloyd’s London formally stated that war-risk insurance premiums for vessels calling at Pakistani ports would no longer be automatically triggered by their classification under listed areas. This is expected to reduce shipping costs and improve the commercial attractiveness of Karachi, Port Qasim and Gwadar, removing a reputational disadvantage that had affected Pakistan’s ports for more than a decade.

The committee also addressed the longstanding problem of auctioned containers occupying valuable port space. Customs authorities allowed these containers to be shifted to licensed off-dock facilities, freeing terminal capacity, facilitating faster cargo handling and enabling shipping lines to redeploy their containers for fresh business.

Another breakthrough was permission for less-than-container-load (LCL) transshipment. This involves importing smaller consignments, consolidating or deconsolidating cargo, undertaking value addition and re-exporting it. Pakistan has long sought to develop this business along the lines of Jebel Ali. One major US-based shipping company has already selected Pakistan over India for its LCL transshipment operations.

Gwadar Port also witnessed a notable increase in activity, receiving more than a dozen vessels carrying around 200,000 tonnes of cargo, including steel plates, machinery and fertiliser, within three months. This exceeded the vessel and cargo activity recorded during the preceding three years. Five additional vessels conducted anchorage operations.

To improve competitiveness, reduced port and terminal tariffs were introduced for transshipment cargo, with concessions linked to the proportion of such cargo handled. A Far Eastern shipping company has consequently expressed interest in shifting its transshipment operations from India’s Mundra Port to Karachi.

The committee also took up complaints about excessive and retrospective war-risk and emergency conflict surcharges imposed by shipping companies, including on cargo that had sailed before the conflict began. Customs authorities directed shipping lines and their agents to ensure transparency, disclose charges in advance and refrain from unjustified retrospective levies. A mechanism was established for affected importers and exporters to submit documentary evidence for scrutiny.

Importantly, revised customs procedures will allow consignees to choose between on-dock and off-dock terminals for cargo clearance. This will enable cargo to be moved directly to off-dock facilities, where shipping containers can be emptied and returned promptly, reducing detention and demurrage costs while improving port turnaround times.

The committee’s recommendations were subsequently submitted to the prime minister, who constituted the National Coordination and Management Council to coordinate decisions concerning the economic, trade and energy consequences of the Middle East conflict.

The next phase offers further opportunities. The Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Port Qasim Authority are working on a proposed automobile import and re-export zone where used vehicles could be imported, refurbished and exported. Much of this business is currently conducted in Dubai and Sharjah, often by Pakistani operators. A proposed energy city at Port Qasim or another suitable location could also provide strategic petroleum storage outside the Strait of Hormuz. International energy companies have reportedly expressed interest.

The potential economic gains extend beyond port revenues to shipping, logistics, storage, transportation and employment. Each transshipment container handled in Pakistan could generate an estimated $150 in associated economic activity. An additional throughput of 500,000 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) is achievable within one to three years, rising to one million within five years.

The crisis has demonstrated that trade facilitation is essential to Pakistan’s economic competitiveness. A proposed trade facilitation board is expected to examine remaining bottlenecks in cargo clearance and logistics costs. Sustaining these gains, however, will require consistent policies, institutional coordination and a lasting commitment to removing regulatory friction.

The writer is chairman Pakistan Ship’s Agents Association and former board member of KPT, PQA and GPIA

Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, November 23rd, 2026

articles.title: What deters companies from reinvesting profit
articles.summary:
Limited access to finance is often presented as a key challenge preventing businesses, and the economy, from growing. Last year, the State Bank governor argued that weak investment is “directly linked” to low savings. The argument has serious consequences. Taken at face value, governments and policymakers should focus on promoting higher savings, encouraging foreign money to enter the economy, and decreasing the cost of financing. No doubt, successive governments have gone to great lengths to make elaborate foreign trips, sign memoranda of understanding, offer incentives and fast-track approvals through ad hoc arrangements in their attempts to attract foreign investment.

Yet, the overall story remains that of a failure. Foreign direct investment has averaged just under one per cent of GDP between 2006 and 2025, among the lowest in the world. The world average is 2.6pc. At home, governments have pushed for greater access to financial instruments to increase household savings, promoted Islamic finance to respond to people’s religious preferences, and launched schemes to decrease the cost of borrowing for businesses. However, between 2005 and 2025, investment averaged just 15.7pc of GDP, against an average of 29.8pc for lower-middle-income countries. Only eight of 168 countries invested less. Private investment has been even lower, at close to 10pc of GDP in recent years.

What if the problem has been misdiagnosed and access to finance is not the central problem facing the country? To see this, consider what the largest businesses – non-financial corporations listed on the stock market – do with the internal finance they already have in the form of profits. Data published by the State Bank of Pakistan show that, between 2005 and 2025, these firms earned, in today’s prices, Rs20.7 trillion after tax and paid out Rs10.7tr, more than half, as cash dividends. This result is not driven by a high payout in a few years. Instead, firms paid out more than half of their profits in dividends in 15 of the 21 years, and paid out Rs500 billion in FY25 alone. The share is higher still in food (63pc), autos (59pc), other manufacturing (59pc) and chemicals (57pc). Put simply, Pakistan’s largest firms are not short of money. Instead, they are short of reasons to invest it.

Policy measures must focus on reducing uncertainty for firms by providing a stable macro environment, consistent enforcement of regulation, and the rule of law, which ensures trust in the judiciary

The high dividend payout ratio is not driven by weak firms. The fifth of privately owned firms with the highest returns on assets earned 83pc of all private firms’ profits and paid out 54pc of them. The payout is even higher in the case of multinational subsidiaries, which paid out 68pc of their profits. In other words, while governments court new foreign investors, those already in the country send much of their profits home.

Paying dividends is not undesirable in itself. However, how much firms pay out also depends on the opportunities they have to invest. In a study published in 2000 in The Journal of Finance, La Porta and co-authors examine 4,000 firms across 33 countries and find that, in common-law countries, faster-growing firms pay lower dividends. Pakistan’s high payouts are consistent with the explanation that firms see few opportunities to invest at home. High dividends are, therefore, a symptom, not the problem.

What, then, is missing? Investment in plants and machinery takes years to pay back and is difficult to reverse. As a result, firms invest only when returns are predictable and contracts can be enforced. Pakistan performs poorly on both counts. First, the economy swings from boom to bust every few years, and the current IMF programme is the country’s 24th. Such uncertainty makes firms delay investment.

Second, institutions are weak. The World Justice Project’s 2025 Rule of Law Index ranks Pakistan 130th of 143 countries, 129th for civil justice and 127th for regulatory enforcement. This matters because complex production, which relies on contractual relationships with many suppliers, develops mainly when courts can be trusted and contracts are expected to be enforced.

Together the evidence points to a different diagnosis. While access to finance still matters, particularly for smaller firms, it cannot explain why the largest and most profitable ones pay out so much of what they earn. Another scheme focusing on providing cheap credit or another investment conference aimed at foreign investors is unlikely to change what firms do with their profits. Instead, policy measures must focus on reducing uncertainty for firms by providing a stable macro environment, consistent enforcement of regulation, and the rule of law, which ensures trust in the judiciary. The test of success is straightforward: whether Pakistan’s most profitable firms start reinvesting their own profits at home.

Recent policy, however, points the other way. Rather than strengthening the predictable rules and institutions that encourage investment, the government has increasingly relied on discretionary arrangements. The Special Investment Facilitation Council (SIFC), set up in 2023, can recommend relaxing regulations for individual projects, replacing rules that apply to all with case-by-case decisions. Even the government’s own reform agenda warns that limited transparency around SIFC initiatives could undermine policy predictability.

Nor can firms count on the courts. The International Commission of Jurists called the 26th constitutional amendment “a blow to judicial independence” and the 27th a “flagrant attack” on it, warning that the latter “will significantly impair the judiciary’s ability to hold the executive accountable.”

The writer is an Associate Professor at the University of Bristol and a member of the independent Economic Advisory Group (EAG).

Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, November 23rd, 2026

articles.title: ‘Global food import bill up 1.9pc in 2026’
articles.summary:
ISLAMABAD: Global expenditure on food imports is expected to increase moderately in 2026, with the global food import bill projected to reach $2,267 billion, up 1.9 per cent from the revised estimate of $2,224.8 billion, according to a new United Nations report.

According to the Food Outlook published by the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), import bills are expected to rise for most food groups in 2026, led by animal products and the oil seed complex, while cereals are also projected to record an increase.

Prospects for the remainder of 2026 and 2027 remain subject to several unce­rtainties, including firming prices of some food commodities, higher energy costs, weather conditions and financing constraints faced by some importing cou­ntries. Since mid-year, international prices of cereals and sugar have risen after remaining lower earlier in the year, while vegetable oil prices remained firm.

FAO warns energy costs and supply disruptions may raise bills in 2027

Higher energy prices have raised freight costs, while renewed disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz could restrict fertiliser supplies, affecting crop yields in 2027, despite fertiliser prices easing from their April peak.

The El Nino phenomenon, which is now established and strengthening, has added to the uncertainty, with its effects likely to vary across regions and crops.

FAO has urged timely financial support and expanded funding for food and fertiliser imports, warning that rising commodity prices and delays in assistance could increase pressure on vulnerable importing countries in 2027.

In most years of rising import bills over the past decade, high-income countries (HICs) accounted for between half and nearly all of the increase, including 79pc in 2025. However, their share of the increase in 2026 is projected at just 13pc, while upper-middle-income countries (UMICs) are expected to account for about two-thirds, the report says.

Import bills for cereals, the main staple foods, and oil seeds are rising for the first time in four years, while expenditure on vegetable oil imports continues to increase. The cereal import bill is expected to rise by 3pc, or $8.9bn, mainly reflecting a partial recovery in purchases by some UMICs following steep cuts in 2025.

In the oil seed complex, strong demand from processors and firm international prices are pushing import bills higher across both product groups.

The import bill for oil seeds and oleaginous fruits is projected to increase by 9.9pc, or $12.7bn, with most of the rise concentrated in middle-income economies. UMICs are expected to account for about 70pc of the increase, while lower-middle-income countries (LMICs) will contribute much of the remainder. Ani­mal products and other food items are also making substantial contributions to the increase in the global import bill.

In contrast, the import baskets of low- and middle-income countries are more heavily weighted towards staple foods. Their combined food import bill is projected to increase by 4.9pc, or $36.5bn, in 2026, led by oil seeds and cereals.

Most of this increase is expected to be concentrated in UMICs, whose import bill is projected to rise by 5.1pc, or $28.3bn, largely driven by the same food groups.

The food import bill of LMICs is expected to increase by 3.1pc, or $5.3bn, mainly due to higher spending on vegetable oils and oilseeds, while their import bills for cereals and sugar are projected to decline.

articles.title: Rice exports up by 0.35m tonnes in four months
articles.summary:
LAHORE: Pakistan’s total rice exports surged by 353,000 tonnes to reach 1,351,000 tonnes during the first four months (July-October) of the current fiscal year 2026-27.

The exports were propelled by a massive 62pc jump in Basmati shipments that defied severe maritime disruptions across the Red Sea, the Strait of Hormuz, and the broader Middle East.

According to trade figures for the July-Oct 2026 period, Basmati exports climbed by 116,000 tonnes compared to the corresponding period last year to stand at 301,000 tonnes. Meanwhile, non-Basmati shipments expanded by 140,000 tonnes year-on-year to reach 1,049,000 tonnes.

The remarkable expansion in Basmati export volume came despite heightened geopolitical tensions involving Iran, shipping route diversions, skyrocketing ocean freight charges, and elevated marine insurance premiums.

Market analysts attribute the resilience of the premium grain segment to a combination of domestic policy support and strong agricultural fundamentals. Specifically, the extension of the Drawback of Local Taxes and Levies (DLTL) scheme through September, substantial carryover stocks, an expanded cultivation area, double-cropping in select regions, higher per-acre yields, and favourable weather conditions combined and culminated in a bumper Basmati harvest.

In the coarse grain segment, Pakistani exporters managed to post a 16pc increase in non-Basmati shipments despite fierce price competition from heavily subsidised Indian rice as well as aggressive offers from Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia, and Myanmar.

The country-wise trade data for October 2026 shows that the Philippines emerged as the single largest buyer of Pakistani rice during the month with imports of 87,478 tonnes, followed by Tanzania at 43,747 tonnes and Kenya at 33,078 tonnes. Other major destinations during October included the United Arab Emirates with 25,305 tonnes, the European Union with 21,200 tonnes, Central Asia with 16,400 tonnes, China with 11,949 tonnes, and Saudi Arabia with 7,655 tonnes.

Published in Dawn, November 23rd, 2026

articles.title: India fails Gujarat pogrom survivor Bilkis Bano
articles.summary:
THE latest judicial intervention in the Bilkis Bano case raises questions extending well beyond the liberty of two convicted men. It once again tests India’s ability to deliver justice where communal violence, political power and the rights of vulnerable citizens intersect.

The Supreme Court’s decision to grant bail to Bipinchand Kanaiyalal Joshi and Pradip Ramanlal Modhiya, suspending their life sentences while their appeals are considered, does not amount to an acquittal.

Their convictions remain intact. The period already spent in prison and the severe disability of one appellant are relevant considerations in determining bail. Yet the legal permissibility of a decision does not automatically settle questions about its appropriateness or wider implications.

The Bilkis Bano case is exceptional not merely because of the brutality of the crime but because of the institutional failures surrounding its prosecution. The investigation had to be transferred out of Gujarat amid concerns about the possibility of a fair trial. Eleven men were convicted in 2008, and the Bombay High Court upheld their convictions in 2017.

That the survivor had to depend on judicial intervention to secure accountability was itself an indictment of the circumstances in which the crime was investigated. The subsequent premature release of all eleven convicts by the Gujarat government in 2022 compounded the damage. The Supreme Court’s decision in January 2024 to quash the remission orders demonstrated that executive discretion cannot override jurisdiction and legality. The public celebrations that greeted the convicts’ release raised disturbing questions about the social and political acceptance of impunity.

A fuller explanation of why suspension of sentence was warranted, given the gravity of the offences and the findings of the courts below, would have helped preserve public confidence. Communal violence cannot be addressed through periodic assurances of equality and constitutional protection. Their credibility depends on whether minorities can expect the law to protect them without having to wage a lifelong battle against institutional indifference.

This case is therefore a test of India’s constitutional promise that citizenship, dignity and access to justice do not depend on religious identity or political circumstances. The Supreme Court has not overturned the convictions. But it must ensure that its intervention does not deepen the perception that justice remains uncertain for survivors of communal violence. A system that repeatedly makes victims fight to preserve the fruits of a successful prosecution risks turning justice into an endurance test. No constitutional democracy should expect its citizens to pay such a price.

Published in Dawn, November 23rd, 2026

articles.title: Conveyor belt failure at bulk terminal disrupts coal imports
articles.summary:
• Coal discharge rate falls from 30,000 to 3,000 tonnes per day
• Jamshoro Power Company warns of $2-3 million demurrage on five incoming vessels; fears Rs2.2 billion monthly capacity payment losses

ISLAMABAD: The one and only coal-handling conveyor system at Pakistan Intern­ational Bulk Terminal (PIBT) at Port Qasim has been out of operation since Nov 18, disrupting imported coal supplies to power plants and industries, including cement and textiles, at a time when the power sector is already facing LNG supply disruptions and reduced hydroelectric availability.

Public and private sector power plants and their coal suppliers face mounting demurrage charges as vessels wait to discharge cargo, besides potential power generation problems, penalties and revenue losses.

With coal discharge rates at the terminal falling to one-tenth of their normal level, PIBT has dec­lined requests from power producers and suppliers to declare force majeure, which they say would help them pursue insurance claims and avoid financial losses.

According to PIBT, the terminal’s conveyor was damaged on Nov 18 during the discharge of coal from the vessel ‘Pegasus 8’ due to the “excessively dusty nat­ure of the Tanzanian coal” and the presence of “foreign materials, particularly sharp pieces of iron mixed with the cargo”. Repairs could take eight to 10 days, it said.

The state-run Jamshoro Power Company (JPC) reported that “vessels are being discharged manually at a significantly redu­ced rate (3,000MT per day versus the usual 30,000 MT per day)”.

In a letter to PIBT and the federal government, JPC said it dep­e­nded on “uninterrupted coal rec­eipts” through the terminal and that “this disruption puts that supply at immediate risk with serious and compounding consequences”.

The company said delayed coal receipts threatened critical stocks at its plant and, consequently, its operations and electricity generation for the national grid, besides causing port congestion and demurrage charges.

Slower discharge would lengthen queues at PIBT and expose waiting vessels to demurrage, increasing the cost of imported coal and, subsequently, electricity generation.

The company warned that del­ays to incoming shipments would also disrupt critical supplies and raise future procurement costs due to demurrage on vessels already en route or ordered.

“Based on our five upcoming vessels, demurrage exposure is expected to exceed $2-3 million (Rs556m-Rs834m). Furth­ermore, the disruption could result in potential capacity payment losses of approximately Rs2.2 billion per month to JPC due to insufficient coal inventory,” it said.

Given these consequences, JPC called on PIBT to declare force majeure in view of the nature and scale of the failure.

“JPC requests that PIBT form­ally declare force majeure without delay,” it said, warning “all dem­­urrage, detention, additional exp­enses, damages and losses ari­sing out of or attributable to the disruption shall be borne by PIBT”.

A shipping line has warned that it would seek compensation for the prolonged wait for discharge as well as any damage caused to its vessel during conventional unloading.

However, PIBT rejected the requests, saying the breakdown was not “an event giving rise to any declaration of force majeure on our part, as the discharging operations are ongoing, albeit thr­ough conventional means”, which were “understandably going to be slower”.

Sources said the terminal’s dependence on a single jetty, coal berth and conveyor system had compounded the problem. A second conveyor proposed in 2021 to increase annual handling capacity from 12m to 17m tonnes has yet to be built.

Published in Dawn, November 23rd, 2026

articles.title: Varma century in vain as Pakistan Shaheens down India A in Asia Cup Rising Stars clash
articles.summary:
Pakistan Shaheens overcame a late challenge from Tilak Varma to beat India A by 48 runs in their Asia Cup Rising Stars match in Doha on Sunday, defending a total of 313 after bowling out their opponents with five balls to spare.

Skipper Varma struck a century before becoming the last man dismissed for 100 off 149 balls, while Shahbaz Ahmed made 56 in a seventh-wicket stand that briefly revived India’s hopes.

But Pakistan’s bowlers held their nerve in the closing overs, with Hasan Nawaz claiming three wickets and Ali Raza taking three for 56.

India’s chase had begun to unravel after an explosive start from Abhishek Sharma. The left-hander made 70 off just 42 balls, hitting six fours and six sixes, but his dismissal at 93-3 in the 16th over left the visitors with considerable ground to make up.

Pakistan’s spinners then tightened their grip. Sufyan Moqim bowled Kumar Kushagra for two before Hasan removed Rinku Singh and Suryansh Shedge, leaving India struggling at 129-6 in the 26th over.

Varma, who had struggled to find the boundary during the middle overs, found support in Shahbaz.

The pair added 112 runs for the seventh wicket, taking the score to 241 before Raza broke the stand by having Shahbaz caught by Hasan for 56 off 49 balls.

Raza then bowled Vipraj Nigam for a duck, while Imran Randhawa dismissed Harshit Rana to leave India nine down.

Varma reached his second century of the tournament, but the milestone offered little consolation as Ahmed Daniyal had him caught by wicket-keeper Rohail Nazir in the 50th over to seal Pakistan’s victory.

Controversial toss

Earlier, Pakistan had posted 313 after winning a dramatic toss and electing to bat on a slightly dry surface.

The toss decision was initially called incorrectly by the match referee, who announced tails after Varma flipped the coin on Pakistan skipper Abdul Samad’s call of heads.

Samad pointed out the error and the officials corrected the decision in Pakistan’s favour. The captains did not shake hands, continuing the protocol observed in recent encounters between the sides.

Pakistan’s openers Shamyl Hussain and Maaz Sadaqat gave their side a flying start, putting on 66 for the first wicket. Shamyl made 33 off 23 balls before Ayush Badoni had him caught by Harshit Rana at short third. Rana then trapped Rohail leg-before for a duck, with Pakistan on 67-2.

The exchanges between Rana and the Pakistan batters had added an edge to the powerplay, with the Indian fast bowler involved in heated verbal exchanges and giving Shamyl an animated send-off.

Maaz and Hasan rebuilt the innings, with the former scoring 59 off 63 balls for his second successive half-century.

Hasan went on to make 79 off 82 deliveries, while Farhan Yousaf’s 56 off 48 balls and Imran’s quickfire 23 helped Pakistan push past 300, which was proven enough for the side at the end.

articles.title: More than 2,300 Indian Sikh pilgrims arrive in Pakistan to mark Guru Nanak's birthday
articles.summary:
LAHORE: Over 2,300 Indian Sikh pilgrims arrived in Pakistan through the Wagah Border on Sunday to attend celebrations marking the 557th birth anniversary of Baba Guru Nanak Dev Ji, the founder of Sikhism.

The visiting pilgrims were received by Evacuee Trust Property Board (ETPB) Chairman Qamar Zaman, Secretary Nasir Mushtaq, Pakistan Sikh Gurdwara Prabandhak Committee (PSGPC) President and Punjab Minorities Minister Sardar Ramesh Singh Arora, the committee’s secretary general Satwant Kaur and other officials at the Wagah border, where the jatha leaders were presented with bouquets.

Indian Sikh pilgrims wave to the camera after arriving in Lahore through the Wagah Border to attend celebrations marking the 557th birth anniversary of Baba Guru Nanak Dev Ji, on Nov 22. — White Star

According to ETPB spokesperson Amir Hashmi, 2,339 Sikh pilgrims arrived from India here on Sunday to take part in the festivities in Nankana Sahib.

The Pakistan High Commission in New Delhi had reportedly issued around 3,100 visas to Indian Sikhs.

Special counters were set up at the Wagah Border to facilitate immigration and baggage screening, while Rangers were deployed to ensure security.

Indian Sikh pilgrims arrive in Lahore through the Wagah Border to attend celebrations marking the 557th birth anniversary of Baba Guru Nanak Dev Ji, on Nov 22. — White Star

The ETPB had also established currency exchange facilities at the border, while its teams promptly issued identity cards and bus tickets to the pilgrims to ensure a smooth onward journey, he added.

“The pilgrims subsequently left for Nankana Sahib in three separate convoys under tight security to attend the main ceremony on Nov 24 marking Baba Guru Nanak’s birth anniversary at Gurdwara Janam Asthan, his birthplace,” Hashmi said.

He added that over 20,000 Sikhs — from Pakistan and across the globe — are expected to take part in the formal festivities, which begin today and continue until Nov 24.

Indian Sikh pilgrims gather after arriving in Lahore through the Wagah Border to attend celebrations marking the 557th birth anniversary of Baba Guru Nanak Dev Ji, on Nov 22. — White Star

Federal Minister for Religious Affairs Sardar Muhammad Yousuf, along with other federal and provincial ministers, will attend the event as special guests.

The event participants will perform religious rituals, including Bhog and Akhand Path Sahib, followed by a traditional palanquin procession, known as Nagar Kirtan.

Speaking on the occasion, ETPB Chairman Zaman said the board was making every effort to ensure that the visiting pilgrims faced no inconvenience during their stay in Pakistan.

He said the Indian Sikh pilgrims would return home with fond memories of love, peace and brotherhood.

Indian Sikh pilgrims including a wheelchair-bound woman arrive in Lahore through the Wagah Border to attend celebrations marking the 557th birth anniversary of Baba Guru Nanak Dev Ji, on Nov 22. — White Star

Minister Arora urged the Indian government to immediately reopen the Kartarpur Corridor, which provides Sikh pilgrims with access to Gurdwara Darbar Sahib in Kartarpur, one of the holiest sites in Sikhism.

India suspended movement through the Kartarpur Corridor in May 2025 amid the four-day conflict between the countries.

Kaldeep Singh Gurgaj, a leader of the Akal Takht authority from India, said the Sikh community shared a deep bond of reverence with Pakistan, where its members were always treated with respect and honour.

“Our gurdwaras in Pakistan are safe and preserved in their original state,” he said.

Parmjeet Singh, a leader of a Delhi Gurdwara Management Committee delegation, said Pakistan held special significance for Sikhs as the land associated with their guru.

“Pakistan is the land of our guru, and we love it very much,” he said.

Indian Sikh pilgrims arrive in Lahore through the Wagah Border to attend celebrations marking the 557th birth anniversary of Baba Guru Nanak Dev Ji, on Nov 22. — White Star

After attending the main ceremony, the Sikh pilgrims will visit Gurdwara Sacha Sauda in Farooqabad on Nov 25 before proceeding to Hassan Abdal, where they will stay overnight at Gurdwara Panja Sahib.

They will travel to Gurdwara Darbar Sahib in Kartarpur, Narowal, on Nov 27.

The visiting devotees will then spend Nov 29 and 30 visiting various historic gurdwaras in Lahore before returning to India through the Wagah border by road on Dec 1.

Sikh pilgrims frequently visit Pakistan to observe events of religious significance. In June, around 600 Sikhs arrived from India to observe the death anniversary of Guru Arjan Dev Ji, known as Jore Mela; before that, about 2,800 visas were issued to pilgrims to celebrate the Baisakhi festival in April.

articles.summary:
By Moses Akaigwe

The Director-General of the National Automotive Design and Development Council (NADDC), Chief Joseph Oluwemimo Osanipin, and the Corps Marshal of the Federal Road Safety Corps (FRSC), Shehu Mohammed, have confirmed their attendance at the 19th Nigeria Auto Journalists Association (NAJA) International Auto Awards, scheduled for Thursday, December 3, 2026, in Lagos.

The two prominent government officials are expected to join leading automobile manufacturers, distributors, policymakers, industry captains and other stakeholders at the prestigious ceremony, which will hold at the Civic Centre, Victoria Island, Lagos.

Osanipin’s confirmation is particularly significant, given NADDC’s strategic role in driving the Federal Government’s automotive industrialisation agenda, including local vehicle assembly, technology development, capacity building and the transition towards cleaner mobility.

Under his leadership, the Council has continued to engage industry stakeholders on initiatives aimed at strengthening Nigeria’s automotive value chain, promoting local manufacturing and encouraging investments in alternative-energy vehicles.

Similarly, the presence of the FRSC Corps Marshal as a Special Guest underscores the importance of road safety in the development of Nigeria’s automotive and transportation sectors.

The FRSC remains a critical stakeholder in vehicle regulation, road safety enforcement, driver education and the promotion of safer motoring practices across the country.

Chairman of the 2026 NAJA Awards Planning Committee, Frank Kintum, said the committee was encouraged by the confirmation of the two senior government officials, noting that their participation would further enhance the significance of the annual industry gathering.

He said preparations were in top gear to deliver a memorable ceremony that would recognise outstanding achievements, innovation and professionalism across Nigeria’s automotive industry.

The NAJA International Auto Awards, now in its 19th edition, has evolved into a major platform for celebrating excellence among automobile manufacturers, vehicle assemblers, distributors, after-sales service providers and other players in the automotive value chain.

Chairman of NAJA, Theodore Opara, said the awards remained committed to recognising organisations and individuals making measurable contributions to the growth and transformation of the Nigerian automotive industry.

The 2026 edition is expected to attract major players across the sector, with awards covering vehicle manufacturing and assembly, automotive distribution, alternative-energy mobility, after-sales services, commercial vehicles and individual industry contributions.

A major attraction at this year’s ceremony is expected to be the Car of the Year category, which is likely to generate keen competition among established automotive brands and emerging manufacturers.

Other categories include Bus of the Year, Pickup of the Year, SUV of the Year, among others.

articles.title: Nigerian Sinotrucks, Sterling Bank partner to expand vehicle ownership, advance mobility solutions
articles.summary:
By Moses Akaigwe

Nigerian Sinotrucks Limited has entered into a strategic partnership with Sterling Bank Limited to widen access to vehicle ownership and advance integrated mobility and financial solutions in Nigeria, in a collaboration both organisations say will create new opportunities for individuals, entrepreneurs and businesses.

Collaboration seeks to bridge vehicle acquisition financing gaps, strengthen commercial mobility and unlock new opportunities for businesses and individuals.

The agreement, formalised through the signing of a Memorandum of Agreement (MoA), underscores a shared ambition to address one of the major constraints in the mobility market: access to appropriate financing for vehicle acquisition.

Anchored on the theme, “From Partnership to Progress: Advancing Integrated Mobility and Financial Solutions”, the collaboration brings together Nigerian Sinotrucks Limited’s commercial vehicle expertise and market presence with Sterling Bank’s financial capabilities to create a more accessible vehicle ownership proposition.

For Nigerian Sinotrucks Limited, the partnership represents another significant step in its broader ambition to deepen its footprint in Nigeria’s automotive and transportation ecosystem, while making its vehicle solutions more accessible to a wider customer base.

Speaking on the significance of the agreement, the Managing Director of Nigerian Sinotrucks Limited, Alfred Okugbeni, said the collaboration was driven by the company’s determination to go beyond vehicle supply and provide solutions that respond to the broader needs of customers.

“At Nigerian Sinotrucks, we understand that access to reliable vehicles is only one part of the mobility equation. Access to appropriate financing is equally important. Our partnership with Sterling Bank is a deliberate effort to bridge that gap and create greater opportunities for individuals and businesses to acquire the vehicles they need to grow.

“We believe that when mobility and finance work together, the benefits extend beyond vehicle ownership. They translate into stronger businesses, improved logistics, greater productivity and wider economic opportunities,” he said.

For Sterling Bank, the agreement reinforces its commitment to using strategic partnerships to deliver financial solutions that address real economic needs, with transportation and mobility forming an important part of that agenda.

Speaking at the signing, Akporee Idenedo, Divisional Head, Commercial Banking at Sterling Bank, said the partnership reflects the Bank’s conviction that financial institutions and mobility providers have to work together to unlock growth.

“Transportation is the backbone of commerce. Every truck on the road is a supply chain moving, a business expanding, jobs being created and sustained. Yet for many entrepreneurs and businesses, the cost of acquiring the right vehicle remains a major barrier. Through this partnership with Nigerian Sinotrucks, we are bringing financing directly to the point of need, so customers can access quality vehicles on terms that are practical and fit their realities.

“At Sterling Bank, we believe the most meaningful financial solutions are the ones that solve real problems. This collaboration lets us support individuals and businesses who want to own their vehicles, while helping to build a more efficient and productive transportation ecosystem for the country,” he said.

The agreement also builds on Nigerian Sinotrucks Limited’s broader customer-support proposition, which extends beyond vehicle sales to include after-sales services, maintenance, genuine spare parts and technical training for drivers and mechanics.

These capabilities are particularly important in commercial transportation, where vehicle reliability, maintenance support and operational efficiency have direct implications for business performance. 

The company, which is wholly Nigerian-owned and was incorporated in 2012, is a Federal Government-recognised vehicle manufacturer and assembler, as well as an authorised distributor of Sinotruk products in Nigeria. It received Federal Government recognition as a vehicle assembler in January 2015. 

Its portfolio spans heavy-duty commercial vehicles, including HOWO tractor heads, dump trucks, tippers, cargo trucks, tankers and other specialised vehicles. The company has also expanded its alternative-energy offerings, with CNG and LNG-powered trucks, alongside its recent introduction of Sitrak electric commercial trucks into the Nigerian market. 

This evolving product offering reflects the company’s determination to respond to changing demands in the transportation industry, particularly as businesses seek more efficient, cost-effective and sustainable ways to move goods and manage logistics operations.

The partnership with Sterling Bank is expected to complement this ambition by bringing financing more directly into the vehicle acquisition process, helping to address the capital constraints that can prevent individuals and businesses from investing in the vehicles they need.

Industry observers have increasingly pointed to the need for stronger collaboration between vehicle distributors, financial institutions and other mobility stakeholders to address the high cost of vehicle acquisition and improve access to transportation assets.

Against this backdrop, the Nigerian Sinotrucks-Sterling Bank partnership represents a practical approach to connecting vehicle solutions with financial accessibility, with the potential to support businesses across logistics, manufacturing, distribution, construction and other sectors dependent on transportation.

The signing ceremony was marked by the exchange of duly executed copies of the agreement, followed by a handshake between representatives of both organisations and a brief celebratory moment, symbolising the formal commencement of the collaboration.

More than a ceremonial milestone, the occasion represented a shared commitment to building a stronger mobility ecosystem in which financial access and reliable vehicle solutions work together to unlock progress.

For Nigerian Sinotrucks Limited, the partnership reinforces its position as a mobility solutions provider with ambitions that extend beyond the supply of commercial vehicles to supporting the wider transportation and automotive value chain.

As the collaboration takes shape, both organisations will be looking to translate the agreement into tangible customer benefits, expanded access to vehicle ownership and greater opportunities for businesses to move, grow and compete.

From partnership to progress, the message is clear: when mobility meets finance, progress moves forward.

According to the Managing Director, Nigerian Sinotrucks Limited, Alfred Okugbeni, ‘Nigerian Sinotrucks is not simply putting more vehicles on Nigerian roads; it is helping create the financial and mobility partnerships that make progress possible.’’

articles.title: Versat Automobile signs exclusive distribution agreement with EXEED
articles.summary:
By Moses Akaigwe

Versat Automobile Limited has signed an exclusive Distribution Agreement with Chery Group, formally securing its appointment as the authorised General Distributor of EXEED in Nigeria. 

The agreement marks a significant milestone in the company’s expansion within the Nigerian automotive industry and lays the foundation for introducing the premium brand to the Nigerian market in 2027.

The signing ceremony took place in Wuhu, Anhui Province, China. Alhaji Francis TntñtjlOgboro, Non-Executive Director of Versat Automobile Limited, signed on behalf of Versat, and Mr. Heaven Hai, Regional Director of Chery Group, signed on behalf of Chery Group. Mr. Umoh Ekanem, Head of Commercial Vehicles at Versat Automobile Limited, and Mr. Shane Ni, National Director at Chery Group, were also in attendance. 

Under the agreement, Versat Automobile will be responsible for the distribution and representation of EXEED in Nigeria. The mandate covers passenger cars (electric vehicles, hybrid vehicles, internal combustion engine vehicles l) and after-sales support. 

This framework establishes the brand’s local operations and reflects a shared vision to introduce a premium automotive offering that responds to the changing expectations of Nigerian consumers, with better access to quality vehicles, innovative mobility solutions, and dependable ownership support.

Speaking on the significance of the agreement, Alhaji Francis Ogboro said: “This partnership represents an important development in our commitment īto bringing quality automotive brands and innovative mobility solutions to Nigeria. 

Securing the exclusive distribution rights for EXEED is a responsibility we take seriously, and we are committed to establishing the brand on a strong foundation. We recognise the opportunities within the Nigerian automotive market and look forward to building a lasting partnership that delivers value to customers while contributing positively to the industry’s development.”

Nigeria remains an important market for automotive distribution, supported by a large population, growing urban centres, expanding business activity and evolving consumer expectations. As mobility needs change, vehicle quality, technological advancement, reliability, efficiency and dependable After-Sales services matter more than ever. Against this backdrop, EXEED broadens the range of premium choices available to Nigerian consumers and contributes to the development of the country’s automotive distribution landscape.

For Versat Automobile, the agreement is more than an addition to its portfolio. It is a strategic commitment to building a recognised automotive brand in Nigeria through structured distribution, market development and sustained customer engagement. As General Distributor, Versat will lead EXEED’s market representation and distribution activities, working closely with Chery Group to put the necessary commercial and operational framework in place. A key feature of the agreement is that it goes beyond vehicle distribution to include After-Sales (Services and Genuine Parts). A successful brand introduction takes more than making  vehicles available for purchase. It also needs the infrastructure, technical capability and service standards to support ownership throughout the vehicle’s lifecycle. Versat will develop an after-sales framework for EXEED customers, including genuine parts, technical support and service arrangements designed to maintain performance, reliability and customer confidence.

The inclusion of Electric and Hybrid Vehicles also reflects the changing direction of the industry. As alternative powertrains gain attention, the Nigerian market will need distributors able to support different vehicle technologies and their ownership requirements. Versat will work with Chery Group to align its local operations with the brand’s standards while accounting for the needs of Nigerian customers and the realities of the local market.

Mr. Umoh Ekanem said: “The agreement gives us a clear mandate to develop EXEED’s presence in Nigeria across vehicle distribution and After-Sales. Our focus is on putting the right structures, resources and support systems in place to ensure that customers receive a complete ownership experience. We are working towards building a distribution and service framework that reflects the standards of the brand and provides the level of support Nigerian customers expect.”

Speaking on the partnership, Mr. Shane Ni commented: “We believe that EXEED’s collaboration with the Versat team will bring more opportunities to the region and better embody our philosophy of ‘in somewhere, be somewhere, for somewhere.”

The signing took place during the 2026 EXEED International User Summit, which brought together 120 user representatives from 26 countries and regions. During the summit, EXEED unveiled its “Future Luxury” design language, rooted in its Perpetua philosophy, and held its 12th track experience event at a professional circuit. 

Versat Automobile and Chery Group will continue preparing for the official introduction of EXEED in Nigeria in 2027. The launch will be the next major milestone, giving the brand a formal introduction to Nigerian  consumers, automotive stakeholders, business leaders and the media. 

Until then, Versat will continue work on distribution planning, customer engagement, after-sales readiness and other operational requirements. 

Further details on the launch, product availability, distribution arrangements and customer-facing activities will be shared through the company’s official channels in due course.

Alhaji Ogboro added: “We see significant potential for EXEED in Nigeria, and we intend to build a brand presence that is both commercially sustainable and responsive to the needs of the market. We are approaching this partnership with a long-term perspective, recognising that establishing customer confidence requires consistency, quality and dependable support. 

We look forward to introducing EXEED to Nigerians and building a relationship with customers that extends well beyond the point of purchase.”

The signing marks an important new chapter for Versat Automobile. With both organisations committed to 2the partnership, the focus now shifts to turning the agreement into a structured market presence supported by effective distribution, reliable after-sales services and a strong customer-focused approach.
