articles.title: Beyond the showroom: Why car buyers in Nigeria must demand more than 4 wheels
articles.summary:
By Moses Akaigwe

For many Nigerians, buying a brand-new vehicle represents a major financial commitment, often involving years of savings, bank loans or carefully planned investments. Yet, the excitement of driving a new car home can quickly turn into frustration when the vehicle develops a fault and the dealer suddenly becomes difficult to reach.

This growing disconnect between the promises made at the point of sale and the support customers receive afterwards has brought the issue of after-sales service into sharper focus in Nigeria’s automotive industry.

Consumer rights advocate, Akonte Ekine, knows this experience firsthand. He recalled purchasing a brand-new vehicle through a bank only for it to develop a problem barely two weeks after delivery. His attempts to obtain assistance from the seller and insurance company, he said, yielded little response.

“I once spent my good money to buy a brand-new car through a bank and just two weeks after, the car developed a problem. I complained to the seller and to my insurance but they didn’t even show interest in the situation,” Ekine told BusinessDay.

His experience raises an important question for automobile manufacturers, distributors and dealers: What happens to the customer after the money has changed hands?

For Ekine, the answer should be straightforward. Businesses must deliver the quality of service promised to customers, regardless of the market in which they operate.

“The consumer is the same everywhere. What he or she wants is simple quality service based on the brand promise,” he said.

The concern goes beyond individual experiences. In Nigeria, where vehicle ownership involves considerable financial sacrifice, access to genuine spare parts, qualified technicians, warranty services and timely repairs can significantly influence the overall ownership experience.

Importantly, consumers are not without legal protection.

The Executive Vice Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC), Mr Tunji Bello, has reinforced this position, insisting that businesses cannot evade their statutory obligations through restrictive company policies.

Speaking at a stakeholders’ engagement organised by the FCCPC and Lagos State Consumer Protection Agency (LASCOPA) in Lagos on July 29, 2026, Bello said consumers were entitled to appropriate remedies when goods failed to meet legally required standards.

“They must also know that where the law gives them the right to a refund, replacement, or repair, that right will be respected,” he stated.

He further emphasised that: “Every transaction also carries an implied warranty that goods supplied will be of acceptable quality and fit for the purpose for which they were purchased.”

The Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act 2018 provides for consumers’ entitlement to goods of acceptable quality, while Section 132 establishes an implied warranty of quality and provides remedies for qualifying defective products.

For the automotive industry, this should serve as more than a regulatory reminder. It is a call to rethink customer relationships and recognise that a vehicle purchase is the beginning, not the end, of a business relationship.

Automobile brands that invest in responsive customer care, transparent warranty arrangements, accessible service centres and reliable spare-parts networks stand a better chance of earning consumer confidence and securing repeat patronage.

Ultimately, the real test of an automobile brand is not simply how attractive its vehicles look in the showroom or how aggressively they are marketed. It is how the company treats customers when the excitement of a new purchase gives way to the realities of vehicle ownership.

For Nigerian buyers, the lesson is equally important: before collecting the keys, ask what happens when something goes wrong. A good vehicle should come with the assurance that the people who sold it will not disappear when their customers need them most.

articles.title: Amnesty condemns killing of village head, six others in Niger village
articles.summary:
Amnesty International has condemned the killing of seven people in an attack on Lumma Ba’are village in the Borgu Local Government Area of Niger State, calling on the authorities to do more to end escalating bloody attacks on villages and communities across parts of the state.

This is contained in a Monday statement shared by the rights group on X.

Amnesty said the brutal attack carried by gunmen widely referred to as bandits, which occurred around 5:00pm on Saturday, also resulted in many homes and shops getting burnt to ashes.

“The Nigerian authorities must do more to end escalating bloody attacks on villages and communities across some parts of Niger state,” Amnesty said.

The organisation stated, “The gunmen particularly targeted a mosque in which people were performing dawn prayers and killed the village head and other worshippers.

“This attack had torn the community apart, with many people still missing. The gunmen also kidnapped unspecified number of people.”

It added, “Clearly, the spate and scale of these attacks are indication that the Nigerian authorities have left rural communities in the north at the mercy of rampaging gunmen who have been killing people and burning down entire villages.”

Amnesty said terrifying attacks on rural communities in the north of Nigeria have been going on for years, describing the ongoing failure of security forces to take sufficient steps to protect villagers from these predictable attacks as utterly shameful.

“Gunmen and other armed groups have been intensifying bloody attacks on Borgu. The majority of the people in these communities depend on farming for their livelihoods, but they are now too afraid to go to the fields.

“The government has an obligation to protect its population. The rising death toll in the north of Nigeria shows just how badly the authorities are failing in this responsibility,” it further stated.

articles.title: Afreximbank unit completes equity investment in D’Banj’s C.R.E.A.M. Platform
articles.summary:
By Faheem Lawal

CANEX Creations Inc., a subsidiary of Afreximbank’s Fund for Export Development in Africa (FEDA), has completed a strategic equity investment in C.R.E.A.M. Platform Limited, the Nigerian digital platform founded by Afrobeats star D’Banj.

The completion was announced at a ceremony during CANEX WKND 2026 in Lagos on 6 November. CANEX Creations, set up to invest in, develop and commercialise African intellectual property, was represented by its Chief Executive Officer, Osahon Akpata. D’Banj, whose full name is Oladapo Daniel Oyebanjo, represented C.R.E.A.M., which he founded.

The investment closes out a deal first announced at the Afreximbank Annual Meetings in 2025, when the two sides signed a term sheet setting out the framework for the transaction.

The funds are expected to support the platform’s scaling, including the rollout of CREAM 3.0, expansion of services and content, and targeted marketing to grow users and revenue. C.R.E.A.M. says it will also gain institutional backing as it works to support African creative talent.

D’Banj cast the deal as bigger than a signing. “As I have always said, content is the new crude,” he said. “This is beyond a deal signing. It is history being made: Africa’s creativity becomes Africa’s capital. African creatives now have access to the financial infrastructure to compete globally, while owning and retaining our IP in Africa.”

C.R.E.A.M. gives independent creatives tools to showcase their skills, distribute content, connect with industry opportunities and earn income. Its monetisation channels include content distribution, caller ring back tunes, streaming platforms, copyright protection, royalty collection and intellectual property management.

Akpata said the investment reflects C.R.E.A.M.’s position as “an African-owned platform that discovers talent, distributes and monetises their creative content”, and fits CANEX Creations’ mandate to back commercially viable, high-impact projects in Africa’s creative and cultural industries. He said it also supports Afreximbank’s wider creative-economy strategy of building the infrastructure, platforms and market links that African creative businesses need to scale, and the Bank Group’s aim of turning creative potential into enterprises, jobs and income.

Akpata added that C.R.E.A.M.’s mobile-first, USSD-enabled model suits African market realities and reaches emerging and grassroots talent that international distribution platforms may underserve. He expressed confidence that the investment would strengthen the platform’s ability to connect creatives with discovery, distribution, audience engagement, monetisation and future financing, and support its expansion beyond Nigeria.

articles.title: Makinde kicks against politicians’ children working in govt offices
articles.summary:
Oyo State Governor and Allied Peoples Movement (APM) presidential candidate, Seyi Makinde, has said he does not support the practice of children of political office holders occupying positions around their parents in government offices.

Makinde said his children should be allowed to pursue their individual ambitions and build independent careers without relying on their father’s political position.

He made the remarks in an 87-second video clip from an interview on The Rooftop, which he shared on his X account on Monday.

During the interview, the governor said his children preferred to maintain private lives and contribute to society independently rather than associate themselves with government offices.

“Of course I am. That’s why you can’t see any of my children, you know, around the government offices,” he said.

Asked whether he considered it inappropriate for children of people in power to work around government offices, Makinde replied, “No, I am totally, totally opposed to it.”

He said he would want anyone who could identify his children in Oyo State to come forward, maintaining that they were pursuing their own paths in life.

“For my children, they are on their own trajectory in life. My own job is to advise them, give them necessary support, and with the way they have been brought up, we know that they will go on to make their own mark in life,” he said.

However, Makinde said he would support his children if they independently decided to venture into politics, although he would not encourage them to do so.

“No, I won’t advise them to go into politics, but if they choose politics, I will support them,” he added.

His comments come amid renewed attention on the participation of children of prominent Nigerian politicians in elective offices ahead of the 2027 general elections.

The post Makinde kicks against politicians’ children working in govt offices appeared first on The Sun Nigeria.

articles.title: 2027: Tinubu orders APC leaders to reconcile, mobilise for victory
articles.summary:
President Bola Tinubu has directed leaders of the All Progressives Congress (APC) to resolve internal disputes, reconcile aggrieved members and mobilise voters ahead of the 2027 general election.

He also urged party members and supporters to obtain their Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs) and work towards securing overwhelming votes for the ruling party, warning against complacency.

Tinubu gave the directives on Sunday at a prayer session organised by his extended family at the Yoruba Tennis Club, Onikan, Lagos.

Acknowledging divisions within the party, the president urged its leaders to put aside personal differences, embrace forgiveness and strengthen internal cohesion to consolidate the gains of his administration ahead of the election.

“We must generate enough votes to overwhelm the opponents,” he said, reaffirming his commitment to providing purposeful leadership, strengthening national unity and justice, and building a prosperous country for Nigerians.

He called on party members to return to door-to-door mobilisation, urging them to visit their neighbours and encourage eligible voters to collect their PVCs.

“The challenge of today is much easier than that of yesterday, but we cannot take it for granted. You must knock on your neighbour’s door, tell them to collect their PVC.

“If you have PVC, you have the power of January 16th and February 6th, and that’s what I want to ask you to exercise,” he said.

Tinubu specifically directed his Special Adviser on Political Matters, Alhaji Ibrahim Kabiru Masari, and former Minister of Defence, Alhaji Abubakar Badaru, who were among those present, to help resolve disagreements within the party.

Apparently reacting to reports of a disagreement between Katsina State Governor Dikko Umar Radda and Masari, the president ordered his aide to return home and reconcile with the governor.

“Alhaji Kabiru Masari, go back home and reconcile with everybody. That is the president’s order. When you finish that, you move to Jigawa.

“You move to other places and reconcile them, beg them because we have to reconcile and every anger must dissipate and evaporate,” Tinubu said.

He gave a similar directive to Badaru, a former governor of Jigawa State, urging him to work towards resolving differences among party leaders.

The president cited his own experience of overcoming political disagreements in 2021 and 2022, recalling his relationship with the late former President Muhammadu Buhari as an example of the importance of forgiveness and political accommodation.

“I had my own anger in 2021-22. I can invoke the memory of Muhammadu Buhari. When he called me, I said, okay, he said you are the coordinator, co-chairman of the campaign. I said, oh yeah. I had my own anger full of hurt feeling, but I let go,” he said.

Tinubu also drew lessons from his recent visit to the Holy Ka’aba, emphasising faith, gratitude and forgiveness. He urged supporters to extend to others the forgiveness they seek from Almighty Allah.

He warned that political disagreements should not undermine the party’s collective objectives, calling on members to replace resentment with reconciliation and renewed commitment to its electoral ambition.

On voter participation, the president expressed concern about low turnout in Lagos State, questioning why an electorate of about seven million registered voters would produce only between 100,000 and 200,000 votes.

“Even if you win, and you say a win is a win. No. You have to generate the maximum. And to all of you, it’s not anger. Anger will not do it,” he said.

He urged party supporters to encourage eligible Nigerians to register and collect their PVCs, stressing that electoral victory should be backed by substantial voter participation.

Recalling his use of the Emilokan slogan during the 2022 presidential campaign, Tinubu told supporters that the responsibility of securing his re-election now rested with them.

“It is now your turn (Eyinlokan) to make the re-election possible,” he said, appealing to Lagos residents to turn out in large numbers on election day.

The president also recalled the economic difficulties and cash shortages that preceded the 2023 general election, attributing his eventual victory to divine intervention and the determination of his supporters.

“We invoked the spirit of Almighty Allah and said, ‘Kun faya kun (Be, and it becomes). It got us there, and we have the presidency. Allah gives power to whom he wants, and he takes it from whoever he wants,” he said.

Tinubu thanked members of his family for their longstanding prayers and support throughout his political career. He also urged young Nigerians to embrace leadership responsibilities and contribute to national development.

Reaffirming his administration’s commitment to infrastructure and development, he expressed confidence in the country’s ability to overcome its challenges through collective effort.

“We can do it in this country. There’s nothing we cannot do. Nothing. Go to Abuja, we’ve moved mountains. In Lagos, we’ve tamed the Atlantic. In Abuja, we’ve moved mountains to give way to development. Nothing we cannot do if we put our heart at it,” he added.

The president thanked the organisers and clerics who prayed for him, his administration and the country.

The session was attended by Muslim and Christian clerics, as well as the governors of Lagos, Kaduna, Kwara, Ogun and Imo states.

Other dignitaries included the National Security Adviser, Mallam Nuhu Ribadu; Chief of Staff to the President, Femi Gbajabiamila; Lagos Deputy Governor, Kadiri Obafemi Hamzat; Minister of Education, Tunji Alausa; and Speaker of the Lagos State House of Assembly, Mudashiru Obasa.

Also present were the Grand Chief Imam of Lagos, Sheikh Sulaimon Oluwatoyin Abou-Nolla; Chairman of the Board of Trustees of the Coalition of Northern Groups, Dr Nasturah Ashir Sharriff; members of the Tinubu family and party faithful.

Earlier, Lagos State Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu described the president as an epitome of justice, fairness, equity and inclusive governance, saying the virtues were essential to building a united, peaceful and prosperous Nigeria.

Badaru said Northerners appreciated Tinubu’s support for Buhari’s victories in the 2015 and 2019 presidential elections. He urged voters in the region to reciprocate the gesture and support Tinubu’s re-election bid.

The chairman of the occasion, 94-year-old elder statesman Alhaji Lateef Femi Okunnu, pledged to canvass votes for the president and vote for him on January 16, 2027, saying Tinubu had done enough to merit another term.

Okunnu also stressed the need for justice and praised the administration’s focus on the economy and infrastructure, particularly the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway and the Sokoto-Badagry Superhighway, as well as efforts to strengthen the naira and foreign reserves.

In their vote of thanks, representatives of the Tinubu family, Alhaji Rafiu Tinubu and Alhaja Iyalode Bintu Tinubu, thanked God for the family’s blessings and urged Nigerians to support the president’s efforts to deliver the dividends of democracy.

Chairman of the Lagos State Government House Chapel, Rev. Honsu Oluremi, referenced the Bible and urged Nigerians to pray for the success of their leaders.

The coordinator of the prayer session, Abou-Nolla, also read from the Qur’an and prayed for Allah to grant the president success and good health.

The post 2027: Tinubu orders APC leaders to reconcile, mobilise for victory appeared first on The Sun Nigeria.

articles.title: 2027: Lagos APC declares ‘Awa lo kan’ movement for Tinubu
articles.summary:
The Lagos State chapter of the All Progressives Congress (APC) has declared that President Bola Tinubu’s re-election bid in 2027 has evolved from a personal political ambition into a collective national movement, describing the emerging slogan as “Awa lo kan” (It is our turn).

The party said the political movement that began with Tinubu’s “Emi lo kan” declaration ahead of the 2023 presidential election had grown into a shared determination among Nigerians to consolidate the administration’s reforms and sustain the country’s progress.

Lagos APC spokesman, Seye Oladejo, stated this on Monday, saying the shift reflected a defining moment in the country’s political evolution, where an individual aspiration had become a collective conviction.

According to him, the emerging “Awa lo kan” sentiment represents Nigerians’ desire to protect the gains of the Tinubu administration, expand opportunities and sustain the country’s journey towards prosperity.

The party said the movement was about ordinary Nigerians, including traders seeking a more predictable business environment, farmers demanding improved productivity, graduates looking for jobs, entrepreneurs seeking affordable credit and families hoping for a better standard of living.

“It is about a nation that cannot afford the luxury of abandoning its reform trajectory halfway through the journey,” the party stated.

The Lagos APC maintained that Tinubu had demonstrated the political will to confront structural challenges that previous administrations either postponed or approached with hesitation.

It cited the removal of the fuel subsidy, unification of the foreign exchange markets and investments in infrastructure, education, healthcare, agriculture and economic diversification as some of the administration’s major interventions.

However, the party acknowledged the difficulties associated with the reforms, saying responsible leadership required recognising both the present challenges and the opportunities being created for the future.

“The answer to transitional difficulties cannot be a reckless return to the policies and practices that contributed to the problems being collectively overcome,” it said.

On national unity, the APC said Tinubu’s administration had demonstrated commitment to inclusivity and representation across geopolitical zones, ethnic groups, religious affiliations, gender and social backgrounds.

It argued that the administration’s appointments, policies and development priorities reflected an understanding that Nigeria’s strength lay in its diversity and that national progress must benefit all sections of the country.

The party also pointed to efforts to strengthen the nation’s security architecture, saying interventions, operational improvements and increased investments in security capabilities represented steps in the right direction, despite continuing challenges in some parts of the country.

It accused the opposition of dismissing every improvement and amplifying setbacks for political purposes, insisting that national security should not be reduced to partisan propaganda.

The Lagos APC said the growing “Awa lo kan” campaign was not a call for complacency but an appeal for collective responsibility and commitment to sustaining the administration’s policies.

It added that the benefits of governance should be consolidated and expanded rather than sacrificed through what it described as political experimentation.

The party also criticised opposition groups, accusing them of being preoccupied with internal disagreements, ideological differences, leadership disputes and struggles for political relevance.

“Their inability to present a coherent, credible and sustainable alternative to the Renewed Hope Agenda makes their promises of an imaginary national rescue increasingly unconvincing,” it said.

The APC argued that Nigerians deserved more than political rhetoric and criticism, insisting that opposition parties should explain what they intended to do differently, how they planned to achieve it and why their proposals should be trusted over the current administration’s reforms.

It described the 2027 presidential election as a contest that would go beyond political parties and personalities, saying it would be a choice between continuity and uncertainty, consolidation and disruption, as well as sustained reforms and a return to what it called unsustainable policies.

“For the Lagos APC, the message is unmistakable: the Tinubu presidency has laid important foundations, and the responsibility before Nigerians is to ensure that these foundations translate into enduring national prosperity,” the statement said.

The party said the transition from “Emi lo kan” to “Awa lo kan” captured the evolution of Tinubu’s political project from an individual declaration into a collective aspiration centred on continuity, opportunity and shared destiny.

“In 2027, it is not simply about giving President Bola Ahmed Tinubu another term. It is about giving Nigeria the opportunity to complete the transformation that has begun.

“It is about our collective future. It is about our shared prosperity. It is about our common destiny. Awa lo kan! Nigeria’s turn to consolidate, progress and prosper,” the Lagos APC stated.

The post 2027: Lagos APC declares ‘Awa lo kan’ movement for Tinubu appeared first on The Sun Nigeria.

articles.title: 2027: ‘Tinubu won’t be part of my government’ – Makinde
articles.summary:
The presidential candidate of the Action Peoples Movement, Seyi Makinde, has said President Bola Tinubu will not be part of his proposed government of national unity if he wins the 2027 election, citing an agreement he claimed the President failed to honour before the 2023 polls.

Makinde, however, said his government would be open to appointing qualified Nigerians from the ruling All Progressives Congress, stressing that political affiliation would not prevent capable individuals from serving.

He made the remarks during an interview on The Rooftop Podcast, where he was asked whether he would accommodate political figures such as former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar, Peter Obi and Tinubu in his proposed administration.

“Perhaps not President Tinubu, but there are still decent people in APC as well. I’ll tap them and they are Nigerians,” Makinde said.

When asked why he would exclude Tinubu, the governor referred to his political relationship with the President ahead of the 2023 general election.

Makinde said he had supported Tinubu at the time based on an understanding that an inclusive government would be formed after the election, but alleged that the agreement was not honoured.

“Well, not in that context. I mean, I worked for him in 2023. We agreed on a government of national unity. He did not fulfil it,” he said.

The governor explained that the arrangement was among the issues raised by the PDP G5 governors, who broke ranks with the party’s leadership before the 2023 presidential election.

According to him, the group wanted an administration that would bring together competent people from different parts of Nigeria rather than limit appointments to members of the ruling party.

“We came from the PDP as G5 and we said, ‘Look, this is not going to be a government of APC. It should be a government where you tap people from all across the country. Go to every corner of the country, pick and choose people that can help you know to sort some of this out,’” he said.

To explain his position, Makinde recalled how former military Head of State, General Sani Abacha, brought prominent Nigerians into his government after the annulment of the June 12, 1993 presidential election.

He mentioned former Lagos State Governor Lateef Jakande and businessman Alex Ibru among those appointed, arguing that their inclusion was intended to ease political tensions and accommodate aggrieved groups.

Makinde said he wanted to adopt a similar approach by bringing people with the right skills and experience into government, irrespective of their political backgrounds.

He faulted Tinubu’s approach to appointments, alleging that the President had largely favoured individuals from his political circle.

“Tinubu didn’t do that at all. All his appointees are from Bourdillon,” he said.

The APM candidate maintained that his proposed government of national unity would prioritise competence and national inclusion in selecting people to help address the country’s challenges.

articles.title: Iran says it will use all its tools to confront US naval blockade
articles.summary:
DUBAI, Nov 23 (Reuters) - Iran will use all its tools to confront the US naval blockade, Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said in a weekly news conference on Monday.

The US blockade on Iran-related oil exports was imposed on April 13, lifted in June after Washington reached a draft understanding with Tehran, then restored on July 14 after the agreement collapsed.

"We will definitely not tolerate it (the blockade) and we will use all our tools to confront this US aggression," Baghaei said.

articles.title: COP flop triggers backlash in Australia; Pacific nations express despair
articles.summary:
By Praveen Menon and Lewis Jackson

SYDNEY/ANTALYA, Turkey, Nov 23 (Reuters) - The finger pointing to assign blame for the collapse of UN climate talks in Turkey began on Monday with calls for the resignation of the Australian minister leading them, while the Pacific island nations most at risk expressed their despair over the failure of countries to collectively address global warming.

articles.title: Bad COP, worse COP: What's next after climate talks fail?
articles.summary:
The collapse of marathon climate talks in Turkey has renewed questions about reform of their consensus requirement, and galvanised calls for legal action and ambitious side agreements between like-minded countries.

The "conference of the parties" talks, better known as COP31, ended without agreement and two days over schedule on Sunday, as countries deadlocked on fossil fuels, finance, science and carbon-removing technologies.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia's influence loomed large over failed COP31 deal
articles.summary:
By Valerie Volcovici and Sarah McFarlane

ANTALYA, Turkey, Nov 23 (Reuters) - As the COP31 climate conference drifted into what proved to be record overtime, a negotiator from a small island state complained that a promised meeting with the talks' Turkish and Australian presidents had been cancelled yet again.

Saudi officials, meanwhile, had regular access, allowing them disproportionate influence at the Antalya conference, according to negotiators from Europe, small island states, Latin America, Asia and Africa.

articles.title: Analysis-Can climate diplomacy build on the collapse of COP31?
articles.summary:
By Peter Hobson, Simon Jessop, Valerie Volcovici and Sarah McFarlane

ANTALYA, Turkey, Nov 23 (Reuters) - The collapse of COP31 talks in Turkey on Sunday without a political agreement left exhausted negotiators questioning the future of a process that for three decades has led the global fight against climate change.

For the small, vulnerable countries most exposed to rising sea levels and the increasingly extreme weather scientists link to rising carbon emissions, annual UN conferences are their chance to draw the world's attention to their plight and seek financial help.

articles.title: Iran strike wounds two in Bahrain, Saudi condemns 'criminal' attacks

Iran's Revolutionary Guards have repeatedly said they targeted US facilities in Bahrain, where Iranian strikes resumed on November 13 after a lull since early September.

"In the wake of the criminal Iranian attacks suffered yesterday (Saturday) by the Kingdom of Bahrain... a Bahraini national with a disability was wounded," Bahrain's interior ministry said on X.

articles.title: Libya's eastern government suspects drone attack caused explosion on Russian ship

Nov 22 (Reuters) - A suspected drone attack caused an explosion aboard a Russian ship docked at the Benghazi naval base in eastern Libya, the country's eastern-based government said on Sunday after a preliminary investigation.

No one has claimed responsibility for the suspected attack, and there was no immediate reaction from Russian authorities.

Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Ukrainian forces have repeatedly used naval drones and missiles to target Russian warships and naval facilities, mainly in the Black Sea.

articles.title: Drone strikes hit homes, UN building in Sudan's capital

A drone strike destroyed a house, a witness said, while a Sudanese army source said the drones had been launched from Ethiopia.

Earlier, multiple countries and negotiating blocs said they could not accept the version of the text put before them.

"There will be no new text from now on. We will not be carrying out work on a new text in an environment where there is no consensus," Kurum said.

(Reporting by Tuvan Gumrukcu, writing by William James)

articles.title: In an Egypt village, generations of Palestinians denied a normal life
articles.summary:
Shamma Abu Hussein is possibly the last person in her village of refugees to have lived in historic Palestine. Living in Egypt, she has watched three generations of her family grow up in legal limbo.

She was among the hundreds of thousands who fled or were expelled during the creation of the State of Israel in 1948, whose descendants number in the millions.

Now she fears that the effects of the Gaza war and rhetoric from Israeli ministers calling for Gazans to be expelled means history is repeating itself.

articles.title: Syrian Christian town demands security after resident kidnapped
articles.summary:
When Amina saw her nephew's motorbike knocked onto the ground and a car speeding away from his home in central Syria, she thought there had been a crash.

Instead, 38-year-old jeweller Maher Sankari had been kidnapped, an incident that plunged the Christian town of Suqaylabiyah into fear and prompted church leaders to demand authorities take action against repeated attacks and kidnappings of Christians.

Sankari's captors are demanding an eye-watering ransom of 120 kilogrammes (265 pounds) of gold.

articles.title: COP31 climate talks collapse as EU and others reject deal
articles.summary:
By Peter Hobson, Lewis Jackson and Ezgi Erkoyun

ANTALYA, Turkey, Nov 22 (Reuters) - UN climate talks ended in collapse on Sunday as the European Union and others rejected a final deal put forward by COP31 presidents Turkey and Australia, saying it was too weak to advance the fight against global warming.

The failed talks reflect the struggle by governments across the world to muster ambitious action to address the worsening consequences of climate change — including heatwaves, wildfires, floods and powerful storms — as wars and economic pressures compete for their attention.

One of the strike drone impacts occurred in a courtyard near a nine-storey residential building in the city centre. Cars and a flat on the fifth floor caught fire as a result of the strike.

At another location, a fire broke out in a residential area, damaging houses.

Emergency services report that all seats of fire have been extinguished.

articles.title: "She put a little of herself into every student": Russia kills primary school teacher near Kyiv
articles.summary:
Maryna Moichenko, a 36-year-old primary school teacher, has been killed in a Russian drone strike on a Novus supermarket in Vyshneve, Kyiv Oblast.

Source: Vyshneve Academic Lyceum Osnova, the primary school where Maryna worked

Details: Her colleagues described Maryna as a kind and compassionate person who put her heart and soul into teaching every student.

"For the little ones, she became their first mentor, teaching them kindness, openness and a love of learning. For us, she was a dependable colleague and a true friend. Her smile, warmth and wisdom will remain in our memories forever," the school wrote on its Facebook page.

Maryna is survived by two daughters. One of them, Sofiia, attended dance classes at L&G Studio in Vyshneve.

"Maryna was an incredible mother to two wonderful girls, a vibrant and positive person, an excellent primary school teacher, and someone who was exceptionally active, sincere and full of life," the studio said.

Former students remember Maryna as someone who had been there for them from the very beginning of their school lives.

"She welcomed the children, taught them, supported them and gave a part of herself to each of them. She was an incredible teacher and a person we will always remember with warmth and gratitude," wrote Daneliia and Melaniia Mykolaienko, two of Maryna's former students.

Background: On the evening of 22 November, Russian forces struck a supermarket in Vyshneve. Three people were killed and 15 were injured.

articles.title: Russian fibre-optic drone strikes vehicle carrying bread in Sumy Oblast – photos
articles.summary:
Russian forces have conducted a drone strike on a vehicle delivering bread and other food supplies in the Krasnopillia hromada in Sumy Oblast. The ensuing fire was extinguished by firefighters. [A hromada is an administrative unit designating a village, several villages, or a town, and their adjacent territories.]

Photo: State Emergency Service in Sumy Oblast

Photo: State Emergency Service in Sumy Oblast

The strike occurred just as the goods were being unloaded. The vehicle caught fire. Due to its close proximity to a shop, there was a threat of the fire spreading to the building. Firefighters extinguished the blaze and prevented the flames from spreading to the shop."

Details: Early reports indicate that no one was injured.

articles.title: Western intelligence warns that Russia is preparing to deploy nuclear weapons in space
articles.summary:
Western intelligence services are warning of a new nuclear threat from Moscow: Russia could launch a satellite carrying a nuclear warhead into orbit within the next few weeks.

Source: WDR; NDR; Süddeutsche Zeitung, as reported by European Pravda

Details: Several NATO countries have recently received a warning about Russia's intentions.

The German Armed Forces (Bundeswehr) have reportedly informed Defence Minister Boris Pistorius and other government officials about the threat.

Western intelligence services and military agencies, including the German Armed Forces and the Federal Intelligence Service (BND), believe that Russia could launch a satellite carrying a nuclear warhead into space at any point over the coming weeks.

The satellite, named Sputnik-S, would reportedly become operational once placed in orbit. It is said to be fully assembled and to have been in storage near Moscow for some time.

Deploying nuclear weapons in space would pose an enormous military threat to the West. Once a nuclear-armed satellite is in Earth's orbit, there would be virtually no effective way to counter it or prevent its weapon from being used.

Experts believe that the consequences of a nuclear explosion in space would be severe. According to WDR, NDR and Süddeutsche Zeitung, US Space Command chief Stephen Whiting recently warned that such an explosion would probably disable around a third of all satellites in low Earth orbit within hours or days, with the remainder gradually failing over the following months.

Another concern would be the extremely powerful electromagnetic pulse generated by a nuclear explosion in space, which could also potentially cause widespread failures of technical systems on Earth.

Major General Armin Fleischmann of Germany's Cyber and Information Domain Service (CIR) noted that if such a device were detonated, the consequences for life in Germany would be enormous: power outages and severe restrictions on communications and navigation.

In response to enquiries from WDR, NDR and Süddeutsche Zeitung, the Russian Embassy said it had no information about the events described. It categorically rejected what it called unfounded accusations concerning Russia's space activities, describing them as part of a propaganda campaign.

Background:

Seven European Union countries previously called for the proposed European Space Shield to be restructured around protecting EU space systems, while keeping military space capabilities at national level.

Paris and Berlin have long been sceptical of the European Space Shield, an initiative proposed by Brussels last year as part of the Defence Readiness Roadmap 2030.

articles.title: Zelenskyy confirms Ukrainian naval drones sank Russian corvette Merkury off Libya – video
articles.summary:
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has confirmed that Ukrainian naval drones sank the Russian corvette Merkury with a Ka-27 helicopter on board and struck the dry cargo ship MV Angara, which Russia was using to transport weapons, near the Libyan port of Benghazi.

Source: Zelenskyy; Security Service of Ukraine (SSU)

Quote from Zelenskyy: "It all took place off the coast of Libya. Our warriors deployed seven Ukrainian-made naval drones.

Despite all the enemy's efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk. It's one of their newest ships, commissioned in 2023, during the full-scale war. A Ka-27 combat helicopter was also destroyed along with the corvette."

An exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia’s war. I thank the warriors of the Security Service of Ukraine and all our Defense Forces of Ukraine who took part in carrying out these tasks. I received detailed briefings on the operation’s steps yesterday and today – the… pic.twitter.com/eW6DGfPuIZ

https://x.com/ZelenskyyUa/status/2124764825049850041?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw

Details: The SSU said the Merkury, pennant number 734, was part of Russia's Black Sea Fleet. The corvette regularly escorted Russian convoys at sea, including the dry cargo ship MV Angara, the operation's second target.

The SSU added that Russia had been using the sanctioned dry cargo vessel to transport military equipment, including along the supply routes known as the Syrian Express and Libyan Express. [The Syrian Express is the name used to describe Russia's maritime supply and logistics network, which has been used since 2012 to transport weapons, military equipment, troops and supplies between Russian ports and the Syrian Mediterranean port of Tartus.]

Quote from the SSU: "Both vessels were legitimate military targets for Ukraine, as they were directly supporting Russian military capabilities."

Background: Two Libyan officials previously told the Associated Press that the Russian corvette Merkury suffered serious damage as a result of a strike on a naval base in Benghazi, and a fire broke out at the base. Citing an initial investigation, the AP wrote that the ship may have been hit by Ukrainian naval drones.

articles.title: Ukrainian forces hit Rubicon S base in Kursk Oblast and debunk false Russian claims – video
articles.summary:
Ukraine's defence forces have denied false Russian claims that they remotely laid mines in the city of Rylsk in Russia's Kursk Oblast.

Source: 8th Air Assault Corps of the Armed Forces of Ukraine

Quote: "The Russians turned a police station in central Rylsk into a drone workshop and ammunition depot. Now they want to shift responsibility for the explosions in the city centre away from themselves."

Details: Intelligence officers from the 8th Air Assault Corps identified the location of the Rubicon S special UAV unit in Rylsk, Kursk Oblast. The unit had set up its workshop inside a local police station. Unmanned systems units of the 8th Corps carried out precision strikes, hitting the workshop and the accommodation used by Rubicon S personnel. The location where drone pilots from Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) were based was also struck.

Russian forces had set up an ammunition depot inside a police station in the city centre, violating all safety requirements. The strikes caused the ammunition to explode. Storing ammunition in the middle of a city poses a threat first and foremost to civilians. It was the Russians who created this danger.

Following the powerful explosions, the local authorities had a new task: shifting the blame onto Ukraine. The Russians launched an information campaign claiming that Ukraine had used drones to scatter mines across central Rylsk.

Quote: "We state unequivocally that this is yet another Russian lie. We did not carry out any remote mining using drones. The explosions in central Rylsk were caused by the detonation of an ammunition depot inside the local police station."

articles.title: Industrial facility damaged in drone attack on Russia's Perm Krai, fire at oil refinery reported – photo, video
articles.summary:
The Russian authorities have reported that an industrial facility in Perm Krai has been damaged in a drone attack. A fire has been recorded at a Lukoil oil refinery, according to monitoring Telegram channels.

Source: Perm Krai Governor Dmitry Makhonin; Exilenova+ Telegram channel; Latvia-based Russian media outlet Meduza

Quote from Makhonin: "Air defence forces and mobile fire groups are repelling an attack by enemy drones. An industrial facility has been damaged as a result of the attack. Early reports indicate that there are no casualties. Emergency services are working at the scene."

Details: Monitoring Telegram channels posted footage showing fires and smoke in the vicinity of the oil refinery. The Russian authorities urged residents not to post any information online about aircraft or air defence operations.

Reports on social media indicate that the Kaleikino oil pumping station in Almetyevsk, in Russia's Republic of Tatarstan, came under attack on the night of 22-23 November.

The Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery in the city of Novoshakhtinsk, Rostov Oblast, was reportedly struck again on the night of 22-23 November. However, the resulting fire may have broken out at the privately owned company Tata-Gaz instead.

Quote: "Damage to civilian and railway infrastructure facilities in the oblast has been recorded as a result of enemy attacks over the past day and during the night."

articles.title: Russian warship Merkury in Libya may have been hit by Ukrainian drones – AP
articles.summary:
The Associated Press has suggested that Ukrainian naval drones were likely behind the explosions that hit the Russian corvette Merkury in Benghazi, Libya.

Source: Associated Press (AP), citing sources

Details: Two Libyan officials told AP that a strike on a naval base in Benghazi, eastern Libya, has seriously damaged the Russian corvette Merkury and sparked a fire at the site.

Citing Libyan sources, AP reports that "several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship from a base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya, according to an initial investigation into the attack. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship".

The officials, who represent the self-proclaimed Libyan National Army, which controls eastern and southern Libya, spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the press, AP said.

AP recalls that Libya has been divided since 2011, when a NATO-backed uprising toppled the decades-long rule of dictator Muammar Gaddafi, who was subsequently killed. A UN-backed government is based in Tripoli, while a rival administration is located in the east of the country. The oil-rich nation remains the epicentre of a prolonged competition between Russia and the West.

The government based in eastern Libya said in a statement that the strike on 22 November caused an explosion and a fire at the base, which was subsequently extinguished.

Satellite television channel Almasar aired footage showing the vessel engulfed in flames. The channel reported that the Libyan navy had rescued the crew of a Maltese-flagged vessel.

The vessel had docked at the Libyan base to refuel and take on supplies under a cooperation agreement between Russia and the government in eastern Libya. No further details about the ship or its cargo were provided.

Furthermore, the statement indicated that a joint investigation has been launched together with Russia to "uncover the circumstances of the attack, its source, and the party behind it".

AP adds that there was no immediate comment from either Russia or Ukraine.

A European official, also speaking to AP on condition of anonymity, said the vessel had been identified as a Russian corvette but that there was no assessment yet of what caused the incident.

The government of western Libya expressed concern about "dragging Libyan ports and civilian facilities into external conflicts", which AP suggests is an apparent reference to the war in Ukraine.

"The government reaffirms its categorical rejection of turning Libya into an arena for international conflicts or a theatre for external powers to settle scores," the western Libya government's statement reads.

Background: An explosion occurred on board the Russian Steregushchiy-class missile corvette Merkury in Benghazi. The warship is believed to have been destroyed.

articles.title: Oil refinery ablaze in Russia's Novoshakhtinsk following attack – video
articles.summary:
Users on Ukrainian and Russian social media platforms suggest that the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery in Russia's Rostov Oblast was hit once again overnight on 22-23 November, although the fire reported in the area may have broken out at the privately owned company Tata-Gaz instead.

Source: Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+; Russian media outlet Astra; other Telegram channels

Details: Exilenova+ reported that the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery was hit at around 01:00.

The refinery can process up to 7.5 million tonnes of crude oil a year and produces diesel fuel, marine fuel, heating oil, fuel oil and petrol fractions.

Ukraine's General Staff said the refinery directly supplies Russian forces with fuel, including diesel and jet fuel. It is one of the main suppliers of petroleum products in southern Russia.

The Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery has been attacked on several occasions: on 22 June 2022; 4 May 2023; 13 March, 6 June and 19 December 2024; 21 August and 25 December 2025; and 25 August and 25 September 2026.

Update: Local residents report that Novoshakhtinsk is under a massive UAV attack. Numerous explosions and air defence activity can be heard in the city. A fire near the local oil refinery and a glow in the sky have also been reported.

Residents of Rostov Oblast say the blaze is visible from many kilometres away.

Astra reported that the attack on Novoshakhtinsk has been going on for three hours. Explosions were also heard in the distance in Rostov-on-Don and near Platov International Airport.

The outlet later reported a major fire near the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery and a fuel trading company.

Astra said the blaze was in the direction of the two facilities, where "storage tanks may have exploded".

The facilities concerned are the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery and Tata-Gaz LLC, a privately owned company involved in fuel trading, storage and logistics.

Tkachenko subsequently reported that the number of people killed in the Russian attack on Dymer had risen to 11 after another body had been recovered from under the rubble.

Search and rescue operations are ongoing.

Early reports indicated that two people had been killed and four injured in the Russian attack. One of those killed was an 18-year-old man.

Rescue workers were searching for 11 people, including two children.

Before that, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported that a Russian drone strike on Dymer had partially destroyed one section of a five-storey apartment building.

articles.title: US envoy Kushner explains when Trump would approve Article 5-style security guarantees for Ukraine
articles.summary:
Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's special envoy and son-in-law, has said that Trump would approve NATO Article 5-style security guarantees for Ukraine, subject to congressional approval, if the overall European security architecture made it highly unlikely that those guarantees would ever need to be invoked.

Source: Kushner on X (Twitter)

Details: Kushner said that Trump's willingness to consider providing Ukraine with security guarantees similar to those under NATO's Article 5 was "a critical feature to achieving lasting peace". He described Russia's willingness to discuss such guarantees as "a major step forward and potential indication that it is serious about peace".

Kushner noted that such guarantees, together with deterrence and conflict prevention mechanisms, could significantly reduce the risk of another war.

"President Zelenskyy is right that these guarantees must be specific, credible, and clearly documented. That is exactly the work Steve Witkoff and I are undertaking together," he wrote.

Quote: "These are among the most significant commitments the United States can make and require careful consideration.

Donald Trump would have to approve any proposed guarantee, subject to constitutional and congressional processes. He would take such a step only if he believed it clearly served America's national interests and the broader security arrangements made it highly unlikely that the guarantee would ever be invoked.

This is why security guarantees for Ukraine cannot be finalised in isolation from post-war European security architecture. The two must be considered together."

Background:

Earlier, Kushner said that Washington had succeeded in securing Russia's readiness to consider a concept under which any security guarantee agreement for Ukraine would be based on a mechanism modelled on NATO's Article 5.

In response to Kushner's remarks, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed doubts that Ukraine and the US share the same understanding of the phrase "security guarantees similar to those provided under NATO's Article 5".

Meanwhile, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov said that any forms of Ukrainian "quasi-membership" of NATO as part of security guarantees are "unacceptable" to Moscow.

Zelenskyy said on 21 November that he does not know what exactly partners mean by "NATO Article 5-style" security guarantees, but is certain that Ukraine needs guarantees lasting far longer than Trump's time as US president.

articles.title: Russian attack damages 18 trolleybuses in Dnipro, halts metro services and disrupts water supply – photos

articles.title: Cop31: Why the UN climate summit ended in victory for fossil fuel producing nations
articles.summary:
The UN’s annual two-week climate summit, Cop31, has ended in failure. Countries could not find consensus on a final agreement. It is the first such failure in more than 20 years.

The summit started relatively smoothly. In fact, the conference agenda was adopted within a few hours on day one, as country parties found nothing objectionable. At the time, this event looked like it might be smooth sailing: another summit simply focused on implementing policies agreed in previous years.

But week two became explosive. First, the draft agreement – which if adopted would have been known as the Antalya Accords – conceded that we have failed to keep global temperature rise below 1.5˚C and that the world is entering a period of “overshoot”. Second, oil and gas producing nations fought to keep the root cause of climate change – namely fossil fuels – out of any deal. And they succeeded, as the agreement fell through.

The frustration felt by many was summed up on day ten (November 19) by Panamanian environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro, who said: “While we listen to endless oratory, the planet is being destroyed.” The country’s delegation then said enough is enough – they were not about to put their name to an outcome that does not adequately address the crisis.

We are climate experts at UCL who have written about the outcome of these summits for The Conversation since Cop26 in Glasgow, and we were in Antalya this year too. Here’s why we think this year’s summit failed.

Disagreement over ‘fossil fuels’ caused the collapse

Every Cop meeting since 2003 has resulted in a global agreement. This year, however, countries failed to reach consensus on a final deal, after negotiations broke down over whether to explicitly address fossil fuels.

Inside the negotiation rooms at Cop31 in Turkey.
Simon Chin-Yee

The draft agreement presented to the summit for approval omitted any mention of fossil fuels, after pressure from oil, gas and coal producing nations led by Saudi Arabia. The EU, Panama and many vulnerable island nations refused to agree to any text that did not explicitly address them. This disagreement ultimately prevented the summit from reaching consensus.

This has been the modus operandi of these summits – they start with a more ambitious draft text that gets weakened as it comes closer to adoption. Last year at Cop30 in Brazil countries agreed a watered-down text with no mention of fossil fuels just to get an agreement. But removing fossil fuels from a climate text is like removing mention of cigarettes in an anti-smoking campaign – it was simply too much for many countries to accept.

A push for electrification, without a fossil fuel phase-out

There were some positives to come out of the summit. Electrification was a key focus this year, for instance. In this context, it refers to using electricity in transport, industry and other sectors, rather than burning fossil fuels. The summit hosts said the target was 35x35 electrification: making electricity account for 35% of the world’s final energy consumption by 2035.

In the last days of the summit, an electrification delivery package was launched with support from more than 150 countries plus the EU, as well as 37 cities and 150 businesses. This included plans for power utilities and energy companies to investment US$156 billion (£119 billion) a year in renewables and energy storage.

But electrifying transport and industry will only cut emissions if the electricity itself is clean. Countries pushing for a shift to renewable-powered electrification also wanted a clearer commitment to moving away from fossil fuels. With the negotiations ending without agreement, there was no collective commitment to ensuring electrification would reduce dependence on fossil fuels.

The most climate-vulnerable nations were left disappointed

Pacific island nations were left deeply disappointed. Many are low-lying coral atolls, where sea-level rise and increasingly severe storms, floods and other extreme weather are threatening their very existence.

But Cop31’s failure to agree on stronger action on fossil fuels or adequate adaptation finance exposed the widening gap between what vulnerable countries need and what international negotiations are delivering. Countries have very different responsibilities for tackling climate change. Small island states and least developed countries like the Marshall Islands have emitted very little in the past and have very little to mitigate today. The largest emitters and fossil fuel producers, meanwhile, have a much greater responsibility.

Ambassador Albon Ishoda of the Marshall Islands said: “Disappointing is probably not strong enough a word … We have money for wars but not to save communities.”

In short, this was an “implementation Cop” which turned into one of the worst ever climate summits. As the world enters a period of overshooting 1.5˚C, the failure to agree on a clear path away from fossil fuels is a big win for the countries that produce them – and another setback for those least responsible for climate change but most exposed to it.

Mark Maslin is Pro-Vice Provost of the UCL Climate Crisis Grand Challenge and the Lead for Climate, Health and Security at the UNU. He is the Chair of the Carbon Trust Scheme Owner Impartiality Committee. He is a member of the Climate Crisis Advisory Group. He is an advisor to Sheep Included Ltd, Lansons, NetZeroNow and has advised the UK Parliament. She is a Trustee for Wilton Park Foundation. Research funding sources include UKRI, Royal Academy of Engineering, Water Aid, British Academy, Bboxx Ltd, UCL, Royal Society and British Council. articles.title: How did the COP31 climate agreement fall apart – and what happens now?
articles.summary:
Chris McGrath/Getty

Two days after the COP31 global climate summit was supposed to finish, the talks in Antalya, Turkey, have come to an end – but not as we might have hoped.

Agreement simply could not be reached. The sticking point was the omission of fossil fuels in draft texts. The European Union led a revolt, shattering the consensus needed to adopt the cover text proposed by the Turkish and Australian conveners.

In a year of unprecedented climate disasters, a supercharged El Niño and as the world heads inevitably past 1.5 °C of warming, the EU and other nations said that the international process did not meet the moment.

Some coverage has suggested the rejection of the cover text is a sign the entire summit was a failure. This isn’t quite right.

These texts have always been add-ons to the formal negotiation process. Countries have regularly agreed these political, overarching statements, particularly since the Glasgow meeting in 2021, but they are not a requirement.

Its failure does not signal the end of the COP process – or the breakdown of the Paris Agreement. What it may mean is that international climate cooperation will look different from this point onwards.

Chris Bowen, the COP31 president of negotiations and Australia’s Minister for Climate Change, speaks to the media after the final session during the second overtime day of the climate talks.
Chris McGrath/Getty

No mention of the ‘F’ word

For many observers, the litmus test for success at COP31 was whether countries could make any headway on the root cause of climate change – fossil fuels. Unfortunately, fossil fuels proved unmentionable.

Three years ago at COP28 in Dubai, countries agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels”, marking the first time fossil fuels had explicitly been mentioned in an official decision text in decades of negotiations.

The Dubai text was hailed as “the beginning of the end of the fossil fuel era”. But there was little sign that hope would be realised in Turkey.

In a repeat of last year’s fraught negotiations at COP30 in Brazil, major fossil fuel producing nations Saudi Arabia and Russia banded together to block any reference in the negotiating outcomes and proposed cover text.

Australia and Turkey proposed a compromise – no fossil fuel language in exchange for support for electrification “with the greatest possible use of clean energy”.

This seemed to get Saudi Arabia over the line but drew backlash from the European Union, Panama, the Marshall Islands, Vanuatu, and Belize, who rejected the cover text.

Brazil took a different approach to the same problem last year. In a bid to break the deadlock, Brazil committed to develop a global strategy to phase out fossil fuels outside the formal negotiating agenda.

The roadmap was launched at this year’s summit in Turkey and managed to attract support from big fossil fuel producers such as India, Germany and Nigeria. Countries across the European Union are launching similar roadmaps.

Frustration over fossil fuels at COP31 is likely to lead more nations to go outside official talks to progress phase-out efforts. Earlier this year, 57 nations attended the first conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels in Santa Marta, Colombia. Another meeting is planned for next year, co-hosted by Tuvalu and Ireland.

Neither the Turkish hosts nor their Australian partners seemed keen to mention fossil fuels. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan was untroubled by the optics of announcing two huge new oilfields in Turkey in his speech at the summit opening. While Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese highlighted the existential risks to Pacific countries from climate change, he made no commitment to stop approving new Australian coal and gas projects.

Both leaders much preferred to talk about electrification, namely the flagship “35 by 35” electrification pledge. The goal here is to boost electricity’s share of final energy use globally from around 23% at present to 35% by 2035.

Efforts to embed this goal in the cover text failed. But the electrification pledge drew strong support outside official negotiations. More than 75 countries and 180 businesses signed on, including the European Union and China.

Activist Greta Thunberg attends a protest at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.
Burak Kara/Getty

The “COP of action” fails to deliver

This year’s climate summit was billed as an “implementation COP”, focused on delivering the pledges countries had already made to address climate change.

Overseen by Australia in its role as “president of negotiations”, the formal talks largely focused on the actions countries are taking to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change, whether their response is sufficiently urgent and whether funds aimed at supporting the most vulnerable countries are adequate.

It was abundantly obvious that longstanding divisions had not been overcome. Developed countries called for emissions to be cut faster, while developing countries responded by pointing to a lack of financial support to do so.

African countries, in particular, stressed that an “implementation COP” was meaningless if rich nations failed to provide the actual resources needed to act.

Despite the general gloom, these talks did achieve progress in a few areas. Nations moved forwards on supporting a just transition (shifting to clean energy fairly) via a “phased approach”, as well as improving alignment in climate adaptation, which will help the poorest nations to implement their adaptation plans.

But broader efforts to find a way forward on the Paris Agreement’s Global Goal on Adaptation were left unresolved.

Decisions stalled in many negotiating rooms in the face of hard “red lines” declared by different blocs of countries.

Countries failed to reach any agreement on the vital question of cutting emissions, after Saudia Arabia and Russia blocked a proposed decision. Both are among the world’s top fossil fuel exporting nations.

This failure has left the world without any dedicated negotiating process on cutting emissions under the Paris Agreement. It’s possible nations could agree to renew a work program on climate mitigation at next year’s COP32 talks in Ethiopia.

What about money for adaptation?

Who pays for the costs of climate change has long been a contentious point. Developing countries face the brunt of damage from climate change, but have emitted far less – and have much less money to spend on adaptation.

Ahead of COP31, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said talks on new climate finance commitments were “dead in the water”. He urged delegates to focus on implementing existing pledges rather than try for fresh funding.

The summit failed to meet even these low expectations. No concrete progress was achieved on the goal of tripling funds for climate adaptation pledged last year at COP30 in Brazil.

Ahead of the summit, the Australian government flagged the need to boost global contributions to the official Pacific climate fund.

This, too, didn’t eventuate. Rich nations – including Australia – merely re-announced their existing pledges, leaving the Pacific fund A$450 million short of its 2026 target of $749 million.

Ironically, the most notable pledge came from the Solomon Islands, a small Pacific nation. Prime Minister Matthew Wale pledged $600,000 to the global Green Climate Fund. “The Pacific did not create this crisis,” he declared. “But we will not stand by and wait for others to act”.

A few new commitments arrived by the end of the two week summit from nations such as Canada and Norway.

Press and participants watch as a man dressed as a dinosaur performs as part of the Fossil Of The Day award at the COP31 UN climate summit.
Burak Kara/Getty Images

Defending the science

Unusually, climate science was front and centre at COP31.

This year, a small bloc of fossil fuel-producing countries has been obstructing the publication of key scientific reports from the world’s leading body of climate scientists, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.

This year marks the first UN summit since it was officially confirmed the world will overshoot the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C goal by 2030.

With the collapse of support for the cover text, statements supporting release of the latest climate science didn’t get approval. All that remained were technical conclusions which “expressed utmost concern” that climate impacts will continue to increase with every increment of global warming.

IPCC chair Jim Skea at the opening ceremony of COP31. Previously, he described the stymied outcome of the meeting in Ethiopia as frustrating and disappointing.
Chris McGrath/Getty Images

Australia on the global stage

COP31 gave Australia a unique global role. After being outmanoeuvred in their bid to host the summit, Australia secured a role in overseeing negotiations.

Australian Climate and Energy Minister Chris Bowen and his team had the unenviable task of seeking consensus between 195 countries and the European Union.

After the cover text was rejected, Bowen declared Australia had left “nothing on the field” but had faced “unbridgeable red lines.”

Hours beforehand, Fijian Climate Minister Lynda Tabuya acknowledged Bowen’s efforts, noting the failure was “not yours to carry […] it is the responsibility of all parties.”

Are COP summits still worthwhile?

This year’s climate summit took the unenviable record of the longest ever. With consensus seemingly impossible, some civil society representatives dubbed it “the worst COP ever.”

Outgoing UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres blamed “powerful fossil fuel interests”, including fossil fuel exporters and corporate lobbyists.

Some nations are now calling for urgent reform to negotiations long paralysed by vetoes and disconnected from science.

Unfortunately, any change to official voting processes would itself require a consensus decision.

Consensus is hard to achieve, but powerful. The power of the Paris Agreement draws on the fact it represents the view of nearly every country – big or small, rich or poor.

COP31 President Murat Kurum began the summit expressing hopes this year’s talks would leave a legacy of “working together.”

That was a false hope. A more realistic hope is that the collapse of consensus may be the shock the world needs to change course.

As former UN climate chief Christiana Figueres has said, we should not see the refusal of more than 130 countries to sign an inadequate deal as a failure. Rather, it might be “a sign of courage”.

Jacqueline Peel receives funding from the Australian Research Council. She is affiliated with the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, serving as a coordinating lead author in Working Group III (mitigation) for the Seventh Assessment Report.

Kathryn Bowen receives funding from Australia's Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade and Department of Climate Change, Energy, Environment and Water, the World Health Organisation, Wellcome, the Global Fund, Green Climate Fund, Global Environment Facility, Asian Development Bank and World Bank. She is affiliated with the Port Philip EcoCentre and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change where she is a lead author for the Sixth and Seventh Assessment Reports (Working Group II - Impacts, Vulnerability and Adaptation).

articles.title: Why fossil fuel-producing countries are stalling this crucial climate report
articles.summary:
Muhammad Fajri/Getty

After a year of record-breaking weather and a “super” El Niño underway, there’s no doubt climate extremes are wreaking havoc across the globe.

For decades, scientists have warned us this would happen. Their research made the case for reducing fossil fuel dependence. And we’ve relied on their expertise to assess the severity and extent of climate change.

But a small bloc of fossil fuel-producing countries is now obstructing the publication of a key scientific report from the world’s leading body of climate scientists, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).

This threatens global cooperation on tackling the climate crisis. And it has created deep concern at the COP31 climate summit, currently in its final hours in Turkey, also known as Türkiye.

A truly global report

First, it helps to understand why this report is so significant. The IPCC is the UN body for assessing the science related to climate change. Established in 1988, it provides political leaders with independent scientific assessments on climate change and strategies for response.

This panel has produced six pivotal reports to date, which have collated and reviewed the latest knowledge on climate change science. And over the past two years, more than 640 experts from around the world have been meeting to write the seventh.

The authors are leading researchers who volunteer their time. More than half of the authors working on the current seventh report, called the Seventh Assessment Report, or AR7, are from developing countries. I am a lead author for the Sixth and Seventh Assessment Reports in the working group that looks at impacts, vulnerability and adaptation.

Work on this seventh report kicked off in December 2024, and its timeline for completion was never officially finalised.

What’s the hold-up?

Originally, the plan was for the seventh report to be released in 2028. But five countries are objecting to this timeline and pushing for a later release in 2029.

India, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Kenya and China are ostensibly arguing that countries from the global south lack the resources and capacity to meet the current deadline.

However, these countries also happen to be among the world’s largest fossil fuel producers.

If recent reports are anything to go by, the evidence of global warming in this seventh report is likely to be alarming. It will highlight the evidence for much greater action, including deep and urgent reduction in fossil fuel production and use.

Extending the release date means IPCC contributors would have even more information they would have to assess. This delay would increase, not alleviate, the demands of authorship and reviewing for those contributors from developing nations.

The disagreement resulted in the suspension of the latest IPCC meeting in October in Ethiopia, with no confirmed timeline for the report release or budget for 2027. This threatens the very existence of the IPCC.

Nations seeking delay argue that tight timelines are unfair to developing countries. But the least developed countries (LDC), a group comprised of 44 nations, expressed “deep disappointment” when the meeting in Ethiopia was suspended.

Why the deadline matters

Every five years, the UN’s climate body does a global stocktake of how effectively the world is responding to climate change.

Intended to ramp up climate action, these stocktakes take a long hard look at the state of the planet, identify the gaps in our approach and suggest a path forward. To be truly effective, these must be based on the latest science.

Delaying the seventh report would mean the most recent science is not fed into the 2028 global stocktake. This has grave implications for future climate action, and any delay in our response could have catastrophic effects on the wellbeing of planetary and human health.

Science vs politics

While major fossil-fuel-emitting countries often attempt to impede phaseout efforts, undermining the IPCC follows a recent trend of discrediting science for political ends.

After a UN report in September found that limiting global warming to 1.5°C was no longer possible, Saudi Arabia jumped to question the credibility of the science, contending the research was not peer-reviewed. In fact, the report had been written over the course of a year by 44 experts, and reviewed by a further 44.

Conflict at COP31

Despite opposition to delaying the IPCC report, those pushing for it have remained unmoved at COP31. Speaking to media at the summit, former US Vice President Al Gore accused Saudi Arabia of trying to sabotage the IPCC’s work.

“Saudi Arabia is trying to destroy the IPCC in order to prevent the next global stocktake from using the accurate scientific data on fossil fuels,” he said.

At climate negotiations where the phrase “fossil fuels” is routinely vetoed from the text, finding a resolution to the IPCC issue has even broader implications. If countries can’t agree on this, how will nearly 200 countries agree on a robust final COP31 outcome?

Seeking resolution

While the clock ticks down on the COP31 negotiations, a resolution to the IPCC issue is unlikely in Turkey. However, it is hoped a timeline and budget can be nailed down at meetings in early December.

As the world’s most authoritative global body on climate change, the role the IPCC plays in driving climate action is critical to our future wellbeing. And the science in this seventh report will be fundamental to a truly effective global stocktake.

In a time when the world often feels divided, settling this issue amicably and in good faith would offer countries a much-needed reminder that we are capable of cooperation in pursuit of a better future.

Disclaimer: the author’s views do not reflect those of the IPCC
