articles.title: Weight-loss drugs could free up an area of farmland larger than Italy – new study
articles.summary:
Greta Rosati / shutterstock

GLP-1 weight-loss medicines such as Ozempic and Wegovy could affect much more than the waistlines of the people who take them. If widely used, our new research suggests these appetite-suppressing medicines could transform the global food system and free up vast areas of agricultural land.

The global food system is ultimately driven by demand. If people eat less, producers respond, affecting production, prices, trade and how much land is needed. We used a powerful computer simulation to explore scenarios ranging from GLP-1 use concentrated in high-income countries to widespread global access.

With widespread use of these medicines among adults living with obesity, we estimate that reduced calorie intake could prevent up to 6.6 million deaths each year by 2050, while freeing up as much as 32 million hectares of agricultural land – an area slightly larger than Italy – for other uses.

The biggest effects, however, occurred when reduced calorie intake was combined with a shift towards healthier diets. In this scenario, up to 7 million deaths could be avoided each year by 2050, while around 46 million hectares of agricultural land would have become available for other uses. This suggests that alongside weight-loss medicines, we need to make healthier options more widely available, affordable and more appealing.

About 100 million people already use GLP-1 weight-loss medications worldwide.
IM Imagery / shutterstock

The food system could respond in unexpected ways

Food systems are interconnected across countries. If demand falls in one part of the world, this can affect farming, trade and food prices elsewhere, with consequences for people who are not taking the medications at all.

Lower demand from GLP-1 users, for instance, could make food cheaper. That sounds positive, but cheaper food could also encourage greater consumption among non-users, offsetting some of the intended benefit. The effects of widespread GLP-1 use, in other words, cannot be understood just by looking at individual patients’ weight loss. They ripple through the global food system.

It’s tempting to read these findings as an argument for putting more people on weight-loss medication. That would miss the bigger picture.

Obesity has often been framed as a “lifestyle disease”, blaming individual people for not having enough willpower. But diets are shaped by what food is available, what it costs, how it’s marketed, where shops are located and what’s most convenient. In many high-income countries, it is remarkably easy to consume large amounts of cheap, energy-dense food. Society tells people to make healthier choices while surrounding them with an environment that often encourages the opposite.

The UK government commissioned national food strategy, finalised in 2021, made this point clearly: improving diets can’t simply be about asking individuals to choose better. The wider food environment needs to change to make the better choice the easy one.

Our findings shouldn’t be taken to mean that people living with obesity have a responsibility to lose weight to reduce the environmental impacts of food production. Rather, our research examines the wider consequences that changes in food demand could have across the food system.

Changing the food system alongside medicine

A healthier diet is not necessarily just a diet with fewer calories. It could mean more fruit, vegetables and other nutritious foods, alongside less excessive consumption of foods linked to poor health. These changes affect not only human health but also agriculture, land use and the environment.

Rather than asking whether GLP-1 medications or healthier diets are the answer, let’s ask how they can work together. Imagine a food system where healthier foods are affordable and accessible, unhealthy options aren’t relentlessly promoted, agricultural policy supports nutritious and sustainable production, and people who need medical treatment can access it. That combination could be far more powerful than any single intervention.

GLP-1 medicines can play an important role in tackling obesity, but they shouldn’t become a technological fix that allows the wider food system to escape scrutiny. They can help people eat less in an unhealthy food environment, but the long-term goal should be to make it easier and more affordable to have a healthier, more sustainable diet.

The remarkable thing about GLP-1 medications may not be that they change how much food people eat. It may be that they show us, with new clarity, just how closely human health, food production and environmental health are connected, and how much could be gained if we tackled all three together.

Peter Alexander receives funding from UKRI and Wellcome.

Roslyn Henry does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Three decades of free school meals in India: dignity, aspiration and the social meaning of food
articles.summary:
poltu shyamal/Shutterstock

Debates about the provision of free school meals often focus on eligibility, nutrition and health, programme costs and reducing child poverty. These are important questions. But there is another critical question that receives much less attention: How do families themselves understand and respond to school food?

This question is at the heart of addressing the gap between eligibility and uptake that plagues school meal programmes around the world.

India offers a useful place to look for answers. Its midday meal scheme, now known as PM Poshan, marked its 30th year in 2025. It is the world’s largest – and one of the longest-running – school feeding programmes. It provides a free cooked meal on school days to 112 million children attending pre-primary and Classes I–VIII (aged from around six to 14) in more than a million government and government-aided schools on all school days across India.

Our new research offers important insights into how families perceive and experience school meals. We carried out interviews with members of 86 households in Uttar Pradesh and Goa, basing our analysis particularly on in-depth conversations with 134 adults and 112 children.

While the scheme aims to improve children’s nutrition and educational participation, our findings show that its significance extends beyond these outcomes. Children talked about the food’s taste and whether it filled them up. Parents, on the other hand, largely mentioned the meals’ nutrition only when prompted. Instead, they weighed the scheme against their aspirations, their sense of dignity and the pressures of precarious lives.

For low-income families, accepting a free school meal is rarely a simple yes or no. It is weighed against everything else the household needs: food at home, the cost of getting to school, children’s contributions to household work and family livelihoods, and their hopes for the future. How families make that calculation can decide whether a school meal programme reaches the children it is meant for.

Food carries social meaning

School meals were also shaped by what food signalled to others. Some children felt uncomfortable queuing for meals, adding their names to the monthly register, or asking for a second helping when portions were small. Each of these made a child’s need visible to classmates and teachers. For some, how others perceived their need for a meal mattered as much as the need for food itself.

Parents, too, attached meaning to how their children ate. Some fathers felt that relying on school food conflicted with their responsibility to provide, while mothers kept packing lunch boxes from home as an expression of maternal care.

Caste and class shaped eating as well. Reflecting purity norms, some families sent their own plates for their children. Some better-off parents kept their children away from the meal entirely, distancing themselves from those they saw as in need of help.

Some families sent their own plates for their children.
PradeepGaurs/Shutterstock

Because free school meals are only provided in government and government-aided schools, the choice of school is also a choice about food. Some families who could have benefited from the programme moved their children to low-cost private schools, giving up the free meal altogether. They associated these schools with English-medium teaching, greater accountability, more attentive teachers and better prospects.

This did not mean food was unimportant to them. Some households cut back on food at home to pay private school fees. For these families, going with less now was the price of hope for later. Choices that look puzzling from the perspective of a programme made sense from the perspective of a family investing in its children’s futures.

The scheme is designed around the individual child, but food insecurity is lived by whole households. For the poorest families, a single meal could not outweigh the hidden costs of free schooling, such as daily transport, or the income an older child could earn. Some children were kept at home or withdrawn from school altogether. Girls bore the heaviest share, more often leaving school early to care for younger siblings and run the home.

None of this diminishes the scheme’s importance. For families facing sudden hardship, school meals became a lifeline, sometimes the only place children still ate vegetables. A programme that was less of a priority for one family could be an essential safety net for another.

Lessons beyond India

The step between programme eligibility and take-up is where household trade-offs and social meanings do their work. A child who feels awkward about being seen to claim support, or a parent who feels judged for accepting it, may not show up in eligibility figures, but both shape whether a programme works. Programmes routinely count who is eligible and who eats. They rarely ask families why they do or do not take part.

India’s universal design offers an important, practical lesson. When every child eats the same meal, the meal itself reveals little about a family’s circumstances. As England and other countries debate means-testing and the design of school food, stigma and family meanings belong at the centre of those decisions.

Putting food on the plate is essential. But understanding what that meal means within family life may be just as important to making school meal programmes work as intended.

Swayamshree Mishra is employed as a Postdoctoral Research Associate on the UKRI-funded Food Security for Equitable Futures project, led by Professor Jasmine Fledderjohann through a Future Leaders Fellowship (grant numbers MR/T021950/1 and MR/Y033965/1).

articles.title: The US-China AI race is real – but Trump’s recent moves on ‘super intelligence’ are unlikely to give America any advantage
articles.summary:
Donald Trump is insisting that people drop their use of the term artificial intelligence (AI), in favour of “super intelligence”. This started on September 29, when he signed an executive order telling federal agencies to call AI super intelligence, because, in the president’s view, “artificial” makes it sound fake.

On October 4, he followed up with a super intelligence force to coordinate the federal government’s effort “to ensure that America continues to lead the world in Super Intelligence”.

This AI force is led by Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence and a former chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission. Alongside him sit Federal Trade Commission chair Andrew Ferguson, the Pentagon’s technology chief Emil Michael and Scott Kupor, who runs the federal workforce.

The force reports to the president and his chief of staff and has 120 days to report on the risks and opportunities AI poses.

Is this serious national strategy or a branding exercise? The label itself tells us very little. What matters is whether the force can marshal what actually decides who leads in AI: compute, capital, talent and infrastructure. This is now a race, and the countries and organisations that move fastest and mobilise the most resources will hold a significant advantage.

Supporters can point to a genuine coordination problem. Responsibility for AI in Washington is scattered across intelligence, defence, competition policy, procurement and the civil service, which rarely act in concert.

Putting several of those agencies under one roof, reporting directly to the White House, could cut through that. Clayton has given a blunt assessment: “The risk of not being first is high.”

America also has a strong hand. According to Stanford’s 2026 AI Index, US private investment in AI reached US$285.9 billion (£217.24 billion) in 2025, roughly 23 times China’s US$12.4 billion (£9.42 billion). America’s largest tech firms are on track to spend more than US$650 billion on capital investment this year.

A body that helps clear bottlenecks the private sector cannot – grid connections, data centre permitting (approval), hiring technical talent into government – could add real value. Including the head of the federal workforce is a telling choice: governments have long struggled to recruit the people they need for AI.

Deeper problems?

Critics see something much thinner. The White House has not disclosed a budget, nor said whether the force will have regulatory powers or merely advise. It arrived shortly after leading firms, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and Nvidia, had signed a one-page White House accord committing to internal evaluations, external audits and board reviews.

Trump called it “morally binding”. But Democrat lawmaker Mark Warner, senior senator from Virginia, was scathing: “The president’s response? To rename it and tell the companies developing it to regulate themselves,” he said.

To my mind, there are three deeper problems. First, the US does not control the trajectory of AI. The same Stanford report found that the performance gap between the best US and Chinese models has narrowed to 2.7%, down from double digits in 2023.

The performance gap between US AI models and Chinese ones, like Alibaba’s Qwen series, has been narrowing.
hxdbzxy / Shutterstock

Beijing will pursue its own strategy whatever Washington calls its task force.
Second, the actors that matter most are private. The frontier AI labs (those at the cutting edge) have enormous commercial and strategic incentives of their own – and the previously mentioned investment figures are overwhelmingly made up of private money.

The companies will cooperate where interests align, on energy or export controls, for example. But I would not expect them to commit fully to a government programme. A voluntary accord with no enforcement mechanism shows where the leverage lies.

The third problem is timing. The US midterm elections heavily shifted control of Congress in the Democrats’ favour. This could reshape both funding for AI and oversight. Building national AI capability is a multi-year effort, and what is created by executive action can be undone the same way. For instance, President Trump revoked Joe Biden’s AI executive order on his first day back in office.

There is also a tension in the mandate itself. The force is asked both to win a race and to protect the public, yet its leadership is drawn from the intelligence, defence and competition enforcement sectors rather than from AI safety. Those goals do not always point the same way, and the announcement about the super intelligence force says little about how they will be balanced.

Is this better than nothing? Absolutely. Coordination has value, and the force could become a serious mechanism for concentrating resources at a scale commensurate with the stakes. But the test is not the name. It is whether the body secures a substantial budget, gains real authority over approval for infrastructure, procurement and hiring, and survives the political cycle.

AI policy is at a turning point. Yet a name, like super intelligence, is just a slogan. Until we see what resources the super intelligence force can command, and whether it can execute quickly and sustain that effort, I would put relatively little faith in it changing the trajectory of AI.

Ram Gopal does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Switching devices off standby can save £45 a year – practical advice on energy bills from an expert
articles.summary:
Simple changes at home can save pounds. Nanci Santos Iglesias/Shutterstock.

As the weather turns colder and with energy bills predicted to rise, it’s the time of year when we look for ways to heat our homes more cost-effectively.

Gas and electricity bills for a typical UK home are predicted to rise by 26% from January. Some financial support is promised by the government, including the household energy payment of £100 to many households in England and a VAT cut on electricity bills until July. In most cases, though, these measures will not offset the increase in bills, which is projected to be around £443 for a typical household.

The UK has a high proportion of older properties, with 78% having been built before 1980. This means UK homes are often not as energy efficient as they could be, making them expensive to heat. Heat pumps, batteries, solar panels and full retrofit projects may ultimately reduce energy bills, but are expensive. Just 1.1% of homes in England and Wales reach an energy performance certificate score of A, and the vast majority (around 72%) score C or D, so there opportunities for all of us to improve our homes.

Reduce draughts

Draughts (cold air entering the house from outside, or entering a warm room from a colder one) dilute the warm air in the room with colder air, meaning our heating has to work harder to replace it. What’s more, draughts can make us feel cold even in a warm room, because air movement across our skin has a cooling effect.

The most common sources of draughts are windows, doors and letterboxes. Walking around your home on a cold or windy day will highlight any draughts. In many cases, draught-proofing can be a relatively cheap DIY job. Guidance from charity the Centre for Sustainable Energy explains how to go about it. A DIY draught excluder for the bottom of the door can be quite easy to make, and cut out some of the cold. A curtain behind the door is also effective, but make sure it’s wide enough to cover gaps around and below the door.

How to make a DIY draught excluder.

Energy advice charity the Energy Saving Trust suggests that professional window and door draught-proofing could save around £55 per year, and a chimney draught excluder could save another £45 per year.

Insulate

If the heat in our homes escapes, our heating has to replace it, which uses energy and costs money. Insulation stops this happening. Our homes should be insulated on all sides. This means the floor, walls, and roof.

In homes with a loft, this is often the easiest place to insulate. Loft insulation helps reduce heat loss through the roof. Insulating a loft now will reduce bills for years to come. This can be a DIY job, or can be done by a professional. Organisations such as the National Insulation Association can help find an installer.

If your loft is already insulated, you can add more insulation. The current minimum recommendation for new properties is 270mm, and increasing yours from 120mm to this level could save around £17-£20 per year. If you currently have less insulation, the saving will be much greater.

If you have a hot water cylinder, it’s also worth checking its insulation and adding or improving it. Insulating an uninsulated cylinder could save £200.

In properties with single glazing, heat loss from windows will be large. While installing double glazing is a big job, long term benefits are large.

Heat to suit your home

It is sometimes suggested that leaving your heating on at a low level can lead to lower total energy use than turning it on and off. Whether or not this is true depends on your house, your heating, and you.

A detached house with thick stone walls will take a long time to become warm, but will stay warm for longer (this is also true in summer, and is the reason churches and old buildings remain cool in summer). A newer house with brick and plasterboard walls will heat up more quickly, but also loses heat more quickly.

It’s often better to maintain temperature in the thick walled older house, so here it might be better to adopt the “low and slow” method, particularly if you have a heat pump or a modern boiler. If you have a newer house, turning the heating on and off is likely to be the cheaper option in the long run. Using a smart meter, it’s possible to test both options for a week or so, then adopt the best option.

Not just heating

Heating is a major contributor to energy use, but it’s not the only one. Cooking, lighting, hot water and appliances all play a part. If you have any old-fashioned light bulbs, swapping them for LEDs immediately can save around £45-£55 a year. Using lids on pans, only boiling the water you need, turning off your oven and letting food finish cooking in the leftover heat, and avoiding the tumble dryer wherever possible are all good ways to save energy and money.

There are many other practical options, such as reflecting film behind your radiators, to reduce your energy bills without too much hard work. Just switching devices off standby could save £45 annually. Then of course there’s also looking at changing your energy supplier or making the most of cheaper electricity overnight. We haven’t included every option here, but energy advice services such as the Energy Saving Trust and charity the Fuelbank foundation can all help.

Bigger projects

If you’re considering a bigger project and want to really understand how your house loses heat and prepare yourself for the winter, there are charities and organisations across the UK who offer surveys, or may have infrared cameras available to borrow.

A survey will tell you where your house is losing heat so you can target your efforts in the right place. Some are available for free, and even if you’re not planning major work can provide useful information on cold spots and missing insulation. You could start with charity the National Energy Action.

Stuart Walker is affiliated with the Grantham Centre for Sustainable Futures, University of Sheffield, and Hope Valley Climate Action.

articles.title: Paramedics need time and support to recover between emergency calls
articles.summary:
Paramedics can go straight from one emergency to the next, with little time to take in what happened on the last call. Rawpixel.com/Shutterstock

When a paramedic arrives at your door, they may have come straight from someone else’s emergency. “I don’t know how you do your job,” people often tell me. I think about how little time there can be to take in what’s happened on one call before the next one comes in.

I’m a paramedic and an academic specialising in paramedic science. Ambulance staff deal with death and serious injury, and they can encounter violence on the job. There are pressures between calls, too. A review of research on ambulance work describes how long shifts, unpredictable work and limited time to recover can add to the strain.

In a separate UK study carried out during the COVID-19 pandemic, ambulance staff reported worsening shortages and raised concerns about having too little time to do the job. In ambulance work, there’s an expectation that we’ll be resilient and raise a hand if we’re struggling. I find that second part difficult, and I doubt I’m the only one.

Researchers describe resilience as a process of adapting in the face of serious adversity. When I hear that we’re expected to be resilient, I think of something springing back into shape. I’m uneasy about applying that image to people. I can be ready to help the next patient and find, at the end of my shift, that I’m still thinking about the previous call. If getting on with the job is taken as a sign that we’ve recovered, it falls to us to say when the strain is getting too much.

I prefer to think about fortitude – the strength and courage it takes to face the demands of the work. That can include telling someone when a call has stayed with you. What interests me is where that strength comes from. Having a colleague you trust and time to talk can make it easier to say how you’re doing before the strain builds any further.

When it’s hard to give patients the care they need

Paramedics describe caring well for patients as one of the most rewarding parts of the job. That same commitment could make some calls especially painful. When staff felt unable to give a patient the care they believed was needed, they described a strain known as moral distress. It’s what you can feel when something prevents you from doing what you believe is right.

A separate study looked at how paramedics decide when to stop trying to revive a patient whose heart has stopped. Some described following guidelines that required them to keep going even when they believed further attempts would do no good. The guidelines are there to protect patients. Following them can still be difficult when a paramedic’s judgement about the person in front of them pulls in a different direction.

A conversation after a difficult call can help a crew make sense of what happened. If staff keep raising the same problem and see little change, it can be hard to see the point of speaking up again.

In interviews at one ambulance service in England, staff described feeling that senior managers put pressure on crews to work faster while giving too little attention to their wellbeing. When crews repeatedly flag something that makes it harder to give patients the care they need, managers should look into what’s causing it and tell staff what they’re doing about it.

Support crews feel able to use

Talking to someone they trusted helped people in my interviews make sense of difficult calls. That might be a colleague or someone outside work. In another interview study, paramedics said they wanted time to talk privately after a call, often with the colleague they worked with regularly.

An ambulance service can offer counselling, but staff still have to feel able to use it. Staying composed is often part of caring for a patient in an emergency. If people feel expected to appear unaffected once the call is over, it can be harder to say they’re struggling.

An ambulance service might offer extra support after a major incident. A crew can also reach the end of a shift worn down by a series of calls, even if none on its own would prompt that kind of follow-up.

Training is one place to start. A trial involving 570 student paramedics tested an online programme that taught students how to manage distressing memories and spend less time dwelling on difficult experiences. A year later, students offered the programme were less likely to meet the criteria for post-traumatic stress disorder or major depression than those who continued with their usual training.

I’d also like students to hear, before they start taking calls, how the effects of difficult shifts can build up and who they can turn to when that happens.
Once crews are on the road, support should feel like part of an ordinary shift. That could mean making time to talk privately after a difficult call.

I see that as part of helping staff develop fortitude. It takes trust to say that a call has got to you, especially when you’re still working out what you need. The way a service responds when someone does speak up can make it easier for the next person to do the same.

Rebekah Haimes does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Elizabeth Holmes went from a startup darling to powerful seductress – these gendered portrayals profited investors
articles.summary:
Despite the countless books, podcasts, TV miniseries and documentaries, people continue to be fascinated by the fall of Elizabeth Holmes and her health-tech startup Theranos. We are now being offered a new insight into the founder through the much-hyped documentary, You Can See Everything.

The initial drama of the documentary takes places 34 days before Holmes started her 11-year prison sentence for investor fraud in 2023. In our research, we examined how Holmes was presented across promotional materials, tweets, talks and interviews over the ten year period from her initial appearance on the public stage in 2013 to the same period in which the documentary begins.

Valued at around US$9 billion (£7 billion) at its peak in 2014, Theranos claimed to have built a device that could run hundreds of lab tests from just a few drops of blood. Holmes and co-founder Sunny Balwani hid that the device could not in fact do what they said, leading to its 2018 shutdown and their convictions for investor fraud (and, in Balwani’s case, defrauding patients as well).

For many, the fascination in Holmes’s story lies in the hubris and deception of this young woman who set out to upend the multi-billion dollar diagnostic industry. But popular perspectives on Holmes obscure something important about how we view entrepreneurs, who we celebrate (or vilify) and whose interests this serves. This is something our research explores.

A highly sellable female entrepreneur

In our analysis, we found that gendered stereotypes helped create an attractive female narrative around Theranos and Holmes between 2013 and 2015 that served (predominantly male) investor interests.

Holmes was introduced as a very specific kind of woman entrepreneur – confident, ambitious, authoritative. The prominent venture capitalist Tim Draper, who made his name backing companies like Tesla and was an early investor in Theranos, praised what he saw as Holmes’s entrepreneurial instincts in 2014. He said she was the first entrepreneur he know who kept quiet about her business “so that the competition wouldn’t get a chance to start … She had a winner and knew it”.

In 2015, Theranos board member and longtime Holmes supporter former US secretary of state Henry Kissinger talked about her as combining “fierce and single-minded dedication with great charm”.

Much was also made of her looks, with the media often noting she was a “young, blond, and blue-eyed” woman. She was a refreshing change from the usual men the industry pinned all its hopes on.

Holmes did present a highly sellable vision of a new Silicon Valley that welcomed and celebrated female entrepreneurs. In her 2019 book The Code: Silicon Valley and the Remaking of America, tech historian Margaret O’Mara noted that Holmes’s rise coincided with growing public scrutiny of Silicon Valley’s lack of diversity, and the “tech-bro” homogeneity of the early-to-mid 2010s. At the time, the Valley was also beset by high profile gender discrimination cases.

For investors, Holmes was an attractive answer to a media problem the tech industry had and the media coverage of her rise certainly helped counter some of critics of the Valley’s “brotopia”.

But Holmes’s brand of female founder was not totally new and this also served investors. In many articles she was portrayed as the female reincarnation of the stereotypical “tech bro” – a Mark Zuckerberg with a heart or a Steve Jobs with a social consciousness.

Then there was her intentional self styling, which the media played up as symbols central to her status as a female tech-visionary. Holmes’s signature black turtle necks seemed to be a homage to the uniform of Jobs, who regularly wore an Issey Miyake black turtleneck. She was asked about it again and again, admitting in an interview with Glamour that she owned 150 of them.

Holmes’s founder uniform combined with the fact that she had dropped out of university to pursue her vision, like Jobs, Zuckerberg and Bill Gates, gave her many of the recognisable characteristics of a successful tech founder. She was like all these visionaries but with the added bonus of being a woman. This portrayal fed straight into investor interests by making Holmes at once both familiar and novel, helping her company Theranos’s value to climb to unprecedented heights.

However, when things started to turn sour, our research found that much less flattering gendered stereotypes were quickly deployed. These narratives framed Holmes’ downfall as female weakness in order to protect powerful men.

An ousted ‘villain’

Holmes was vilified, not only as a failed entrepreneur, but also as a seductress who had used specifically female charms to lead competent men astray.

According to Rolling Stone, she “lured” male investors into her fraudulent schemes. Meanwhile, the Evening Standard reported her as having “wooed” the men on her board to do her bidding. Financial journalists described how Holmes “dazzled” normally sober leaders at supermarket chains Walgreens and Safeway who then invested in her scheme.

Holmes’s board of directors – once portrayed as the “most illustrious board in US corporate history” – along with the other powerful men she was seen as having duped could now be presented as innocent victims of malicious female magic.

For investors, this villification of Holmes could help them spin their own narratives in order to preserve public trust in their abilities. They could argue that her monstrous supernatural abilities to bamboozle and manipulate were too strong for them to overcome. In this media framing, the fact that investors appeared not to have conducted basic due diligence before investing hundreds of millions of dollars was neither their fault nor a reflection of their real talent for investment. They were simply good men who wanted to help people but had been fooled by a woman playing on an emotional blind spot. They were credulous rather than gullible.

To be clear, we don’t excuse Holmes or seek to diminish the seriousness of what she did. But her story tells us something interesting about the wider system surrounding tech entrepreneurs, and how we can remain blind to the ways capital interests can fuel – and exploit – popular and idolised archetypes.

You Can See Everything provides a new intimate portrait of Holmes, which will add, change or warp ideas we already have about her. But we also need to turn the focus back onto ourselves and think about the ways in which we idolise or judge people in her position – and the gendered stereotypes we would rather not admit to holding.

In the past ten years Susi Geiger has receive funding from the following public bodies: European Research Council (ERC Grant 2018-2024); Research Ireland (SFI Pathway grant 2024-2029); Horizon Europe MSCA Actions (2023-2026). Susi Geiger is an Ambassador to the European Research Council (voluntary and unpaid role) and a member of the WHO Technical Advisory Group on Pharmaceutical Pricing Policies (voluntary and unpaid role).

articles.title: Duran Duran’s drummer has retired because of tinnitus – here’s why musicians are at higher risk
articles.summary:
After more than 40 years performing with Duran Duran, drummer Roger Taylor has announced he’s retiring because of his worsening tinnitus.

His decision highlights the effect that decades of exposure to loud music can have on musicians and even music lovers. It also illustrates the profound impact tinnitus can have on someone’s relationship with sound and their ability to continue doing something they love.

Tinnitus affects an estimated 740 million adults globally. It’s not actually a disease, but rather a symptom associated with changes in the hearing system and the way the brain processes sound. It is commonly described as a ringing in the ears, though others describe hearing a buzzing, hissing, whistling or humming.

Tinnitus can develop for a number of reasons. One of the most important preventable risk factors for tinnitus and hearing loss is exposure to loud noise. For professional musicians, who are often surrounded by loud or amplified instruments throughout their career, this exposure can accumulate over years of rehearsals, performances and studio recordings.

Research has even found that musicians, whether playing classical, pop or rock music, are more than three times as likely to experience tinnitus as non-musicians. They also face a substantially increased risk of noise-induced hearing loss.

The relationship between sound exposure, hearing damage and tinnitus is complex.

Exposure to excessive sound can damage the delicate sensory structures within the inner ear, contributing to hearing loss and tinnitus. Although symptoms can settle, repeated or intense exposure can permanently damage those cells. Once lost, they cannot grow back and hearing may not recover.

However, risk doesn’t only depend on sound intensity and duration. Factors including previous noise exposure, age, existing hearing loss, genetics and medical conditions such as cardiovascular disease and diabetes, have been linked to an increased risk of both hearing loss and tinnitus.

Managing tinnitus

There’s currently no universally effective treatment or cure for tinnitus. One reason for this is that tinnitus is not a single condition with one underlying cause.

However, the absence of a cure doesn’t mean nothing can be done. There’s a wide range of evidenced-based management options that can significantly reduce tinnitus’s impact on daily life and improve emotional wellbeing and quality of life.

Tinnitus causes people to perceive sounds – despite the absence of an external source.
Crystal Eye Media/ Shutterstock

For people who have tinnitus alongside hearing loss, hearing aids can not only improve environmental sounds and communication, but they may also make tinnitus less noticeable.

Some people may find that introducing gentle background sounds, such as music, natural sounds or white noise, makes their tinnitus less noticeable, particularly in quiet environments.

One of the most effective strategies for reducing tinnitus distress is cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT). Rather than attempting to eliminate the tinnitus sound itself, CBT helps people change how they respond to it. This can help provide sustained improvements for the distress, anxiety and poor sleep that tinnitus can cause.

Research is also continuing to advance our understanding of tinnitus, helping drive more personalised approaches to care and aiming to make tinnitus support more accessible through digital technology.

There are also practical steps that musicians and music lovers can take to protect their hearing and lower the risk of developing tinnitus.

High-fidelity or custom-moulded earplugs reduce sound levels while preserving much of the clarity and balance of music. Scheduling regular quiet breaks during rehearsals or gigs, keeping in-ear monitors and headphones at safe levels, increasing distance from loudspeakers and other intense sound sources where possible and avoiding sudden loud sounds, all reduce risks of hearing damage.

Installing acoustic screens, elevating brass and percussion sections, increasing stage spacing and rotating seating during rehearsals can also help reduce musicians’ exposure to loud sound.

Roger Taylor’s decision to step back is a reminder that hearing is one of a musician’s most valuable assets. Protecting it should be an essential part of making and enjoying music.

Eldre Beukes does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Why AI-enabled scientific research is a double-edged sword
articles.summary:
OpenAI has sparked a backlash in the mathematics community by apparently using AI to solve more than 700 longstanding maths problems in a short space of time. A recent open letter signed by 28 recipients of the Fields Medal (one of the highest honours in maths) goes some way to explaining why.

Mathematicians who have gone through some of the solutions offered by AI say they are opaque in their reasoning. As the open letter explains: “Solving problems is only a tool and proxy for achieving the primary goal of conceptual understanding and insight.”

As famed mathematician and Fields Medal winner Terence Tao put it: “These companies are dumping carcasses of raw meat onto our communal village table and saying: ‘Here you go, I solved your food problem.‘”

OpenAI said it had consulted with the community prior to announcing the latest three results, one of which was in my own field of computer science.

Nevertheless, mathematicians are having to adapt fast to the disruptive arrival of AI in their field. This challenge extends far beyond mathematics and into all other disciplines of science and research.

The impact AI has had on software development through tools such as Claude and Codex, is undeniable. Industry software teams are now routinely using AI tools in their work.

But now, AI is already having a major impact on the practice of science itself. Academic journals and conferences are dealing with exponential increases in submissions from researchers, in a system largely based on volunteer effort for reviewing and editing.

Terence Tao is among the leading mathematicians who signed an open letter expressing concern about the impact of AI on the field.
Institute for Pure and Applied Mathematics, CC BY-SA

Breaking peer review?

This year, the International Conference on Learning Representations, a leading academic meeting on AI, received 60,000 submissions. This has increased from 490 in 2017. One researcher, commenting on the figures, said: “AI is breaking traditional academic peer review.”

This doesn’t seem to be a special case. In 2024, Mark A Hanson, from the University of Exeter, and colleagues, published a paper titled: “The strain on scientific publishing”. In it, the authors note that the total number of available academic articles has grown exponentially in recent years.

This is in part the result of a decades-long trend, predating modern generative AI, with many factors playing a role – including pressure on researchers to publish large numbers of academic articles, known as “publish or perish”. In 2022, just before ChatGPT launched, the number of papers published was about 47% higher than in 2016. The increase has occurred while the number of practising scientists has seen little growth. But AI is undoubtedly accelerating the process.

Yet this raises questions about whether the current trajectory is sustainable – and whether the quality of science will suffer. One academic conference has been testing whether AI could be part of the solution as well as the problem. This year, the NeurIPS meeting, which focuses on AI and machine learning, introduced a voluntary AI-assisted review for those submitting conference abstracts.

Afterwards, scientists evaluated the quality of the review and how helpful it was. But some in the field believe this could compound current problems.

Protecting critical thinking

Anecdotal evidence suggests some members of the public who are not professional scientists are using AI to produce and submit their own academic papers and write books on science. Citizen scientists make valuable contributions in areas such as biodiversity monitoring and astronomy.

But AI should not be viewed as a substitute for the formal training, daily research work, critical thinking and expert input from colleagues that academia offers. While AI and related technologies are powerful tools for democratising knowledge, it took me 13 years from my PhD to write my first book (the only one I have written so far), whereas now the same can apparently be done in weeks. But, as with peer review and maths proofs, humans have to check and interpret these.

As this story plays through and repeats, we may need to resort to new modes of scientific dissemination to deal with the new methods of creating research.

This brings me to the critical thinking that research requires. Currently, I provide the ideas, but increasingly rely on my AI assistant to do a lot of the work of thinking for me, or at least appear to. But the results of AI-enabled research can be obtuse, as the Terence Tao quote above illustrates, or even plain wrong. They can only be sorted out with human time and domain expertise.

I increasingly wonder what this means for the role of the researcher and for training the future generation of scientists, mathematicians and engineers. I am finding that a challenging, long term student project that would normally take several months to complete is at risk of being able to be almost completely automated through providing judicious prompts to an AI agent.

If I am guiding the student while they provide the prompts to an AI system, what do they learn from the process? And in my own research, where AI enables me to undertake projects I would not otherwise have the resources to, if I am providing the ideas but the AI is doing a lot of the “thinking” for me, am I even doing my own research anymore?

This could have an impact on the future generation’s ability to generate novel research questions, as well as their capacity for critiquing AI’s attempts to answer them.

One of my favourite sci-fi short stories is Profession, by Isaac Asimov. In it, the author imagines a future where young adults are educated by direct upload into their brains using technology known as magnetic tapes – which could be seen as a stand-in for AI. At one point, the main protagonist, George, tries to convince another character that humans can learn in other ways – by reading books, for example.

The other person is baffled, seeing this only as an unnecessary expense. Through the narrative, Asimov reveals the risks in the “direct upload” approach to learning. He also explores what is needed for society to progress when some forms of knowledge can be gained so easily.

We seem to be arriving at the science fiction future I once looked forward to where, like a science officer on a starship exploring unknown corners of the universe, or a billionaire genius tech superhero, I can just provide the ideas while getting the computer to do the heavy lifting. Like others, I am exhilarated by this, but also concerned about what it means for the practice and future of my discipline.

James A. R. Marshall does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Shenzhen summit shows the power the US, China and Russia wield – and their limits
articles.summary:
The US, Chinese and Russian leaders each had their own reason to want a three-way meeting in Shenzhen – a historical first in this format.

Xi Jinping got to show that China can convene the world’s great powers. Donald Trump, fresh from his midterm election defeat, got to look like something other than a lame duck. And Vladimir Putin got to sit at eye level with the other two, after years of western efforts to isolate him.

Ahead of the summit, concerns about three strongmen carving up the world into spheres of influence made their rounds. There was widespread fear that Shenzhen would resemble the 1945 meeting between the US, UK and Soviet leaders in the Russian resort city of Yalta.

That meeting paved the way for the cold war division of the world into western and Soviet spheres of influence.

Shenzhen produced a different sort of document: a joint peace declaration. Its first substantive point is a pledge to reform the UN, one of the institutions the allies were laying the groundwork for at Yalta.

The declaration also pledges further talks to reduce the risk of nuclear proliferation, calls for more production and supply of refined petroleum products and takes a swipe at the International Criminal Court (ICC) by stressing state consent and the immunity of officials.

The UN clause deserves particular attention. The three leaders stressed they spoke as permanent members of the security council. The other two permanent members, France and Britain, were not in the room in Shenzhen, but will be somewhat relieved that the prime venue of multilateralism is not forgotten.

Less clear, however, is what kind of reform Xi, Trump and Putin have in mind. Their attacks on the ICC, for example, do not give the impression that their vision of a post-reform UN is one of a rules-based order in which international law applies equally to small, medium and great powers.

Energy gets the second of the Shenzhen declaration’s four points. China, Russia and the US declared they plan to produce and supply more refined petroleum products, which could ease pressure on global energy markets after the repeated disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz caused by the conflict in the Middle East.

The recent Nvidia spy scandal and the resignation of the company’s CEO, Jensen Huang, has added a separate source of market stress. At a time when investors are absorbing both shocks, steadier fuel supplies are important also to keep the energy-hungry AI revolution on track.

The ICC clause reads like a mutual assurance. By stressing the “principle of state consent” and “respect for immunities” of state officials, and warning the court against not to “abuse their jurisdiction”, Xi, Trump and Putin signal a willingness to give one another and their allies diplomatic cover.

Here, Putin has the most immediate stake. The ICC issued an arrest warrant for him in 2023 over the alleged unlawful deportation and transfer of children from occupied areas of Ukraine.

The nuclear question shows how far the three leaders still have to go. The last nuclear arms control treaty between the US and Russia, known as New Start, expired in February 2026 with nothing to replace it. Trump wants China in a trilateral nuclear arms control deal, but Beijing wants the other two to cut their arsenal first – or have them wait for China to catch up.

No Yalta 2.0

The Shenzhen summit was not the feared Yalta 2.0, despite Xi mentioning in his opening remarks that the three leaders must not cross each other’s red lines.

Yalta was able to divide the globe between major powers because it confirmed facts on the ground and the solutions were ripe. The Red Army already held much of Eastern Europe, and the US and UK were in no position to push it out. Nowadays, none of the new “big three” can deliver what dividing the world would require.

China has economic stakes across Latin America. US security commitments run across Asia, to governments with their own reasons to resist Beijing. Russia’s demands in Europe bind no European government just because Washington accepts them. And middle powers like India and Brazil keep ties with all sides precisely so that nobody can assign them to a sphere.

The three leaders put their personal relationships on display in Shenzhen. Xi took the unusual step of greeting Trump as Air Force One arrived. And whenever the cameras were rolling, the three leaders called each other “old friends”.

Ahead of the meeting, Xi had already spent more than two hours in direct talks with Putin, discussing trade and other areas of cooperation. Trump’s separate meeting with Putin lasted about 40 minutes, followed by roughly an hour with Xi before the three sat down together.

The sequence gave Xi room to demonstrate the depth of his relationship with Moscow while giving Trump a conspicuous welcome of his own, with a cheek-to-cheek hug, military guard of honour and cheering schoolchildren.

The Shenzhen declaration gives the three governments a few things to work on together. What is now important is whether they can turn these broad pledges into verifiable commitments. That means agreeing on who does what, in what order and how each side can check that the other parties have followed through.

The G20 summit in Miami in December will show whether anything follows. Washington has invited Putin, but whether he comes, and whether the three meet again, is still open.

By then we will know whether negotiations on details have started behind the scenes, or whether the three leaders still have to make good on the pledges they made in Shenzhen.

Stefan Wolff is a past recipient of grant funding from the Natural Environment Research Council of the UK, the United States Institute of Peace, the Economic and Social Research Council of the UK, the British Academy, the Nato Science for Peace Programme, the EU Framework Programmes 6 and 7 and Horizon 2020, as well as the EU's Jean Monnet Programme. He also regularly provides advice to governments and international organisations. He is a Trustee and Honorary Treasurer of the Political Studies Association of the UK and a Senior Research Fellow at the Foreign Policy Centre in London.

articles.title: Brain stacking: an expert weighs in on whether this TikTok trend can really boost your brainpower
articles.summary:
Brain stacking is a trend popularised on TikTok. Krakenimages.com/Shutterstock

Brain stacking is a new TikTok trend dedicated to making time for activities that engage our mind, such as reading or doing puzzles.

The idea is to allocate specific time to them. People typically “stack” a particular amount of minutes of reading with a specific amount of journalling, for example. That will be followed by stacking a few more minutes of an activity like colouring, and something else like a word search or a sudoku puzzle. But why is this idea considered to be good for the brain? And is there a scientific basis for the idea that engaging in, or combining, activities like these can improve focus, memory or productivity?

If only it was so easy. But maybe there is something useful in brain stacking. Perhaps the more immediate benefit is a sense of wellbeing: joy, happiness or a basic level of contentment.

Let’s unpack what happens when we do some reading at the start of our day. On one level, we purposefully allocate time to ourselves. That can feel good, especially if the rest of the day feels rushed.

Research tracking people in daily life found that, during periods of leisure, they report more positive mood and less stress. That does not prove that a particular morning routine causes these benefits, but it gives us a useful starting point.

Then there is the layer of agency: the feeling that we are the ones deciding what to do. We are not being pushed by someone or something else. Choosing to spend a little time on something we enjoy may be one small way of experiencing that control.

Another thing that can happen when we are involved in an activity is a sense of flow. It involves becoming deeply absorbed in what we are doing, often when the challenge is well matched to our skills. Imagine following a recipe, playing a game or working on a piece of knitting that needs just enough concentration.

With this absorption can come a change in our sense of time. We pay less attention to the clock, so that time can seem to fly. Reading a novel we enjoy can also give us that feeling, even if we would not call every enjoyable reading session a state of flow.

There is another idea behind brain stacking: making room to focus on one task at a time. Multitasking can feel like a necessary evil. But with tasks that demand our conscious attention, what we call multitasking often involves switching between them.

Read more:
Can brain training really shave ten years off brain ageing, as a recent study suggests?

Some activities can be done together, such as walking and talking, particularly when they are familiar and relatively undemanding. The difficulty comes when tasks compete for the same limited resources. Switching takes time, so performance can suffer. We may feel we are doing everything at once, but important parts of the processing are taking turns.

How might brain stacking help, then? By giving us a period with fewer competing demands and interruptions. That is a plausible benefit, rather than evidence that the routine resets the brain or removes stress at a neural level. And if we are already absorbed in our book, we do not need to stop after five minutes just to move on to the next item in the stack.

A useful question is how the activity fits into our lives. Do we enjoy it? Can we choose when to stop? Does it leave room for sleep, other interests and the people around us?

A brain stack in the library.

The evidence

Like trends in general, this one has attracted exaggerated claims. Evidence about leisure, attention and practice does not establish that stacking particular hobbies improves memory, focus or productivity more generally. Getting better at a puzzle is also different from improving our ability to think and remember across everyday life. Research on brain training makes this distinction clear: improvements on the practised task do not necessarily translate into broad improvements elsewhere.

There is also an assumption behind some of these claims: that our focus, memory and productivity all need to be improved. For many of us, a hobby does not need to be justified as a way of making our brain work harder or better. Enjoying it can be reason enough.

If you want to try brain stacking, start with something you already enjoy. Give yourself some uninterrupted time. There is no evidence-based requirement to complete a certain number of hobbies, or to spend a particular number of minutes on each. And do not turn it into another thing to be good at. If it starts to feel like homework, something has probably been lost along the way.

So, yes, do go ahead and brain stack as long as you do not lose sleep or money over it, or force yourself into activities you do not enjoy. Good nutrition, sufficient sleep and a circle of friends and family are important too. Those are not trends, not yet at least.

Irene Reppa does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: ‘Spermmaxxing’ promises better fertility, but the evidence is thin
articles.summary:
Sperm count is only one measure of sperm quality. How well sperm move and the health of their genetic material also influence fertility. Pixel-Shot/Shutterstock

Shining red light on your testicles or sitting in a sauna with an ice pack: social media has plenty of unusual suggestions for improving sperm quality.

This trend, sometimes called “spermmaxxing”, encourages men to take control of their reproductive health. As a reproductive scientist, I welcome that interest – I’ve even written a book about it. Male fertility has historically received less attention than women’s, and many men know surprisingly little about how their own bodies work.

But some spermmaxxing advice is based on experiments that tell us very little about someone’s actual chances of having a baby.

Listen to Michael Carroll speak about spermmaxxing on The Conversation Weekly podcast and on the Strange Health podcast.

A sperm count is only part of the picture. When scientists analyse semen, the fluid released during ejaculation, we examine how many sperm it contains, how many are alive and how well they swim. Their ability to move forwards is called progressive motility.

The World Health Organization’s reference figures include 39 million sperm per ejaculate and 30% moving forwards. These figures represent the lower end of results recorded among men whose partners conceived within a year. They are not a pass-or-fail fertility test.

Someone with a low sperm count may still conceive, while someone with millions of apparently healthy sperm may struggle. Pregnancy also depends on the egg and other stages of reproduction.

And, as my own research has shown, sperm can swim normally while carrying DNA damage that a routine test misses.

Do spermmaxxing hacks work?

Take red-light therapy. A laboratory study found that exposing sperm to particular wavelengths of red or near-infrared light improved their movement.

But shining light on sperm in a laboratory dish is very different from shining it on someone’s testicles. There is insufficient evidence that doing so improves fertility.

Then there are ice packs, sometimes promoted for use in saunas.

The testicles hang outside the body because sperm production works best at temperatures 2-4°C below normal body temperature. Research involving ten men found that regular sauna exposure temporarily impaired sperm production.

But putting ice against the scrotum, the pouch of skin containing the testicles, is not an established fertility treatment and risks injuring the skin. Avoiding prolonged excessive heat is a more sensible approach.

Abstinence advice is equally confusing. Some influencers suggest saving up sperm by avoiding ejaculation for long periods.

Longer gaps can increase the number of sperm in a sample, but an analysis of 13 clinical trials found that shorter periods of abstinence were associated with better forward movement and less DNA fragmentation – breaks in the genetic material carried by sperm.

This doesn’t mean ejaculating as frequently as possible will improve fertility. The optimal interval remains uncertain, and a change in sperm measurements does not necessarily translate into a greater chance of pregnancy.

Another misconception is that taking testosterone will help you produce more sperm.

The hormone is essential for sperm production, but taking testosterone supplements or anabolic steroids can suppress the signals from the brain telling the testicles to produce their own testosterone.

This can dramatically reduce sperm production, sometimes to zero. Production often recovers after treatment stops, but recovery can take months or longer.

Men considering testosterone treatment who want children should discuss fertility with their doctor beforehand.

What a sperm test can miss

Sperm need to carry healthy DNA, the genetic instructions passed from a father to a developing embryo.

In research my colleagues and I conducted, we exposed human sperm in the laboratory to compounds involved in glycation, chemical reactions between sugars and protein molecules.

One compound, glyoxal, increased a marker of oxidative DNA damage without significantly affecting how well the sperm swam.

This experiment does not prove that eating sugar causes infertility. It demonstrates why sperm counts and swimming ability cannot tell us everything about reproductive health.

And what about alarming claims that sperm counts are collapsing worldwide?

A large analysis published in 2023 reported substantial declines across studies spanning several decades.

However, a 2026 Danish study involving 8,320 men found relatively stable semen measurements between 1996 and 2022.

These studies examined different populations using different methods. The Danish findings do not disprove declines elsewhere, but they demonstrate why we need to examine geographical differences and study methods before drawing sweeping conclusions about global fertility.

What actually helps?

There is more reason to focus on general health than expensive fertility gadgets.

Smoking is associated with poorer semen quality. Research has also linked vaping with lower sperm counts, although it cannot establish that vaping carries the same reproductive risks as smoking.

A 2025 review found associations between Mediterranean-style diets, rich in vegetables, fruit, wholegrains and olive oil, and some measures of better sperm quality. However, stronger evidence is needed to establish whether following this diet improves pregnancy rates.

Research also links disrupted sleep with poorer sperm quality. Exercise and maintaining a healthy weight can support reproductive health, although lifestyle changes cannot resolve every cause of infertility.

If conception is proving difficult, both partners should be assessed. The NHS recommends seeking medical advice after a year of trying, or sooner in certain circumstances.

Finally, sperm count is no measure of masculinity. Men experiencing infertility can face considerable isolation and shame, and turning sperm production into a competition risks making that worse.

Greater interest in male fertility is welcome. But improving reproductive health requires understanding what the science can tell us, recognising what remains uncertain and giving men access to reliable information rather than another miracle cure.

Strange Health is hosted by Katie Edwards and Dan Baumgardt. The executive producer is Gemma Ware, with editing and mixing by Anouk Millet. Artwork by Alice Mason.

Listen to Strange Health on your preferred podcast app, download it via our RSS feed or find out how else to listen here.
