articles.title: Cop31: the world is heading for climate ‘overshoot’ – the UN summit must start planning for what comes next
articles.summary:
Sahabi Ware / shutterstock

A surprising thing has happened at the UN climate conference, Cop31, as it gears up to its conclusion in Antalya, Turkey. Negotiators are discussing how to cool the planet.

You might think this should not be surprising, but how to respond to the latest climate science was not on the agenda when the meeting started. Now, the summit’s latest draft decision explicitly recognises a role for carbon dioxide removal (CDR) alongside deep emissions cuts. This is a significant shift, driven by pressure from some of the countries most vulnerable to climate change – the small island states – in response to two alarming scientific reports in the last month.

The World Meteorological Organization has confirmed that the rate at which the Earth is heating up is accelerating. One reason is the planet is becoming less “reflective”: the loss of ice and snow, changes in cloud formation and (paradoxically) reductions in atmospheric pollution means that more solar radiation is being absorbed rather than reflected into space.

The result is that the Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5°C will not be met. There’s a new term for this new warming trajectory: “overshoot”. As a United Nations Environment Programme (Unep) report explains, the best we can hope for now is to exceed 1.5°C but then limit the extent of the overshoot, peaking emissions as soon as possible and then returning to 1.5°C later in the century.

Unfortunately, Unep also notes that this may be easier said than done. The longer temperatures remain above 1.5°C, the greater the risk of triggering irreversible changes to systems such as polar ice sheets and glaciers, ocean currents and the Amazon rainforest, which could make returning to lower temperatures impossible.

Once a rainforest is lost, it can be extremely difficult to restore – with global climate consequences.
finchfocus90

Beyond cutting emissions

Up until now we have thought there were basically two responses to global heating. We needed to cut emissions (mitigation), and cope with the warming we experienced (adaptation). But overshoot means that achieving net zero emissions is not enough. By the time we get there the temperature will be too high.

Overshoot will require two other kinds of response. As well as cutting the flow of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere, we can physically take them out, a process known as carbon dioxide removal or CDR.

And we will also need to consider different ways to increase the planet’s reflectivity. These include limiting aircraft contrails (which trap heat), expanding the white surface areas of the earth (both buildings and crops), or making glaciers more stable. It could potentially include various methods of “solar radiation management”, such as brightening clouds over the oceans, or injecting reflective aerosols into the stratosphere. If any of these “climate cooling” technologies could help bring temperatures down, they need much more carefully governed research.

Removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere is not the same as carbon capture and storage (CCS), which refers to the capture of emissions from industrial plants before they reach the atmosphere. In all net zero scenarios CCS is needed to deal with the residual emissions of fossil fuels. But we now know CDR is going to be required as well – first alongside emissions reduction, to slow warming down, and then to return the global temperature to a safer level.

There are various potential removal methods. Some are familiar and uncontroversial, though not yet being done at anything like the required scale. These are natural processes such as tree-planting, restoring ecosystems and improving carbon in soils.

Other “novel” forms of CDR are still in development. Carbon uptake methods in the oceans include enhancing the ocean’s alkalinity and the fertilisation of phytoplankton by adding iron. On land, enhanced natural processes include adding charcoal to soils (“biochar”), and accelerating the creation of carbonates from rock weathering.

There are also more technological interventions. These include “bioenergy with carbon capture and storage” (Beccs), in which biomass is burned for energy and the emissions captured and stored underground; and “direct air capture”, the removal of CO₂ from the air with advanced machines.

All of these methods are now being piloted, but remain expensive. Some of them also raise environmental risks: before any could be used at significant scale, countries would need to be sure that they would not have negative side-effects. In turn that means the world needs to think seriously about their governance.

The politics of cooling the planet

But there is currently no place for such talks. Neither novel methods of carbon dioxide removal, nor increasing the earth’s reflectivity, are formally part of the Cop negotiations or indeed any other UN policy process.

This is because many countries have believed that any discussion of these would take the pressure off emissions reduction. They have been supported in this view by some of the larger climate NGOs, who have not wanted anything to distract from their campaign against fossil fuels.

But the world has changed. Climate science says emissions reduction on its own can no longer keep us on a safe climate pathway. This surely makes blanket opposition to novel CDR and cooling methods untenable. Governments need to be scaling up research into these methods and considering their governance. At the very least, they should be talking about them.

This is why the latest moves at Cop31 are so important. At this point it is not clear whether countries will agree to a statement on how to respond to overshoot. Some are still opposed. But if the final text does acknowledge that active cooling will be needed, it will mark the beginning of a new era in climate action.

Michael Jacobs receives funding from the Climate Hub, a non-profit organisation aiming to raise awareness of the latest climate science and its implications for policy. He is a member of the Labour Party.

articles.title: Staggered age of consent: a valuable idea, but young people need more than a legal boundary
articles.summary:
New Africa/Shutterstock

Would changing the age of consent better protect teenagers from sexual exploitation? Campaigners proposing a “staggered” age of consent argue that 16- and 17-year-olds should remain free to have sex with people close to their age, while substantially older adults should be prohibited from having sex with them.

In theory, I am in favour of a staggered age of consent, but one measure alone – changing the law – can not be the only approach to the problem of harmful relationships between teenagers and much older adults. There’s the risk that creating a new law is seen as the solution to this problem when wider support and education is also needed.

High-profile cases can expose harms that demand action, but the understandable pressure to respond should not replace careful scrutiny of what extending criminal law would achieve, its possible unintended consequences and the support needed to make it effective.

In England and Wales, the age of consent is 16. However, the law already recognises that 16- and 17-year-olds need additional protection in certain relationships. Defined positions of trust, including particular teaching, caring, sporting and religious roles, restrict sexual activity with under-18s. It is also against the law to engage in sexual activity with an under-18 in certain family relationships, or to pay for a 16- or 17-year-old’s sexual services, even if they agree.

The Close the Consent Gap campaign proposes that sexual activity between someone aged 20 or over and a 16- or 17-year-old should be an offence, unless their age difference is no more than three years.

The close-in-age distinction is important. This is not simply a proposal to prohibit all sex below 18. It seeks to distinguish teenagers’ relationships with peers and young adults from those involving substantially older adults.

And an age-based offence could provide an additional route to accountability. At the moment, prosecutors must establish that the under-18 did not consent, and this change would remove that requirement. That potential value deserves serious consideration.

Close the Consent Gap campaigner Femi Otitoju speaks to BBC Politics.

However, my research with young people on sexual consent examines how interpersonal pressures and wider sexual expectations affect consent. Knowing what consent means does not necessarily make it straightforward to express a preference or challenge a partner.

Differences in money, status, experience, social support and authority may affect someone’s ability to negotiate what happens in a sexual relationship. Someone may use their resources or influence to impose expectations, discourage disagreement or make leaving difficult. Age can play a role in this, but it cannot stand in for all of them. An age difference between partners does not automatically establish coercion.

This matters within similar-age relationships too. Protecting teenagers from substantially older adults should not imply that relationships between peers are necessarily safe. Nor does turning 18 suddenly remove vulnerability to exploitation.

These are reasons to be clear about the purpose of a legal boundary. It can establish circumstances in which sexual activity is prohibited. It cannot certify every relationship outside that prohibition as equal or healthy.

Creating an offence is one policy decision. Making it effective requires decisions about reporting, investigation, evidence, professional practice and support. Reform should explain how each would work.

The offences for which Russell Brand was convicted were already illegal. In his sentencing remarks, the judge described how Brand’s status had protected him until journalists exposed the allegations. A new age-based offence could extend protection, but its effectiveness would still depend on whether people can report harm safely, institutions act on concerns and offences are investigated.

Young people should participate in that process. How would they understand the new boundary? Would they know that responsibility lay with the older adult? What would happen if they wanted support but did not want to describe their relationship as abusive or engage with a prosecution?

Education and support are part of protection

Education should help young people explore how relationships work, including what makes sexual agency possible and whose wishes take priority.

That means opportunities to discuss concrete situations: feeling indebted to a partner, being praised for being unusually mature, worrying about losing affection or finding that gifts come with expectations. These examples should open discussion about context, rather than become a checklist through which every relationship is judged.

Providing that support requires skilled professionals, time and accessible services. It also requires educational continuity. In England, statutory relationships, sex and health education requirements do not apply to sixth-form colleges, 16–19 academies or further education colleges, although provision is encouraged. This means that young people may miss out on education at precisely the age the proposal for a staggered age of consent concerns.

None of this transfers responsibility for preventing exploitation onto teenagers. Adults remain responsible for their conduct, and institutions need clear expectations and routes for challenging it.

Social scientist Jonny Hunt and I sometimes describe conduct as “lawful but awful”. Criminal thresholds cannot settle everything we should expect of intimate relationships or of adults who hold social power.

A staggered age of consent may strengthen protection. Its contribution should be assessed carefully, alongside investment in education, safeguarding and accountability. Young people deserve a legal framework that protects them and support systems that take their experiences seriously.

Emily Setty is co-founder for Reimagining RSE. She receives research funding from Leverhulme Trust, ESRC, University of Surrey and third-sector, commercial and government organisations.

articles.title: Diplomacy, humour and avoidance – what we found when we investigated friendships across class divides
articles.summary:
Milan Ilic Photographer/Shutterstock

Several years ago, the US economist Raj Chetty and his team at Harvard University analysed billions of ties on Facebook in a bid to learn more about social mobility. Their findings highlighted an important link between cross-class friendship and social mobility. Specifically, they found that people from low-income backgrounds who have more friends from wealthier backgrounds tend to have better chances of earning more as adults.

The paper was published in the journal Nature in 2022. Last year, a report from the Behavioural Insights Team came to the same conclusions in the UK. Both have since been seized upon by policymakers seeking to boost social mobility in the general population.

But we were puzzled. Not only did this work seem to rely on a speculative understanding of how friendships actually work, but the conclusions fly in the face of decades of sociological research. Specifically, that friendship rests on reciprocity between friends, not one-way transfers.

In our new paper, we investigated this tension via 42 in-depth interviews with people in cross-class friendships in the UK. We found that these friendships can indeed produce “social capital”. That is, more privileged friends often provide financial support or cultural guidance to less privileged friends navigating elite spaces. Yet our research also underlines the limitations of characterising cross-class friendship in this way.

In our interviews, when support tended to flow only one way, it generated feelings of inequality or indebtedness, and often sent friendships into a downward spiral. Take Tania (not her real name), a researcher who was white and from a lower-middle-class background. She met Florence at Durham University, where Tania was struggling with the “social side of things”.

In these alien environments, Florence, who was privately educated, acted as what Tania called her “pathfinder”. Tania watched how Florence worked a room. She wasn’t comfortable doing the same on her own terms, so she mirrored how Florence “took up space”.

Yet Tania had mixed feelings about this. It had helped her navigate a career in the civil service – she became “posh Tania” at work – but she was troubled by the feeling that the friendship felt contingent on her assimilation. In other words, if she “dropped back down”, Florence might not stick around.

Class diplomacy

Against the arguments of the original study in Nature, the successful cross-class friendships we studied were not based on one-way transfers. Rather, they relied on a careful negotiation of class difference, which we term “class diplomacy”.

Diplomacy is a useful term, because it shows how managing class difference is an ongoing part of these friendships. It requires significant emotion work (although this burden is not necessarily felt equally) and demands certain social skills from both parties.

We identified three modes of class diplomacy: joking, avoiding and confronting. First, many friends used teasing and self-deprecation to voice and defuse class tensions. Humour was present across genders, but it was more overtly connected to class in male friendships. Typically, it played out in terms of mocking oneself or each other in class terms.

Peter, a banker from a white working-class family, explained the enduring role that “taking the piss” played in his friendship with Julian (“your typical private schoolboy jokes”). What was important, though, was that Julian would take this on the chin. In this way, joking – particularly jokes that punched upwards – recognised class difference but also registered how it affected their experiences in different ways.

Humour was used to defuse ‘landmines’.
we.bond.creations/Shutterstock

The second way diplomacy played out was via the choice many had made to avoid discussing class. Avoidance allowed forms of connection to flourish – interviewees told us these would be stymied if they were to confront class.

But at the same time, interviewees were acutely aware of how class difference continually threatened the friendship. Both friends intricately navigated how and when to coordinate their mutual avoidance.

Many described pivoting to other sources of shared connection such as gender, race, sexuality or taste. This did not cancel out tensions – class “landmines” – yet focusing on commonality provided a kind of refuge.

Others chose to confront class difference head-on. These participants, disproportionately women, acknowledged the risks of this honesty, but said that, if accompanied by sensitivity, it could be productive.

Shanthi and Nadia agreed that their different backgrounds had largely been superseded by the “bonding effect” of being two women of colour growing up in a “very white” area. Yet the issue of money was an ongoing tension.

Nadia, whose upbringing had been marked by economic precarity, was uncomfortable with Shanthi continually offering to buy her things. Shanthi realised that even if her offers were coming from a “place of love”, they almost legitimised a power difference.

Class diplomacy paves the way for forms of exchange and reciprocity to flourish between friends. This is vital for friendships across class to persist. In the relationships we studied, this also had a mutually socialising effect that often led to a heightened sensitivity to class inequality.

Friends spoke of how they had been “shaped” by one another. For those from more advantaged backgrounds, this was often about confronting one’s own class privilege and snobbery – of bringing out, as charity worker Marco noted, “behaviours in me that I’m a bit ashamed of and I’m hyper-aware of now”.

For less privileged friends, diplomacy helped them to understand someone they initially saw only through the lens of privilege, and subsequently be more empathetic, while maintaining their critical stance on class inequality.

These results provide a rejoinder to economists who, in a rush to find a magic bullet to social mobility, may have passed over the complexities of cross-class friendship. It’s not just about the creation of these friendships, but their quality and longevity, and fostering the conditions where they can flourish.

This article was co-published with LSE Blogs at the London School of Economics

articles.title: Electric cooking could be as important as EVs in the global energy transition
articles.summary:
Arkadij Schell/Shutterstock

Electric vehicles (EVs) have become the poster child for the green transition. Governments are investing billions in charging infrastructure. Manufacturers are transforming their production lines. Electrifying transport is a central pillar of climate policy.

But there is another potentially enormous driver of electrification that deserves attention: cooking.

I’m currently at the UN climate summit, Cop31 in Turkey, with my colleague Alicia Butterfield. As global manager of the Global Electric Cooking Coalition, she works with governments, development agencies and clean energy organisations to replace polluting traditional stoves with clean, electric cooking appliances.

We have been struck by how many researchers, government representatives and international organisations at this Cop are advocating for electric cooking to be included as a major component of the global energy transition. The question is no longer simply whether we can cook with electricity, but on how doing so can transform electricity systems, stimulate investment and accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels and polluting traditional cooking fuels.

The comparison with EVs is particularly interesting. Not everyone drives a car, but nearly everyone cooks. Cooking takes place in almost every household, as well as in restaurants, businesses, schools, hospitals and other institutions. It is a universal and essential energy service.

If EVs can become a major driver of electricity demand, why should electric cooking not play an equally important role? In terms of the number of people and institutions electric cooking can involve, it could have an even greater reach than electric transport.

Africa is already undergoing rapid electrification. Mission 300, an initiative funded by the World Bank and African Development Bank, aims to connect 300 million people in sub-Saharan Africa to electricity by 2030. Across the continent, electric cooking can help make electricity systems more economically sustainable over the longer term.

For national utilities, increased electricity consumption creates additional revenue. This can improve the commercial viability of investments in electricity generation and distribution networks. For decentralised electricity providers, including mini-grid operators, reliable demand from cooking can improve the return on investment. It can also make off-grid rural electrification projects more financially viable, potentially lowering tariffs for customers.

Of course, this is not a simple process. Adding large cooking loads can increase pressure on grids at evening peak points. Promoting institutional and commercial electric cooking provides a daytime load (higher demand) which can actually help to smooth demand across a 24-hour period. Some innovative approaches are being developed around differential time-of-day tariffs that encourage use of electricity at times of low demand. This can help “smooth demand”.

This transition can happen in many ways. In urban and semi-urban areas, households with grid connections are trialling electric pressure cookers, induction hobs and other efficient appliances. When they do so, the cost of their daily cooking often falls.

But connection to a national grid isn’t essential for energy access. In remote unconnected rural communities, electric cooking can be supported through decentralised renewable energy systems. The economics of adoption in these communities can be more difficult, especially if people are cooking with wood they collected themselves for free.

Research highlights that the costs of traditional biomass (such as wood and charcoal) extend beyond direct fuel expenditure. Costs include the considerable time, physical effort and opportunity costs associated with collecting, transporting and preparing firewood.

So with the right price point, electric cooking can be attractive even where firewood is freely collected. Reducing the time and drudgery of fuel collection can free up time for income-generating activities and other productive uses.

Advances in solar panels, battery storage and energy-efficient appliances, particularly electric pressure cookers, are improving the technical and economic feasibility of off-grid electric cooking. Innovative financial arrangements, frequently supported via carbon finance (incentivising carbon emissions reductions), are driving down appliance costs for the customer.

Global ambitions

Cop31’s 35-by-35 global electrification pledge seeks to increase electricity’s share of global final energy consumption from around 23% today to 35% by 2035. This pledge is not yet a commitment, and at the time of writing, it remains far from clear what kind of an agreement will be reached.

Achieving this ambition requires more electricity generation (from renewables if electrification is going to drive accelerated climate action). It also relies on stronger grids and improved energy storage.

It needs a greater focus on the uses of electricity. The electrification of transport, buildings and industry is essential – so too is cooking.

Read more:
Plastic pollution is a problem we still know too little about

These discussions demonstrate that cooking is increasingly being considered within national energy planning and international investment conversations. There is an important gap: electricity generation and grid infrastructure are often financed separately from the activities that create demand for that electricity.

Progress in Tanzania shows how electric cooking can help bridge that gap. In one remarkable high-level session organised by Sustainable Energy for All (an international initiative hosted by the UN) and the government of Tanzania, delegates heard directly from Samia Suluhu Hassan, Tanzania’s president. She outlined how the country is advancing its energy transition, partly by prioritising clean cooking in schools and health facilities.

Tanzania’s national clean cooking strategy aims for at least 80% of its population to use clean cooking solutions by 2034. Now in its third year, the UK-funded eCooking Scale and Support programme has worked with the Tanzanian energy ministry to encourage the adoption of electric cooking among households, institutions and businesses across the country.

This programme has introduced innovative financial approaches. These include utility on-bill financing of electric cooking appliances (whereby households repay upfront costs through monthly bills) and credit lines (a flexible borrowing agreement) for new appliance suppliers.

A sufuria (cooking pot) is covered in soot from cooking on an open fire in Kenya.
Esther Sweeney / Climate Visuals, CC BY-NC-ND

In school kitchens, polluting stoves (those that burn wood or charcoal) have been replaced with clean electric ones. New repair and maintenance training programmes have been introduced for electric cooking appliances. In collaboration with the Tanzania Bureau of Standards, new standards have been set for electric cooking appliances.

The programme demonstrates how under strong government vision and leadership, electricity utilities, financial institutions, appliance suppliers and development partners can work together to build an effective functioning electric cooking market.

Wider benefits

Energy security is another powerful driver of the move towards locally generated renewable electricity. Reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels and volatile international energy markets makes the case for developing domestic electricity resources even stronger.

Scaling up electric cooking reduces harmful pollution from methane (a potent greenhouse gas with strong links to respiratory health problems) and microscopic particles of black carbon or soot (a short-lived climate pollutant). Moving away from polluting combustion-based cooking can deliver important climate and public health benefits alongside carbon dioxide reductions.

For more households to switch to electric cooking, appliances must be affordable, electricity supplies reliable and people must know what options are available. This electrification transition must be designed around local circumstances and addressed through coordinated policy, investment and innovation. If policymakers look beyond the most visible technologies, cooking could be placed firmly on Cop31’s global electrification agenda.

Ed Brown leads UK Aid's Modern Energy Cooking Services programme (funded via the UK's FCDO under their Ayrton programme). Research that he leads is also currently funded by UKRI and the Climate and Clean Air Coalition.

articles.title: Most children labelled allergic to antibiotics may not have an allergy, researchers warn
articles.summary:
Halfpoint/Shutterstock

It’s seven o’clock on a Saturday night in an urgent care centre. A ten-year-old boy is “proper poorly” with severe tonsillitis and clearly needs antibiotics. Just before I (Rebecca Payne) head out to find a suitable medicine, I ask his mother: “Does he have any allergies?”

“Yes,” she says. “He can’t have penicillin or anything ending in -mycin.”

Finding the right treatment is going to be difficult. Penicillin and clarithromicin are the first-choice antibiotics for tonsillitis, and the alternatives are not recommended as first-line treatments. With an unwell child and a worried mother, this is not the ideal moment to investigate an allergy history that goes back years.

This scenario is a surprisingly common problem. Around one in 20 children in the US has a penicillin allergy recorded in their medical notes. Yet research suggests most children labelled as allergic to penicillin are not truly allergic.

In our recent article in the British Journal of General Practice, we explain how GPs can identify children who may have been wrongly labelled as allergic and remove inaccurate entries from their medical records. A structured conversation with families about what happened when the allergy was first recorded can help establish whether the child really had an allergic reaction.

Why allergy labels stick

Many childhood antibiotic allergy labels begin during viral infections. Viruses can cause rashes that appear while a child is taking antibiotics. Parents and doctors may assume the medicine caused the rash, when the real cause was the virus. Vomiting, headaches, fever and joint pain can also be mistaken for signs of an allergy.

Once an allergy is added to a child’s medical records, it can be difficult to remove. The label may follow them into adulthood, even if they were never allergic in the first place.

This is important because it means children risk receiving antibiotics which are less effective and which kill off a much wider range of bacteria than required. This puts them at risk of infection by superbugs like methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and other pathogens like C difficile. The consequences can include longer hospital stays and higher healthcare costs.

But there is a way to address the problem. Removing an incorrect allergy label from someone’s medical records is known as “de-labelling”. Our recent article outlines how GPs can work with families to establish what actually happened when a child was first labelled allergic.

UK guidance already provides a framework for removing inaccurate penicillin allergy labels in hospitals. Research has also shown that a structured approach can work safely in outpatient clinics and primary care. In that 2024 study, 91% of the children assessed had their allergy labels removed.

Most children labelled as allergic to penicillin are not truly allergic.
Photoroyalty/Shutterstock

How GPs can remove labels

A careful conversation can help GPs place children into three groups, depending on their symptoms and medical history.

The first group includes children whose original symptoms were never typical of an allergy, those who have since taken the same antibiotic without problems and those labelled allergic simply because another family member has an allergy. In these cases, the label can be removed without further tests or a specialist referral. Families can then be reassured that their child can take the medicine.

The second group includes children who developed a mild rash but had no serious symptoms, such as breathing difficulties or feeling faint. After a careful assessment, a doctor can prescribe a single dose of the antibiotic for the child to take at home. The family is then contacted after a week to check for any reaction. If there has been no reaction, the allergy label can be removed. This approach must be overseen by a professional such as a GP or practice pharmacist. Parents should never try giving their child an antibiotic again without medical advice.

The third group includes children who have had a severe reaction, such as anaphylaxis or a serious rash affecting the mouth or other moist areas of the body. Children with severe or poorly controlled asthma may also need specialist assessment. These children should be referred to a paediatric allergy or immunology service. It is vital that children with a genuine allergy are not given the medicine that caused it.

Read more:
Antibiotic resistance is a growing problem, but solutions do exist – expert Q&A

Keeping an uncertain allergy label can feel like the safest option for both parents and healthcare professionals. But leaving an incorrect label in place carries risks too. Reviewing it can help families understand which medicines their child can safely take and allow doctors to choose the most appropriate treatment when they become ill. Reducing unnecessary use of broader-spectrum antibiotics also helps tackle antibiotic resistance, which contributes to keeping these medicines effective for everyone.

If your child has been told they are allergic to an antibiotic, ask your GP whether the diagnosis could be reviewed, ideally when they are well. If the label is removed, you should receive a clear explanation and written confirmation. The change should also be shared with other relevant healthcare professionals. That way, an assumption made years earlier is less likely to dictate a child’s future treatment.

Rebecca Payne receives funding from Health and Care Research Wales and the University of Oxford Reuben-Clarendon Fund. She is Director of the North Wales Centre for Primary Care Research and Chair of the NICE Quality Standard's Committee

Manohar Joishy does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: The philosophical reason AI Christmas ads leave audiences feeling cold
articles.summary:
Alliance Images/Shutterstock

It’s that time of year when Christmas adverts start appearing, and brands offer up a slice of consumerist comfort as you curl up in front of a screen.

Yet companies are increasingly using artificial intelligence (AI) to produce their ads. Last year proved how quickly that strategy can backfire. In the Netherlands, McDonald’s pulled an AI-generated Christmas ad depicting chaotic holiday mishaps after just three days following fierce backlash over the undisclosed usage.

This kind of omission is now restricted under new EU transparency rules that govern how AI-generated content is labelled. Coca-Cola’s 2025 festive campaign drew similar criticism. The advert featured AI-generated scenery and animals that many viewers found uncanny.

Undeterred, this year brands including Very and Plusnet have pressed ahead with AI productions. Because UK law does not require on-screen disclosure, their use of the technology is often tucked away in separate press releases and trade announcements rather than flagged to viewers. Even so, the UK Advertising Standards Authority prohibits misleading omissions if an advert falsely implies human creation to deceive consumers.

Read more:
What does an ‘AI-generated’ label in advertising actually tell us?

Other brands are more subtle with their AI use. While Royal Mail’s 2025 Christmas ad relied on traditional live-action footage, it recently emerged that the campaign used an AI voiceover to narrate the spot.

Replacing human performers – even behind the microphone – has fuelled growing anxiety among both industry insiders and the general public, echoing the fears that sparked the 2023 Hollywood writers’ and actors’ strikes.

AI was used for the voiceover in the 2025 Royal Mail Christmas advert.

Losing trust in animated ads

This growing scepticism means even traditional animation is no longer safe from scrutiny. Dior’s Christmas short film, for example, has generated suspicions among some viewers. Described as hand-drawn and directed by French animator Sylvain Chomet, with an all-star cast featuring Rihanna and Robert Pattinson, it centres on the fashion designer Christian Dior’s friendship with film star Marlene Dietrich.

Commenters praised its authentic visual appearance, while a behind the scenes page was published on Dior’s website highlighting the actors and design sketches, warding off accusations of AI-generation.

Despite this, some viewers believed that Dior’s advert showed several hallmarks of AI. A telltale sign of AI-generated content is garbled hands and fingers. Some viewers pointed to what they perceived as missing fingers and strange hand transitions in the advert.

Dior’s Christmas film.

In an interview with Variety, Chomet and producer Aton Soumache insisted that the advert was hand-drawn and generative AI was never used. But they have confirmed using a process known as “automated interpolation” to generate intermediate frames as “a very small part of the process” for the “repetitive, mechanical part of animation, not the creative work”. Automated interpolation is a standard digital animation tool that precedes AI, but now often involves its use.

The Dior case is illustrative of how vigilant audiences have become about AI use. Just as the presence of deepfakes risks undermining our trust in all images online, a few undisclosed AI-produced adverts can lead to scepticism of all advertising as viewers hunt for evidence of brands cutting corners rather than hiring creatives.

Why care about AI in ads?

Even when specific accusations prove unfounded, the broader shift in advertising toward undisclosed generative AI raises deeper ethical and aesthetic questions for the industry as a whole.

AI models are often trained on artists’ work without compensation and threaten to put them out of work – not to mention AI datacentres’ impact on communities and the environment.

There’s also an irony in major brands baulking at the tedious task of getting the details right, and giving a misleading impression of fully human creation. These moral defects can diminish our aesthetic experience of AI adverts.

But putting aside morality, the revelation of AI use renders ads aesthetically worse in another way. Philosophers of art argue that forgeries are worse as artworks because they misrepresent achievement. We usually appreciate what the artist did in creating a work. So when we learn that a painting is not a genuine Vermeer, but a 20th century forgery by Van Meegeren, we judge it differently. (One philosopher even likens this betrayal to sexual infidelity – perhaps a bit much!)

The praise showered on traditional productions proves that audiences still care deeply about craft.
fast-stock/Shutterstock

Similarly, when we discover a beautiful, animated Christmas ad was produced with AI, we might lose appreciation for its creative process. The appearance of delicately hand-animated characters is a façade, generated not by artistic imagination but raw computational power. It’s not fraud, but it diminishes the experience.

Using AI to assist in creating complex scenery isn’t easy, and there can be skill to its use – some philosophers liken it to gardening. But it’s not the real process of hand-drawing and animation. To present it as such is a misrepresentation of achievement, imitating a style without the requisite labour behind it.

In response to these quandaries, some brands have taken to detailing the human processes behind their animated Christmas ads. Prada’s campaign emphasises traditional hand-drawn animation, with a separate behind-the-scenes video highlighting its artists. Others have followed suit. Barbour and Thatchers Cider each employed Aardman (producers of Wallace & Gromit) to hand-animate their adverts, while Etsy’s festive campaign is not-so-subtly titled “celebrate being human”. There are also video game studios which have detailed their refusal to use generative AI.

The praise showered on these traditional productions proves that audiences still care deeply about craft. A season built on warmth and sincerity cannot be manufactured by an algorithm that has never felt either.

Alex Fisher has received research funding from the Society for Applied Philosophy, the Leverhulme Trust, the Aristotelian Society, and the Royal Institute of Philosophy.

articles.title: Expect to see fewer and smaller potatoes this Christmas – it’s the ‘worst harvest since 1950s’
articles.summary:
Potato prices are rising after a severe drought. BearFotos/Shutterstock

Britain’s potato harvest this winter could be one of the smallest in decades.

This is partly down to the hot summer and a poor growing year. Potatoes have shallow roots and need steady moisture, so dry spells cut yield and size. Where farmers had stored water to regularly irrigate, crops fared better.

With 75% of England in drought in September, and Wales also affected by dry conditions, one model estimated that British potato yields would be 11% below average. It used the 2018 harvest as a guide. Some farmers reported a greater than 50% drop in how many potatoes they were harvesting.

Wholesale prices had already risen by more than 40% by early August. By September, big British buyers were reportedly paying more than £300 a tonne for potatoes.

The Food and Drink Federation has warned of the worst potato harvest since the 1950s.

Growers have warned supermarkets to expect smaller potatoes and tighter supplies this year, so shoppers may need to accept wider variation in size and quality. This is partly because other European countries, which often provide supplies to the UK, suffered the same hot summer, and this affected their crops, too.

But shoppers may not feel the full effect of higher wholesale prices this winter. Potatoes are more likely to become significantly more expensive next year. It is also worth noting that many supermarkets subsidise potato prices.

Lidl has announced that a 2kg bag will cost 9p in the week before Christmas. The supermarket says it is funding the low price itself, so this price tells shoppers nothing about what the crop costs to grow.

Supermarkets agree prices and volumes with farmers well in advance. Retailers may absorb some of the higher costs this year rather than risk losing customers to competitors.

The bigger question is whether British farmers will carry on planting Britain’s favourite vegetable in future, and what happens if more decide it is no longer worth the risk.

How does potato production work?

In 2025, the issue was too many potatoes heading for shops – the UK produced 5.5 million tonnes, 8.5% more than the year before. This caused prices paid to farmers to collapse.

By February 2026, top-quality maris piper potatoes were fetching about £180 a tonne on the open market, less than half the £400 of a year earlier. Contract prices for the following year were also weaker.

Growers did what economics predicts: they planted less. Analysts put this year’s area in Great Britain at around 101,000 hectares, well below the 117,500 recorded in 2020.

Then came the heat and drought.

Why can’t farmers cash in?

Higher prices should encourage farmers to plant more. But a price spike helps only those with potatoes to sell at open-market rates. Most crops are grown under contract, and growers who struggle to deliver the agreed tonnage or quality may miss out.

Some big buyers that normally rely on contracts are buying open-market potatoes as fast as they can, so growers with uncommitted crops may do well.

Meanwhile, costs for farmers keep climbing. Conflict in the Middle East has pushed up energy and fertiliser costs. Labour and machinery are also more expensive.

Meanwhile, the end of the basic payment scheme (an annual payment for farmers that followed environmental guidelines) and controversies about its replacements may have removed a financial cushion that once helped farms through bad years.

The potato contract price is fixed in advance, so growers have little room to pass costs on. Tighter margins are also hitting buyers, packers and processors, but it is growers that carry the bulk of the weather risk.

Economists call this pattern the cobweb cycle. In the textbook version, farmers plant according to last season’s price, so a glut leads to a price crash, then cuts in planting, then shortage and high prices, then over-planting again. Potatoes have followed this familiar cycle almost to the letter this year.

Yet several forces pull the other way. Speaking before the summer’s hot weather and drought, in May, Scott Walker, chief executive of the industry body representing the potato sector, GB Potatoes, said that many growers were weighing up how much exposure they would carry into 2027. The body has warned that growers could leave the business or reduce their crop.

Contract prices were weaker this year, costs are higher, and drought has shown how exposed the crop is. Depressed cereal markets offer little alternative income, so a wholesale exit is not certain either.

Farmers will be looking closely at what supermarkets offer them in 2027. High open market prices alone will not bring growers back.

Two things matter most: the contracts offered this winter, and whether farmers can secure water supplies for next summer. Signs are that water access may remain tight. For instance, the Environment Agency put England’s reservoirs at only 54% of capacity in early October. Higher prices could prompt a rebound in planting, but a normal-weather harvest could tip the market back into glut, forcing prices down again.

Will British farmers stop planting potatoes?

In September 2026, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs saw no indication that winter supplies were at risk but added that it was too early to assess the drought’s full impact on potato production and that there was, at that point, no indication that winter potato supplies were at risk. Registered potato farmer numbers fell from about 2,466 in 2000 to 1,611 in 2020, when the statutory body collating data on potato farmers was discontinued. But each bad year pushes more to ask whether the crop is worth it.

Tim Rooke, National Farmers’ Union potato policy group chair, said in 2025 that the UK imports approximately 1 million tonnes of frozen chips a year, because the risk against return on investment of growing potatoes is astronomically high.

A food system that leaves a shrinking number of growers to absorb the weather and price risk should not be surprised when they plant less. One option could be fairer contracts that share risk, and investment in water storage. But less certain supply chains and more volatile prices could cost shoppers more.

Climate change means water shortages and high temperatures will happen more often across Europe. Potato farmers are, therefore, likely to face these challenges more regularly in the future.

Robin Gowers does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: The nine best books with yearning protagonists for readers who are pining
articles.summary:
Two Girls Reading in a Sunlit Garden by Laura Knight (1910–1914). Danum Gallery, Library and Museum

There is nothing like the agonising yet delicious slow burn of wanting someone you cannot have. Yearning is behind many great romance tropes, from the tragedy of “right person, wrong time” to the tension of “will they, won’t they”.

The cultural critic bell hooks saw yearning as a universal human condition, which could range from a “passionate collective longing for peace and justice” to an individual longing for a lover.

Yearning is a tradition that has flourished in English literature since 18th-century romanticism, a movement that celebrated the personal and the emotional. For such bittersweet desire to take root, there must be a significant hurdle that makes togetherness seem unattainable. That obstacle can take many forms: unrequited affection, painful shyness, or forces external to the pair.

In literature, these commonly include social stigma, geographical distance and mortality. Whatever the barrier, both it and the longing between the two characters must endure. Suspended between memory and fantasy, caught between a lost past and an imagined future, yearning should consume vast amounts of time and energy. The author must allow the reader to access the inner workings of the pining protagonist, so we can sit with their ache and share it.

If you are ready to luxuriate in the angst, here are nine books to pine over.

No one’s 20s and 30s look the same. You might be saving for a mortgage or just struggling to pay rent. You could be swiping dating apps, or trying to understand childcare. No matter your current challenges, our Quarter Life series has articles to share in the group chat, or just to remind you that you’re not alone.

Read more from Quarter Life:

Five ways to find your personal style outside of trends and algorithms

The ick: the psychology of why a romantic partner can suddenly repulse you

Should you cut off your friend? How to tell when a friendship needs repair, change or an ending

1. Eugene Onegin by Alexander Pushkin (1833)

Two of the book’s characters experience yearning and rejection: cosmopolitan Onegin and country girl Tatyana. Moreover, both characters get a turn at being the pursuer and the pursued in their taut encounters.

Pushkin wrote in Russian. English-language translations variously convey the book’s historic and contemporary qualities.

But if they smack too much of the 19th-century for you, try Clémentine Beauvais’ young adult reimagining, In Paris with You (2018). It transposes the story to 21st-century France. Like the original, it tells the story through the medium of poetry, rather than prose.

2. Love in the Time of Cholera by Gabriel García Márquez (1985)

García Márquez won the Nobel prize for literature in 1982. But the yearning in this Colombian novel deserves an endurance award of its own.

Rejected by the beautiful, young Fermina Daza, trainee telegraph operator Florentino Ariza nevertheless continues to love her for 51 years, nine months and four days.

This does not, however, prevent him from having an enjoyable sex life over the decades. In depicting this, the book underscores that yearning and sexual desire are not synonymous. It is just one way in which the book offers an ultimately hopeful take on an initially tortuous experience.

3. Bel Canto by Ann Patchett (2001)

Also set in South America, the action of Bel Canto is condensed into a few months rather than half a century. Events feel further compressed as they occur under a single roof, in an embassy full of guests taken hostage by revolutionaries.

The hostages are initially kept in cramped conditions, under the watchful eyes of the guards. Language barriers abound as captives from an array of nations work through a single translator. For these reasons, the relationships smoulder before consummation.

Some of the yearnings arise within the group of hostages, others between hostages and their captors. However, they are not limited to the sexual or romantic. They include longings for freedom, home and the characters’ previously mundane lives.

4. The Gift of Rain by Tan Twan Eng (2007)

Malaysian novelist Tan Twan Eng should earn a triple entry in this list because yearning is a staple of his writing.

The longings in three of his books (The Gift of Rain, The Garden of Evening Mists and The House of Doors) eschew yearning that is narrowly romantic or erotic for something more ambiguous.

The stories are steeped in the complex social and political contexts of their setting in colonial and wartime Malaya. The yearnings are straight and queer, familial and national, and treacherous for the characters in both political and personal ways.

5. The Painted Veil by Somerset Maugham (1925)

Eng’s novel The House of Doors takes inspiration from Somerset Maugham’s life and works. These include The Letter (1926) and The Painted Veil (1925). That book gets its own entry here for its plot of yearning that jumps tracks from the selfish to the selfless, the unworthy to the worthwhile.

That may sound moralistic, but the novel mines many grey areas as young socialite Kitty Fane searches for meaning in her life as a doctor’s wife in cholera-ridden rural China.

There’s also a gorgeous film adaptation from 2006 to enjoy once you’ve read the book.

6. Under the Udala Trees by Chinelo Okparanta (2015)

Yearning is a characteristic strongly associated with queer literature. This is unsurprising given the legal, religious and cultural prohibitions of, and discrimination against, same-sex relationships.

The publication of homoerotic literature in such contexts required that authors finely balance expression and suppression. Building on hooks’ work, literature professor Elleke Boehmer argues that a “rarefied intensity of desire” emerges in repressive contexts.

Under the Udala Trees is set in one such context, the 1960s Nigerian civil war. The protagonist, Ijeoma, pines first for a classmate, then for a customer. Yet arguably her greatest longing is for self-acceptance and her mother’s acceptance of her sexuality.

7. The End of the Affair by Graham Greene (1951)

The heart-wrenching yearning in this novel comes in the aftermath of an ecstatic affair, with writer Maurice still pining for married Sarah Miles.

Maurice assumes Sarah has forsaken him for her dutiful but dull husband, Henry. But the eventual plot twist that follows is sharper than a hairpin bend.

The novel is one of several by Greene with a strong Catholic focus. As such, the lovers’ relationships with God form a second triangle in this book. Ultimately, Maurice discovers his true rival is not Henry, but the Almighty himself, transforming an obsessive tale of earthly adultery into an agonising collision between human desire and divine grace.

8. Wuthering Heights by Emily Brontë (1847)

“Haunt me then … drive me mad! Only do not leave me in this abyss, where I cannot find you!”

Wuthering Heights is a tale of dark, destructive yearning across several generations of the same two families. It is also widely found on school curricula, so film versions abound. These include Emerald Fennell’s 2026 movie released to coincide with Valentine’s day, proving that the novel’s afterlife is as perverse as its plot and characters.

If you’re looking for a barrier to true love rooted more explicitly in the supernatural, Stephanie Meyer’s third novel in the Twilight saga, Eclipse (2007), draws strongly on Brontë’s love-triangle classic.

9. Mr Loverman by Bernadine Evaristo (2013)

This novel is a reminder that you are never too old to yearn. Or perhaps, that age is a spur to acting on your feelings. Mr Loverman vies with Love in a Time of Cholera for endurance but exhibits a lighter, more worldly-wise tone throughout.

It spans greater distances, from Antigua to Hackney. Barrington’s wife suspects he is consumed with extramarital passion. She manages to indict most of their acquaintances, except the real object of his affection. The book is unashamedly humorous and poignant. The BBC adapted it as a mini-series in 2024.

This article features references to books that have been included for editorial reasons, and may contain links to bookshop.org. If you click on one of the links and go on to buy something, The Conversation UK may earn a commission.

Sarah Olive does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Your brain may be hiding Alzheimer’s from you – and that’s not always a good thing
articles.summary:
Better verbal memory may explain women's brain resilience. superbeststock/ Shutterstock

When scientists examine the brains of older people after death, what they find can often be puzzling. One such puzzle is that around a third of people who showed no signs of dementia when they were alive, had brains which contained key indicators of Alzheimer’s disease.

Neuroscientists describe these people as being “resilient” to Alzheimer’s. They see this trait as a good thing, and have spent decades trying to understand what makes a brain resilient.

The hope is that if we can find out, we may then be able to protect more people from the disease.

But coping with a disease isn’t the same as being protected from it. A brain that copes well may also be hiding the disease – sometimes until it’s too late to act.

Hiding disease

Alzheimer’s disease unfolds in stages. First, proteins called amyloid and tau build up in the brain as plaques and clumps known as “tangles”. Then the brain cells (neurons) are damaged and die. Finally, memory and thinking begin to fail.

Some people never accumulate much amyloid or tau despite having a high genetic risk of Alzheimer’s disease. Researchers call this “resistance”.

Others experience a build up of amyloid and tau, but cope with it. This is resilience.

There are two key forms of resilience. In the first, someone may have plenty of amyloid and tau in the brain but they don’t lose many brain cells.

In the second form, this amyloid and tau build-up does result in the loss of brain cells – but the person may still continue thinking clearly. Or, if there is cognitive decline, it’s very slow – so symptoms are less noticeable.

This second form of resilience should worry us most, because a person can seem perfectly well while their brain is quietly shrinking.

This situation is often seen in women. On average, women have better verbal memory than men throughout life, meaning they have better recall of language-based information such as words, names and stories.

But this can be a problem when identifying Alzheimer’s, as the memory tests used to diagnose the disease rely heavily on verbal memory. Research has even found that women with signs of Alzheimer’s scored better on memory tests than men who had similar signs of the disease.

Read more:
Dementia: how brain resilience, immune health and the menopause play a role in women’s risk

A similar pattern is also seen in people with high “cognitive reserve”. Cognitive reserve is the brain’s ability to adapt and improvise when it faces a setback – such as those caused by ageing or disease. Cognitive reserve is built throughout life by things such as education and mentally demanding work.

People with high cognitive reserve tend to develop Alzheimer’s symptoms later. But once symptoms do appear, brain function tends to decline more quickly. This is usually because by the time symptoms develop the disease is already quite far along.

So although resilience can protect a person’s cognitive health for years, the disease eventually outpaces the brain’s ability to cope. The resilience that was once beneficial to us is suddenly no longer helpful.

This can be a problem for several reasons.

Resilience may hide Alzheimer’s, even when the disease is present in the brain.
ART-ur/ Shutterstock

The first problem is that it can delay diagnosis. This means a person won’t get the support they need at a crucial stage.

Another problem with resilience is that if it hides the disease until it’s in its advanced stages, people may miss the window for when treatment could help most. The only drugs currently approved to slow the progression of Alzheimer’s must be taken in the early stages of the disease to potentially have any effect.

Resilience can also make it difficult when researching and testing new Alzheimer’s drugs. People who cope well decline slowly overall – whether they receive a drug or a placebo. This could make a drug look weaker or stronger than it might actually be. It may also be one of the reasons why a drug may not work equally well for all people who have Alzheimer’s disease.

For example, one Alzheimer’s drug was found to be more effective in people who were less resilient. For people who were highly resilient (even though they had high levels of tau in their brain and similar cognition as the less resilient people), there wasn’t a clear benefit.

Understanding resilience

There’s still much scientists don’t know about resilience.

Although genetics can provide some information about a person’s Alzheimer’s risk and the disease’s likely progression, it unfortunately can’t tell us very much about resilience.

We still need to figure out what’s happening in the brains of people who stay well, and what exactly changes in the brain when that protection starts to fail.

But ongoing research may help us answer these questions someday. Biomarkers, which are measurable signs of a disease, can detect Alzheimer’s from a blood sample. If paired with a cognitive test, this could let researchers see how much disease a person carries, how much damage it’s doing and how well a person’s cognitive function has held up.

Biomarkers could also improve research for treatments by showing which interventions really have an effect in slowing the disease or making people resilient or even resistant.

When it comes to Alzheimer’s, resilience shows us that carrying the disease doesn’t have to mean losing your memory or your independence. But it can also hide signs of the disease until it’s too late.

Uncovering the biology behind resilience could allow us to offer protection to those who need it – and intervene earlier for those who are highly resilient.
